question: 217. Deputy Cathal Crowe asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the main policy achievements of his Department since 22 January 2025; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [23081/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I am proud of the considerable progress by my Department on a broad range of policy, operational and legislative initiatives since my appointment as Minister in January 2025. I look forward to continuing this work on my priorities, in line with the commitments set out in the Programme for Government. I was pleased to recently publish the new Statement of Strategy for my Department for 2025–2028. The Strategy aligns with the Programme for Government, sets out my Department’s strategic direction to 2028 and will further the work towards our shared vision of a safe, fair and inclusive Ireland. Some of the achievements of my Department since January 2025 are set out below. Garda Recruitment and Operations My first priority as Minister for Justice is to get more Gardaí out onto our streets preventing the commission of crime through high visibility patrols. Increased recruitment and appropriate civilianisation where possible are vital to achieving this as is modern technology and equipment and active management of Garda resources. The Programme for Government commits to recruiting at least 5,000 Gardaí in the coming five years. As we strengthen An Garda Síochána, we will see more Gardaí visible in our communities tackling and preventing crime. In 2025, 794 new recruits were welcomed into the Garda College in Templemore. This is the highest number recruited since 2018. This includes an intake of 223 trainees in November, the largest single intake in over a decade. This positive trend has continued, with 215 recruits commencing their training in February 2026, the first of four intakes planned for this year. Recruitment into An Garda Síochána is now gathering real momentum. New Garda recruits are already making an impact in their communities and the ongoing recruitment of new Gardaí will see further progress in increasing Garda numbers across the State. The work completed by the An Garda Síochána Recruitment Training Capacity Group in 2025 has supported the increase in numbers. The Garda Training Review Group, which is currently examining the future training capacity needs for An Garda Síochána, will, I expect, further support the Government’s Garda recruitment commitments. I have also introduced the Garda Síochána (Powers) Bill and the Garda Síochána (Recording Devices) (Amendment) Bill, which will provide additional powers to An Garda Síochána in relation to search warrants and use of facial recognition technology in certain circumstances. Both Bills are progressing through the Houses of the Oireachtas. Domestic, Sexual, and Gender-Based Violence Strategy Combatting all forms of domestic, sexual and gender-based violence (DSGBV) has been a central priority for me since taking office. An allocation of almost €80 million was secured through Budget 2026 to fund initiatives aimed at tackling DSGBV, an increase of 18% (€12.2 million) from 2025. In June 2025, I published the final implementation plan of the five-year ‘Zero Tolerance’ National DSGBV Strategy setting out the delivery targets and collective action to end 2026. The plan contains 95 specific actions across the four pillars of the Istanbul Convention. There is a strong emphasis on delivery, collective responsibility, and meaningful outcomes. I will shortly publish a progress report on implementation in 2025. Amongst the key deliverables are actions already underway in respect of significant legislative reform including: • Prioritising the drafting of the Guardianship of Infants (Amendment) Bill that will, in certain situations, allow for the removal of guardianship rights from individuals convicted of killing the other parent or guardian of their child; • Limiting the disclosure of counselling records in rape and sexual assault cases. • Banning sex for rent under the Criminal Law and Civil Law (Miscellaneous Provisions) Bill 2025; • Introducing the Criminal Law (Sexual Offences, Domestic Violence, and International Instruments) Bill 2025 which will introduce the Domestic Violence Register of Judgments, bringing greater transparency and accountability for serious offenders; • Changing the threshold from a subjective to an objective test for establishing consent in rape and sexual assault cases; • Establishing the necessary legislative basis to provide for Operation Encompass, which will enable An Garda Síochána to share information with schools when a child has been exposed to domestic violence. As part of the Zero Tolerance Strategy, Government committed to doubling domestic violence accommodation capacity in Ireland by the end of 2026 from 141 to 282 family units. By the end of 2026, it is envisaged to have 94 safe homes and 193 refuge units completed, bringing total safe accommodation to 287, with 50 further refuge units under construction. I am continuing to work with Cuan, my Department and the Department of Housing to ensure we are exhausting all measures to increase the pace of delivery for this much needed additional capacity. Immigration It is also a central priority for me to ensure that our immigration system is robust and rules based. My Department has taken action to significantly improve immigration enforcement measures and increase removals. This includes the renewed use of chartered deportation and removal flights. In 2025, 4,700 deportation orders were signed, an increase of 96% compared to 2024, while 2,111 people had their departure confirmed under various mechanisms (i.e. enforced deportation, voluntary return etc.), an increase of 88% compared to 2024. In keeping with the Government commitment to significantly enhance the delivery of public services digitally, phase one of my Department's Immigration Customer Service Portal, which enables applicants to check their immigration application status, book first-time registration appointments, and submit queries, has been operational since October 2024. Since the launch of the Portal more than 285,000 customers have registered, with over 243,000 queries resolved and in excess of 147,000 registration appointments made. International Protection In 2025, the International Protection Office (IPO) delivered over 20,200 first decisions compared to approximately 14,100 in 2024, a 44% increase. The International Protection Appeals Tribunal (IPAT) more than doubled the number of appeals closed from 3,100 in 2024 to nearly 6,300 in 2025. In January this year, the International Protection Bill 2026 was published, which will replace the International Protection Act 2015. It is the most comprehensive reform of immigration law in the history of the State and will implement the EU Migration and Asylum Pact. The Bill has been passed by the Dáil and has progressed through Second Stage and Committee Stage in the Seanad, with Report and Final Stages scheduled for this week. The Pact is a new EU framework to manage migration and asylum for the long-term. The overall objective of the Pact is to provide a fair, sustainable and efficient asylum procedure. These important changes include streamlining the decisions process, streamlining the returns process, a new ‘Border procedure’ with a three-month time limit for decisions, and new institutional arrangements for international protection decisions and appeals. A phased transition that mirrors elements of the Pact is currently underway. Ultimately, improved, faster processing will result in decreasing annual costs by reducing the time an applicant remains in the system. International Protection Accommodation Since taking back responsibility for international protection accommodation in May of 2025, my Department has focused on speeding up applications, reducing the growth in the accommodation system, and applying new procedures, including improved value for money. While current levels of applications are reduced since the end of 2024, application numbers remain well above pre-2022 levels. There were over 13,000 applications in 2025 and pressure on accommodation systems remains high. As part of the strategy to reduce reliance on commercial providers, we have purchased Citywest, renovated other State accommodation, brought on stream modular solutions, all of which contributed to boosting State-owned bed numbers from 900 spaces in early 2024 to over 4,000 today. The purchase of Citywest is central to Ireland’s ability to meet its obligations under the EU Asylum and Migration Pact. The project has been recognised at EU level as an example of best practice, demonstrating accelerated delivery of a fit-for-purpose screening and border facility at scale. The Department is reviewing contracts and improvement in standards, governance, compliance and the introduction of a new rate card model is driving costs down for new and renewed contracts, already saving over €83 million across 147 contracts since May 2025. Commencement of Policing, Security, and Community Safety Act On 2 April 2025, I was pleased to commence the landmark Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024. As a result, the following bodies were established: • The new Garda Board • The Policing and Community Safety Authority (replacing the existing Policing Authority and Garda Síochána Inspectorate) • Fiosrú – the Office of the Police Ombudsman • The Office of the Independent Examiner of Security Legislation • The National Office for Community Safety The Act strengthens and consolidates independent, external oversight of An Garda Síochána; makes community safety a whole of government and multi-agency responsibility and enhances the internal governance of An Garda Síochána by establishing a new non-executive board which is a corporate governance standard across the public and private sectors. Community Safety The National Office for Community Safety established in April 2025 is a central coordinating body to the new whole of government, collaborative, problem-solving approach to community safety as envisaged by the Commission for the Future of Policing in Ireland (CoFPI). Last June, I signed regulations to allow for Local Community Safety Partnerships to begin their work across the country. These regulations allow for a total of 36 Local Community Safety Partnerships to be established across every Local Authority. At a local level, community safety partnerships will play a major role in enhancing community safety nationwide in collaboration with An Garda Síochána, local residents, businesses and state agencies. As of 20 March 2026, members to 35 of these Safety Partnerships have been appointed and 34 are fully operational having held inaugural meetings and elected their Chair and Vice Chair. It is expected that all Safety Partnerships will be operational in the first half of the year. Having launched a call in April last for applications under the Community Safety Fund 2025, I was pleased to announce in October grants totalling €4.4 million from the proceeds of crime, seized by the Criminal Assets Bureau (CAB) and An Garda Síochána, into 42 local projects focused on enhancing community safety. I have also secured an additional €2.5 million in Budget 2026 to support the the establishment of all 36 Local Community Safety Partnerships across the country, alongside increasing the size of the Community Safety Fund to €4.75 million. Youth Justice The Government’s focus on youth diversion and interventions is a keystone in the Youth Justice Strategy, which is a forward-thinking plan designed to address the unique challenges faced by young people in Ireland. At its core, the Strategy emphasises early intervention, prevention, family support, and community engagement. It includes key objectives aimed at promoting positive behavioural change, and it is only by targeting this behaviour that we can break the cycle of offending by young people. YDPs work with young people at risk of crime and anti-social behaviour to divert them away from criminal behaviour and towards better life outcomes. A key intervention under this Strategy is the network of Youth Diversion Projects (YDPs) which work with young people at risk of crime and anti-social behaviour to divert them away from criminal behaviour and towards better life outcomes. Last November, I was pleased to announce with Minister of State, Niall Collins TD, that the State’s network of Youth Diversion Projects (YDPs) has been successfully rolled out nationwide, making these critical interventions available to young people at risk of engaging in criminal activity no matter where they live in Ireland. Criminal Assets Bureau The Proceeds of Crime and Related Matters Bill 2025, approved by Cabinet last July, represents the most significant update to Ireland’s civil asset forfeiture laws since their introduction in 1996. The Bill strengthens the State’s ability to identify, freeze and confiscate assets linked to serious and organised crime. The Bill strengthens CAB’s investigative powers, with new provisions to freeze bank accounts when there is a reasonable suspicion that it is being used to hold proceeds of crime. To address the risk of funds being moved quickly or hidden, a direction can be given to a financial institution to freeze an account for up to seven days. The Bill passed report and final stages in Dáil Éireann on 17 December 2025. Transfers of responsibilities Responsibility for integration, International Protection Accommodation Services (IPAS), and the Ukraine Division transferred to my Department from the Department of Children, Equality, Disability, and Equality on 1 May 2025. This transfer includes the transfer of all staff, approximately 340 people, alongside a substantial budget transfer of approximately €2.1 billion. As my Department had existing responsibility for immigration and migration and the processing of applications for international protection, this transfer underpins a more cohesive and strategic approach to migration and integration. The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) also transferred to my Department from the Department of the Environment, Communications and Climate on 2 June 2025. The NCSC is the lead government agency on cyber security. Responsibility for the Irish Film Classification Office (IFCO) transferred from my Department on 1 August to the Department of Culture, Communications and Sport. This transfer was carried out in line with the Programme for Government and aligns the work of IFCO with the Department responsible for culture. Ahead of the transfer, my Department completed a Periodic Critical Review of IFCO which had a focus on the ongoing business case for the entity, its performance, efficiency, effectiveness, and governance arrangements. The report from the review was published ahead of the transfer. Responsibility for the Property Services Regulatory Authority (PSRA), as well as the Property Services Appeal Board, also transferred from my Department on 1 August to the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage. Cyber Security Ireland’s 2025 National Cyber Risk Assessment published in December 2025, set out a detailed cyber security focused assessment providing a strategic view of the systemic cyber risks facing the State, its Critical National Infrastructure (CNI), and the supply chain ecosystem upon which these services rely. It is also the foundation for Ireland’s third National Cyber Security Strategy. Work is well advanced in my Department on Ireland’s third National Cyber Security Strategy 2030. The Strategy will give rise to a series of measures to build cyber security capability in the State, including in research, development, skills and training. It will also set out the commitment in the Programme for Government 2025 to build a Cyber Security Research Centre of Excellence and providing targeted grant funding for SMEs to improve their cyber security. Ireland is currently transposing the NIS2 Directive via the National Cyber Security Bill. The drafting of the Bill is at an advanced stage and is expected to be published later this year. It will include measures to ensure providers of critical services take measures to increase their cyber resilience and to protect themselves against cyber security incidents. The Bill also establishes the National Cyber Security Strategy as an executive office of my Department and provides the NCSC with additional powers and responsibilities to monitor, detect and respond to cyber security incidents in the State. Establishment of the Gambling Regulatory Authority of Ireland In March 2025, I established the independent Gambling Regulatory Authority of Ireland (GRAI). The GRAI is responsible for a new streamlined, simplified, and coherent licensing framework which reflects the nature of modern gambling in the State and for a robust regulatory regime to regulate gambling in-person and online that will replace the existing, fragmented systems which date back to 1929. The regulatory powers of the GRAI take into account the harms associated with problem gambling and provide safeguards to protect people from those harms, including children, those vulnerable to problem gambling, and those affected by problem gambling. The GRAI will establish and maintain a National Gambling Exclusion Register, funded through licence fees, and establish a Social Impact Fund, financed by a levy on the industry, to support services to treat gambling addiction and fund public education and awareness raising programmes. The GRAI is planning to commence licensing operations in 2026 as part of a phased stand-up of their functions under the Gambling Regulation Act 2024. Data Protection Commission On 17 September 2025, the Government appointed a third Commissioner for Data Protection, with the appointment taking effect from 13 October 2025, for a five-year term. This follows the appointment of two new Commissioners for Data Protection in February 2024. In 2022 the Government approved commencement of a process to increase the number of commissioners. A review was undertaken by the Department of Justice which took account of the evolving organisational structure, governance and business needs of the Data Protection Commission. The appointment completes the process to expand the number of commissioners to 3. As the responsibilities and scope of the DPC continue to grow, the 3 commissioners will now lead and manage this key regulatory body. Improvements to international judicial cooperation Bilateral agreements between Ireland and the United Arab Emirates on extradition and mutual legal assistance (MLA) in criminal matters entered into force on 18 May 2025. The bilateral MLA and extradition treaties will ensure that criminals cannot evade the law. They will also serve to mitigate the harm caused by any perception that criminals can evade the law and benefit from the ill-gotten gains of criminal activity abroad, which itself diminishes the trust and confidence of citizens in the rule of law. Omagh Inquiry Last April, I signed a Memorandum of Understanding with the Chairman of the Omagh Bombing Inquiry on matters relating to the disclosure of materials to the Inquiry. This is a truly important step to delivering on the commitment in the Programme for Government, to “play our full part in legacy processes…including facilitating and supporting the Omagh Inquiry”. That is in the best interests of the victims’ families and survivors . In November, I implemented measures to further support the operation of the Memorandum of Understanding including signing Regulations under section 2B of the Data Protection Act 1988 to support the disclosure of personal data to the Inquiry by my Department. On 13 March 2026, I published the International Co-operation (Omagh Bombing Inquiry) Bill. The Bill is designed to enable the taking of oral testimony before the Irish courts for the purposes of the Omagh Bombing Inquiry. The publication of the Bill is another important step in delivering on the commitment to facilitate and support the Inquiry. Independent Expert In September, following extensive work at official and political levels, the Secretary of State for Northern Ireland and I announced the appointment of Fleur Ravensbergen as the Independent Expert to conduct a scoping and engagement exercise on whether there is a basis for a formal process of paramilitary group transition to disbandment in Northern Ireland. This appointment was made in line with recommendations by the Independent Reporting Commission. I look forward to receiving the report on the outcome of this exercise in the Autumn of this year. Family Justice The ongoing reform of the Family Justice system, for the benefit of families and children, is another of my key priorities. Work has commenced on the implementation of the Family Courts Act 2024. The Act introduces changes to the current delivery of family justice, including the introduction of specialist family law judges assigned and operating within new family court divisions. I intend to shortly bring an implementation plan to Government, with publication expected shortly afterwards. Last May, I published the Review of the Operation of the In Camera Rule in Family Law Proceedings. The review, a key action in the Family Justice Strategy, was conducted by a team from University College Cork and Trinity College Dublin and is an important piece of research which details the perspectives of many stakeholders regarding the current understanding and operation of the in-camera rule in family law proceedings. Importantly, it includes the views of those who have been parties in such proceedings. Officials from my Department are currently engaging with a variety of stakeholders and working on a policy paper regarding how some of the recommendations made in the report could be implemented. Last August, I published two tenders for the provision of new family law services aimed at making our system more transparent and better for children. The first is for a Private Family Law Reporting Project to provide transparency for the public and increase awareness and understanding of family law proceedings while ensuring that children’s and parents’ right to privacy is upheld. I am pleased to say that the Child Law Project has been contracted to deliver the three-year project and work on it has commenced. The second is for a service to provide a new and innovative way to hear children’s voices in private family law proceedings. The Children’s Court Advocate Pilot Project will initially be established in Waterford and Clonmel, ensuring that all children to whom guardianship, custody or access applications relate can have the opportunity to be informed about the proceedings relating to them and have their voice heard without any cost to families. In February 2026, I launched a new online child maintenance calculator to help parents in coming to arrangements on child maintenance payments. The launch of the calculator follows on from the publication of Ireland’s first set of Child Maintenance Guidelines earlier this year. The development of the guidelines was a key recommendation of the 2024 Review of the Enforcement of Child Maintenance Orders. Civil Reform In January, I published the General Scheme of the Civil Reform Bill. The Civil Reform Bill is a key measure that will see the implementation of the Review of the Administration of Civil Justice, also known as the Kelly Report, which was published in October 2020. The Report made over 90 recommendations aimed at improving access to justice for all by making it quicker, more efficient and more cost effective. As part of the Bill, it is my intention to introduce provisions which will codify the existing law on judicial review by placing it on a statutory basis. The measures should achieve greater transparency in the law and lead to a more streamlined review process. Key reforms should ensure that the system cannot be misused on purely technical grounds, that the public interest is placed at the heart of judicial review, costs are reduced where possible and litigants have sufficient standing to properly challenge decisions. Given the significant challenges currently facing our State in terms of housing shortages, energy deficits, inadequate water supplies and climate change, all of which are exacerbated by the demands of a rising population, we can no longer delay on reform of the judicial review system. I am confident that the Bill will remove weaknesses in the current law, eliminate impediments to progress and deliver reform for the public benefit. I am also confident that measures in the Bill preserve the right of the citizen to ensure that public bodies act lawfully and are accountable for their decisions. Judicial numbers The Courts and Civil law (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2025 was enacted in December 2025 to provide for an increase in the maximum numbers of judges in the District Court, the Circuit Court, the High Court and the Court of Appeal. The Act provides for a total increase in judicial numbers of 21, delivering on Programme for Government commitments. General Scheme of the Criminal Law and Civil Law (Miscellaneous Provisions) Bill 2026 In December 2025, I secured Government approval to publish the Criminal Law and Civil Law (Miscellaneous Provisions) Bill 2026 which was subsequently presented to Dáil Éireann on 9 January 2026. The Dáil Second Stage debate took place on 22 January. The Bill responds to a range of pressing challenges for the justice system. Among other provisions, the Bill includes measures to: • criminalise the highly exploitative behaviour commonly known as ‘sex for rent’; • amend legislation relating to disclosure of counselling records in sexual assault trials; • encourage greater use of community service orders as an alternative to imprisonment in suitable cases; • remove the legal prohibition on the possession and use of incapacitant spray by prison officers; • allow the use of more advanced DNA analysis in missing persons cases; • further facilitate video link hearings in the criminal courts by enabling bail bonds and suspended sentence bonds to be taken by Gardaí and prison officers respectively; • establish a permanent regulatory basis under which licenced premises may provide outdoor seating on public land; • provide for the refusal of bail for persons charged with offences relating to forced marriage or coercive control, and • empower the Chief Justice to delegate certain non-judicial functions to other members of the judiciary. In February, I secured further Government approval to introduce additional amendments to the Bill. These amendments concern, inter alia : • the establishment of an application-based legislative scheme for the disregard of certain historical convictions relating to consensual sexual activity between men; • further amendments to provide for a presumption of non-disclosure in relation to counselling notes and other sensitive personal records in sexual offence trials; • an amendment of the Prisons Act 2015 to provide that, where two years or less of the applicable prison term remains to be served, a person may be taken from prison for the purpose of effecting a deportation or removal order; • a further amendment to the Bail Act 1997 to provide for refusal of bail for persons charged with offences relating to witness intimidation or failure to comply with requirements under the Sex Offenders Act 2001. This week, I also secured Government approval to introduce an additional amendment to the Miscellaneous Provisions Bill to provide for the use of Passenger Name Record data for intra-EU flights. Drafting of these amendments, along with a number of outstanding measures from the General Scheme of the Bill, is at an advanced stage and I intend to bring these provisions as amendments to the Bill as it progresses through the Dáil. Prisons and penal reform A multi-year building programme is progressing at several key sites across the prison estate. To accelerate delivery, I sought and secured an exemption from the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation for six major projects (960 prison spaces) to move straight to Approval Gare 2- Pre Tender Approval of the Infrastructure Guidelines. This decision is expected to bring forward delivery timelines on those six projects by 12 to 18 months, while freeing up internal capacity within IPS to advance the wider programme. This acceleration reflects the priority placed by Government on strengthening the prison system’s resilience and providing safe, secure and humane accommodation. This is part of the funded plan to deliver over 1,500 new spaces. In April 2025, I approved the publication of the Probation Service’s 'Community Service - New Directions Implementation Plan 2025-2027. This plan sets out commitments to drive the delivery and support the increased use of Community Service as a robust and meaningful alternative to imprisonment. Engagement with the Judiciary, imbedding the principles of desistence, restorative justice and social justice, and increasing the visibility and accessibility of community service are part of this plan. A key recommendation of the High-Level Taskforce (HLTF) on mental health and addiction was the establishment of a Community Access Support Team (CAST) to divert those experiencing situational trauma or a mental health crisis away from the criminal justice system, and towards the healthcare system. The CAST project commenced in January 2025 and is a partnership pilot between An Garda Síochána and the Mental Health Services of HSE Mid-West Community Healthcare which is currently being trialled in the Limerick Garda Division. This has resulted in multiple diversions from arrest and subsequent detentions under Section 12 of the Mental Health Act 2001 to the benefit of individual patients and increased public safety. Building Pathways Together: Criminal Justice Reintegration Through Employment Strategy 2025-2027 The Building Pathways Together employment strategy launched in November 2024 for implementation during the period 2025 to 2027. To date good progress has been made on implementation of the actions identified, including the establishment of a Criminal Justice Employers Network and Criminal Justice Employment Advisory Committee. Both groups met twice in 2025 and a joint meeting of the groups took place in March 2026 to progress the actions further.

question: 218. answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration An Garda Síochána play a vital role in enforcing road traffic law and in making our roads safer for all road users, including vulnerable road users. question: 445. Deputy Dessie Ellis asked the Minister for Health when she envisages the establishment of a national Traveller mental health steering group which would collaborate in the implementation of a national Traveller mental health strategy; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [23105/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Health As this is an operational matter, I have asked the Health Service Executive to respond directly to the Deputy as soon as possible. Minister of State at the Department of Health (Deputy Mary Butler) I propose to take Questions Nos. 443, 444 and 445 together. The government is committed to working with all stakeholders to improve the health experiences and outcomes for Travellers, in a comprehensive, coordinated, transparent, and sustainable manner. The Traveller Community are recognised as a priority group in national mental health strategies such as Sharing the Vision and the National Suicide and self-harm Prevention Strategy - Connecting for Life. Travellers experience disproportionately high levels of mental health difficulties and suicide rates. In relation to funding, additional funding has been provided annually to address Traveller mental health, with a priority focus on funding Traveller organisations to co-develop mental health services and supports. In Budget 2025, significant additional ring-fenced funding of €365,000 was secured By Minister Butler, Minister for Mental Health for Traveller mental health initiatives. Additionally funding of €200,000 for the National Traveller Counselling service which was allocated on a once-off basis for 2024, was mainstreamed under Budget 2025, bringing the total funding for Traveller mental health to €565,000. An additional €480,000 was allocated by Minister Butler also to support Traveller Mental Health initiatives in 2026, which include co-created Traveller/Roma Led Mental health projects aligned to relevant strategies and action plans and support for the work of the Traveller Mental Health Network, among others. In addition, the HSE National Office for Suicide Prevention (NOSP) received a record allocation of €16m in 2026 to expand crisis supports and suicide. The first full bi-annual report by the National Traveller Mental Health Working Group was developed in November 2025 and covers a range of actions spanning the Department of Health’s and the HSE’s commitments to Traveller Mental Health. The report documents the work that took place between January – October 2025 (Q1-Q3) Q1 – Q3 2025 Policy Level Key Accomplishments 1. Expanded Counselling Services for Travellers - Expansion of Traveller Counselling hubs in Kildare, Mayo, and Cork (NTRIS II, CfL,JCR) Introduction of two youth counsellors for Travellers in Dublin (NTRIS II, CfL, JCR) 2. Research and Evaluation Evaluation of the Traveller Primary Health Care Projects (NTHAP) Commissioned research on Roma Mental Health (NTRMHWG) Partnership with National Suicide Research Foundation to support tracking incidents of suicide in Traveller community (NTRIS II, CfL) 3. Community Programmes and Development Sláintecare Healthy Communities grants awarded (NTHAP, JCR) Development of a Traveller Specialist Group under Sharing the Vision (StV) 4. Service Developments Progression of Ethnic Identifier within Community Connect, the HSE programme that will implement a digital system for managing patient information in all community services (NTHAP, NTRIS II) Pilot project for the development of an implementation guide to support Traveller women at risk of homelessness ongoing in 2025 (NTRIS II) The population health approach that the Sharing the Vision policy advocates contains universal recommendations that benefit everyone in society but also acknowledges that additional work is required to promote positive mental health and build resilience among specific priority groups deemed to be ‘at risk’. To support this Minister Butler requested the establishment of a Specialist Group for Traveller Mental Health. This is based on the need for a specific focus and leadership on supports for Traveller MH given the persistently poor mental health outcomes for this Community. Minister Butler requested the Specialist Group to: • Review existing data and research on Traveller Mental Health, • Identify gaps in service provision and barriers to access, • Include and engage with Traveller representatives and organisations to ensure culturally sensitive approaches, • Develop evidence-based recommendations for policy and service development across Government, • Produce an interim report to inform the 2027 Budget Estimates process • Produce a Traveller Mental Health Action Plan. The Group is being independently Chaired by Dr Fiona Keogh and is made up of members of the Traveller Representative Groups, members of the Department of Health’s Mental Health and Social Inclusion Units, HSE officials, Travellers with Lived Experience, a member of the HRB and the Department of Children, Disability and Equality. The Group was established at the end of January and will produce an interim report and a final Traveller Mental Health Action Plan within twelve months.

question: 195. Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Taoiseach the number of Irish diaspora groups, including but not limited to sporting and cultural organisations, as well as emigrant organisations he and Ministers of State in his Department met for the St. Patrick's Day engagements overseas this year. [21928/26]
answer: Taoiseach (Deputy Micheál Martin) I propose to take Questions Nos. 194, 195 and 196 together. I travelled to Philadelphia and Washington D.C. for a four-day programme of engagements to celebrate St. Patrick’s Day. In Philadelphia, I met with Irish community and business representatives, as well as with Congressman Brendan Boyle, with whom I participated in the St. Patrick’s Day Parade, laid a wreath at a statue of Commadore James Barry, who founded the US Navy, and visited Independence Hall, where the US Declaration of Independence which was signed 250 years ago. I attended the Gala dinner of the Friendly Sons and Daughters of St. Patrick, and I was very pleased to do the official opening of the Irish Diaspora Center’s new premises which carries out excellent work on behalf of the Irish community in Philadelphia, and which is supported by the Government’s Emigrant Support Programme. In Washington DC, I attended the Embassy’s St Patrick’s Day reception attended by a large number of people from political, business, diplomatic and community backgrounds. I also attended the Ireland Funds’ annual Gala Dinner. The Secretary of Transportation, Sean P Duffy, was an honoree at this year’s event. I met with Vice-President, J.D. Vance, and his wife Usha, who hosted me and my wife Mary for breakfast in his residence. I met with President Trump for a bilateral meeting in the Oval Office where we discussed the contribution of Irish and Irish-American people to the development of the US, current bilateral relations, including our strong economic ties, and global issues. The meeting was also attended by Vice-President Vance, Secretary of State, Marco Rubio, and Secretary of Energy, Chris Wright. I also presented President Trump with the traditional bowl of shamrock to mark St Patrick’s Day at a ceremony and reception in the White House. The attendance included a number of senior representatives of the Administration, including members of the Cabinet, with whom I had the opportunity to engage, including Trade Representative Jamieson Greer. I attended the Friends of Ireland lunch on Capitol Hill, hosted by Speaker Mike Johnson. President Trump also attended and participated at the event. I also had a bilateral meeting with Speaker Johnson at which we discussed bilateral relations, political developments in the US and international issues. While on Capitol Hill, I also met with the ‘Friends of Ireland caucus’, co-chaired by Representatives Richie Neal and Mike Kelly. The meeting was also attended by a number of other Representatives, including Mary Gay Scanlon of Philadelphia. While in Washington I also had a programme of economic events at which I met Irish companies with business interests in the US, and US companies with a presence in Ireland. I attended a Business Leaders Lunch hosted by our enterprise agencies, at which I presented the Research Ireland annual academic and enterprise medals. I met with the Strategic Economic Advisory Panel to discuss recent trade and economic developments. I also attended an event hosted by Stripe. Chief Whip Butler visited Malta, Portugal and Spain as part of the Government’s St. Patrick’s Day outreach this year. She met with 16 government/regional representatives in total. She also met with over 15 diaspora groups, both formally and informally, and had over a dozen business engagements across her visit programme. The Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade will provide details on Minister Byrne’s St. Patrick’s Day travel.

question: 204. Deputy Brendan Smith asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade further to Parliamentary Question No. 7 of 18 February 2026, if she has had recent discussions with the United States administration regarding the proposals if any, under consideration in the United States concerning the need to provide a legal pathway for undocumented Irish emigrants in the United States, such as the inclusion of Ireland in the E-3 non-immigrant visa programme; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [21696/26]
answer: Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade Addressing the situation of undocumented Irish emigrants in the United States, and working to secure legal pathways for Irish people seeking to live and work in the US, continues to be important for the Government, as set out in the Programme for Government. Efforts to advance these issues have been made with successive US administrations. The Taoiseach raised the Government's desire to develop a legal pathway for migration during his St. Patrick's Day programme in Washington D.C. During my own recent visit to Washington, I also discussed immigration matters in meetings on Capitol Hill. This included in relation to U.S. immigration policy, its impact on Irish communities and the prospects for immigration reform which could assist, inter alia, undocumented Irish immigrants. However, it is clear to me from these conversations that the challenges faced by such proposals should not be underestimated. The Government remains supportive of efforts to secure an Irish specific E3 visa programme. This would open up a new legal pathway for more Irish citizens to live and work in the U.S. However, it is unlikely that undocumented Irish currently in the U.S. would be eligible for such a programme, if secured. We will continue to provide funding to Irish community organisations, including those that provide trusted immigration information, legal resources and support for those seeking to regularise their immigration status. Some €4.5 million was provided to organisations in the U.S. last year.

question: 207. Deputy George Lawlor asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade if she will arrange for an early and urgent determination of an application for citizenship for a newborn child (details supplied); and if she will make a statement on the matter. [21860/26]
answer: Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade My Department is responsible for processing Foreign Birth Registration (FBR) applications for people who are born abroad and claim Irish citizenship through a grandparent born in Ireland or through a parent who has claimed citizenship also through FBR or Naturalisation. question: 209. Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the number of Irish diaspora groups, including but not limited to sporting and cultural organisations, as well as emigrant organisations her and Ministers of State in her Department met for the St. Patrick's Day engagements overseas this year. [21920/26]
answer: Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade I propose to take Questions Nos. 208, 209 and 210 together. I propose taking questions 208, 209 and 210 together. St. Patrick’s Day is a unique opportunity to promote Ireland’s interests and values around the world. St. Patrick’s Day 2026 saw 38 representatives of the State carrying out programmes across 47 countries focused on trade and investment promotion, engaging with senior business and political contacts, celebrating our diaspora and showcasing Irish culture. As a small, open economy, and a strong proponent of free and fair trade it is more important than ever to make sure that we maximise the value of our national day to engage with key partners all around the world. It is also an opportunity to promote our values around the world. For St. Patrick’s Day 2026, there was an enhanced focus on promoting trade, tourism and investment in line with the Action Plan on Market Diversification with a major focus on priority markets in Europe, US and UK and also in new, emerging and high growth markets across the Asia-Pacific region, Latin America, Africa and the Middle East. The St. Patrick’s Day visits undertaken by me, and Ministers of State Byrne and Richmond were highly aligned with these objectives. My own visit to Boston included high-level political engagement including with the Governor and Lieutenant Governor of Massachusetts, the mayors of Boston and Cambridge, and the members of the Massachusetts Irish American State Legislators' Caucus. I also met President Biden at the Irish American partnership breakfast. I attended the South Boston St. Patrick’s Day Parade, and also met with leaders of the Irish community. Other engagements included visits to the Irish Cultural Centre of Greater Boston in Canton, the Irish Pastoral Centre in Dorchester, and the delivery of a keynote address at the JFK Presidential Library and Museum. I also launched Ireland’s International Sports Diplomacy Strategy in the United States in Boston's Fenway Park. I took part in a number of trade promotion engagements with clients of Enterprise Ireland and IDA Ireland focused in particular on the med-tech and life sciences sectors, Boston being a major hub for these sectors. I also promoted Irish seafood at the Seafood Expo, North America’s largest seafood trade fair in company with Bord Bia client companies. In Poland, Minister Byrne met with his Polish counterpart Ignacy Niemczycki, and the Chair of the European Affairs Committee in the lower house of the Sejm, Agnieskza Pomaska. He attended the embassy’s official reception, and participated in events connected with the St. Patrick’s Day festival in Lódz, where he also met with Irish investors. In Ukraine, Minister Byrne met with the Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs; the first deputy chair of the parliamentary committee on EU Integration, and the first deputy head of the Office of the President of Ukraine, as well as attending the embassy’s St Patrick’s Day reception. In Moldova, Minister Byrne undertook a number of political engagements including with President Sandu; the deputy Prime Minister for European Integration and Moldova’s chief negotiator for EU accession, Cristina Gherasimov. He also met the state secretary in the economic development and digitalisation ministry, and the chair of the Moldova-Ireland Friendship Group in parliament. He attended the embassy’s St Patrick’s Day reception where he met members of the Irish community as well as diplomats and members of parliament. Minister of State for International Development and Diaspora, Neale Richmond, visited Mozambique and South Africa from 11-19 March. In Mozambique, the Minister met with the minister for the economy, and the secretary of state for foreign affairs and cooperation. In Inhambane Province, he met with the governor and two other provincial leaders; its secretary of state and its director of health. He also met with an Irish investor and, at the St. Patrick’s Day reception, met other local business contacts and members of the Irish community. In South Africa, the Minister met with the deputy minister for International Relations and Cooperation, and the deputy minister for correctional services. He also met members of Business Ireland South Africa at a business breakfast, and a range of Enterprise Ireland client companies including at an Enterprise Ireland St. Patrick’s Day event. He participated in St. Patrick’s Day events organised by the Irish South African Association branches in Johannesburg and Cape Town and a business breakfast organised by Business Ireland South Africa Cape Town. All events were attended by many representatives of the diaspora.

question: 225. Deputy William Aird asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the way in which the €16.4 million allocated under the 2025 Emigrant Support Programme is supporting frontline welfare services for vulnerable members of our diaspora; the way in which this funding strengthens Ireland’s long-standing commitment to Irish communities overseas; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [22462/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade The Government is committed to deepening our ties with Irish communities overseas and to ensuring that the welfare of the Irish abroad remains at the heart of our diaspora engagement. Central to our approach is the Emigrant Support Programme (ESP), which in line with our Diaspora Strategy prioritises grants to organisations in the voluntary sector who work with our most vulnerable citizens and communities overseas. The Programme also supports projects that nurture our cultural heritage, promote vibrant networks among the Irish abroad and provide advice for emigrants who wish to return to Ireland. Since its establishment in 2004, the ESP has granted over €265 million in grants to more than 900 charitable and Irish community organisations in 53 countries. The majority of the funding (some 60% annually) is granted to frontline welfare service providers, working with elderly Irish emigrants, and other vulnerable members of our communities These organisations, working closely with our Embassies and Consulates, particularly in Great Britain, the US , Canada and Australia provide crucial support, often at times of crisis, in areas such as elders lunch clubs, advisory, counselling, mental health support, advocacy, information and outreach services for our citizens abroad, including on immigration matters and status. This work is vital, particularly for those from marginalised backgrounds and those with complex needs. In recent years, and reflecting the commitment in our Diaspora Strategy “to seek to heal the relationship with those who left Ireland in crisis, including as a result of institutional abuse” support has also been provided to organisations working with, and advocating for survivors of institutional abuse in Britain, where it is estimated that approx 30% of survivors live. The ESP also supports Irish organisations such as Safe Home Ireland and Crosscare, which support people returning to Ireland, often in challenging circumstances. Full details on the Emigrant Support Programme including the organisations who received grants in 2025 and earlier years is available on our website. Our budget allocation for support for the diaspora in 2026 in €17.5m, the highest allocation to date. Since being appointed as Minister for International Development and Diaspora last year, I have had a chance to meet with many of these remarkable organisations and to hear first-hand about the opportunities and challenges our overseas communities face. I would like to acknowledge the great work they do for our community and look forward to welcoming many of these organisations to Dublin next month for the 4th Global Irish Civic Forum. Ahead of the Forum, we will launch our new diaspora strategy and I can assure the Deputy that the well-being of Irish people overseas and a strong Emigrant Support Programme will remain priorities of our diaspora engagement in the years ahead.

question: 277. Deputy Micheál Carrigy asked the Minister for Transport the status of negotiations regarding a reciprocal driver’s license exchange agreement between Ireland and various United States jurisdictions; if he will specifically address the progress made by the Road Safety Authority (RSA) in its technical assessment of the licensing standards; the timeline for potential implementation of such agreements to alleviate the burden on returning Irish emigrants; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [21428/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Transport I propose to take Questions Nos. 277, 292 and 295 together. I wish to advise that advise that Irish driver licensing operates within a framework of EU law, which sets out the driver licensing legislation with which all Member States must comply. Licence formats, vehicle categories and driving test standards are all set at EU level. As all Member States test drivers to the same standards, there can be mutual recognition of driving licences. Someone who is resident in Ireland must have an Irish or EU licence to drive a vehicle on public roads here. Accordingly, Ireland may make bilateral licence exchange agreements with non-EU states to allow residents from outside the EU to drive here by exchanging their national licence for an Irish licence. In considering whether to enter such an agreement, the relevant authorities on each side compare the two licensing regimes, so that each may be satisfied that they are compatible. As driver licensing protects public safety by ensuring that people licensed to drive on our roads have reached recognised standards, the most important element in reaching a bilateral agreement is that the other jurisdiction's licensing regime applies standards for obtaining a licence which are compatible with our own. Where these standards are not met, no agreement is possible, no matter how desirable an agreement with that jurisdiction may be. For Ireland, this task is carried out by the Road Safety Authority (RSA). US driver licensing operates at state rather than federal level, so there are 50 licensing systems with widely varying standards and road safety performance, many with levels of road fatalities significantly worse than most EU countries. Agreement with any one state would mean taking into account the exchange relationships between that state and the other 49. In line with Programme for Government commitments regarding the easier return to Ireland for emigrants, the RSA has been directed to engage with the state licensing authorities for three US states - New York, New Jersey and Massachusetts. The assessment process for a possible licence exchange agreement is technical in nature between the licensing authorities and is necessarily independent of political involvement. This process is ongoing at present.

question: 368. Deputy Mairéad Farrell asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance whether drafting has commenced at a national level on the proposed EU National Regional Partnership Plans; the way he envisages that this process will take place, including scope for input at parliamentary and civil society level; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [21698/26]
answer: Tánaiste and Minister for Finance The National and Regional Partnership Plans (NRPP) Regulation is part of the European Commission's package of legislative proposals for the EU Budget Multiannual Financial Framework 2028-2034 which were published in July and September of 2025. The package of legislative proposals remain under negotiation in Council. Given the breadth of policy areas contained within the NRPP Regulation, several Government Departments are closely involved in negotiations, including my Department, the Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation and the Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine. More certainty is needed at EU level on the implementation rules of the NRPPs before substantive drafting on Ireland's plan can begin. Notwithstanding this, consultation is likely to be a key feature of the future EU agreement on the NRPPs, as it has been on EU funds in the past. The current draft of the NRPP Regulation provides for a central role for civic society and for each Member State to organise and implement a comprehensive partnership in accordance with its institutional and legal framework. That partnership shall include a balanced representation of the following partners: (a) regional, local, urban, rural and other public authorities or associations representing such authorities; (b) economic and social partners, including farmers, fishers and their organisations; (c) relevant bodies representing civil society, such as environmental partners, non-governmental organisations, youth organisations, and bodies responsible for promoting social inclusion, fundamental rights, rights of persons with disabilities, gender equality and non-discrimination, national human rights institutions and organisations; (d) research organisations and universities, where appropriate. The draft NRPP Regulation also requires that these partners are involved in the preparation of the Plan and throughout the preparation, implementation and evaluation of chapters, including through participation in monitoring committees. This mirrors the approach to the development of the Ireland’s Partnership Agreement with the European Commission for Cohesion Policy Funds (including the European Regional Development Fund, European Social Funds+ and Just Transition Fund) for the 2021-2027 funding period. The development of the Partnership Agreement involved the range of civil society partners in both the Programme Agreement Monitoring Committee and subsequently in the Programme Monitoring Committees overseeing implementation of each Cohesion policy fund. The development of previous Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) plans, including the CAP Strategic Plan 2023-2027, involved extensive stakeholder and public consultation, supported by structures such as the CAP Consultative Committee, which is comprised of representative farming and rural organisations, academics, environmental NGOs and advisory services. Notwithstanding the fact that the negotiation of the NRPP Regulation is still ongoing, the Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine is following a similar approach in relation to the post-2027 CAP process. This includes the establishment of the CAP Consultative Committee and a public consultation launched in February 2026 to gather views from farmers, stakeholders and the wider public to inform Ireland’s approach to ongoing EU negotiations. The Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine and Departmental officials, as has been the case for previous programmes, are also providing updates to the Oireachtas through, for example, appearances at the Committees, Seanad statements and Dail Questions. Civil society is also consulted more broadly by way of public consultation process, including in the preparation of the environmental assessments associated with the plan.

question: 379. Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the number of Irish diaspora groups, including but not limited to sporting and cultural organisations, as well as emigrant organisations he and Ministers of State in his Department met for the St. Patrick's Day engagements overseas this year. [21919/26]
answer: Tánaiste and Minister for Finance I propose to take Questions Nos. 378, 379, 380 and 381 together. The theme for St. Patrick’s Day 2026 highlights Ireland’s place in the world as an open trading economy. In line with this, the St. Patrick’s Day engagements, undertaken by myself and the Minister of State at my Department Robert Troy T.D., focussed strongly on trade promotion and economic engagement. On 10-11 March, I visited Paris to undertake a programme of political and business engagements. France is one of our most valued economic partners in the EU, with two-way trade in goods and services amounting to €45.79 billion in 2024. At political level, I had a wide-ranging and constructive bilateral meeting with my French counterpart, Roland Lescure, Minister of the Economy, Finance and Industrial, Energy, and Digital Sovereignty. I also met separately with Sébastien Martin, Minister Delegate for Industry, and Benjamin Haddad, Minister Delegate for European Affairs. I was also pleased to meet with Mathias Cormann, the Secretary General of the OECD, to reaffirm the value of the OECD to Ireland and in particular the importance of the organisation's economic policy advice and expertise. Engagement with the State Agencies formed a key part of my programme in Paris. I met with several State Agency client companies at the Embassy’s St. Patrick’s Day trade reception for key business contacts, which was attended by over 190 guests. I also had engagements with IDA Ireland client companies Servier and Sanofi, and Enterprise Ireland client Castlebrook. I was pleased to speak at the launch event for Tourism Ireland’s ‘Ireland Week’ campaign, attended by representatives from the leading French air and sea carriers, along with tourism businesses from across the island of Ireland and French tour operators active in promoting Ireland as a tourism destination to the French market. France is Ireland’s fourth-largest source of tourist revenue with over 400,000 French tourists visiting in 2024. In recognition of the ever-closer economic relationship between Ireland and France, I participated in a roundtable discussion hosted by the Paris-based Franco-Irish Chamber of Commerce, NetworkIrlande, alongside 10 senior business leaders from French and Irish companies as well as representatives of the State Agencies. I also visited Station F, the world’s largest start-up facility, where I met with several French start-up companies to learn more about France’s innovation development infrastructure. At the two St. Patrick's Day Embassy receptions that I attended, I also had the opportunity to engage with representatives from 15 Irish diaspora organisations in France, including sporting, cultural, and community groups such as GAA France, An Ghaeltacht-sur-Seine, the Association Irlandaise, and Irish in France. I travelled to London from 14-16 March for the second part of my St. Patrick’s Day programme. In addition to our strong people-to-people and cultural links, Ireland and the UK are close trading partners, with two-way bilateral trade standing at €129 billion in 2024. This is equivalent to around €2.4 billion per week. The UK is Ireland’s largest tourism market, with the value of tourism from the UK in 2024 estimated at around €1.8 billion. As part of the programme, I represented the Government at the St. Patrick’s Day Festival Ball. I met representatives of the Greater London Authority and the Community Advisory Group (comprised of a number of diaspora organisations), as well as meeting with many individual leading members of the diaspora during my participation in the St. Patrick’s Day parade. I addressed an event convened by the British Irish Chamber of Commerce and attended by 28 senior company representatives. I also participated in a Bloomberg Forum attended by senior representatives of a large number of financial services companies. At political level, I had constructive bilateral meetings with the Chancellor of the Exchequer, Rachel Reeves MP, and Deputy Prime Minister, David Lammy MP. Both bilateral meetings underlined the importance of sustained positive cooperation between Ireland and the UK, building on the high-level summit which took place the previous week in Cork. As part of the political programme, I also met with the chair and co-chair of the UK All-party Parliamentary Group on Ireland and the Irish in Britain, Adam Jogee MP and Colum Eastwood MP. My colleague, Minister of State Robert Troy, undertook a series of engagements in the State of Texas as part of the Government St. Patrick’s Day programme. Ireland and Texas share strong political, economic and people-to-people links. Trade between Ireland and Texas totalled $4.8 billion in 2024. Tourism between Ireland and Texas has been bolstered in recent years due to direct flight connections between Dublin and Dallas Fort Worth, with almost 60,000 Texans visiting Ireland and over 8,000 Irish people visiting Texas in 2023. As part of his programme, Minister of State Troy, visited both Dallas and Austin. He engaged with political leaders, including the Texas State Secretary, Jane Nelson, and Mayor of Austin, Kirk Watson, and also met with five State representatives. He also held a number of meetings with senior business leaders, including visiting both the Texas Stock Exchange and the Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas. In Austin, he participated in a series of events in Ireland House at South by Southwest, a world-renowned festival at the intersection of innovation, technology, culture, and business. Minister of State Troy also met with members of the Irish diaspora, including the Celtic Cowboys GAA Club and the Dallas Irish Business Network.

question: 408. Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation the number of Irish diaspora groups, including but not limited to sporting and cultural organisations, as well as emigrant organisations he and Ministers of State in his Department met for the St. Patrick's Day engagements overseas this year. [21925/26]
answer: Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation I propose to take Questions Nos. 407 to 410, inclusive, together. I wish to advise the Deputy that I visited Senegal and Nigeria as part of the St. Patrick’s Day 2026 programme. The visit to Dakar, Senegal provided an important strategic opportunity to enhance the profile of Ireland’s newest embassy in Africa and to highlight the political, economic, cultural, and people-to-people connections between the two countries and reaffirm Ireland’s commitment to strengthening the bilateral relationship. My visit involved engagements reflecting the broad range of the Embassy’s work, with a particular focus on the development aid programme. I met with several UN development partners, including the UN Resident Coordinator for Senegal; International Fund for Agricultural Development (IFAD) Country Director and Head of Regional Hub; World Food Programme Regional Director for West and Central Africa; Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) Sub-Regional Coordinator for West Africa; Head of UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs Regional Office for West and Central Africa; and UN Women West and Central Africa Deputy Regional Director. I visited a number of development cooperation projects supported by Ireland, including an Irish Aid funded Youth Project: Yakaar Environnment; two IFAD Agri-Jeunes projects supporting youth working in agriculture; and an FAO and Irish Aid partnership project training young agricultural entrepreneurs. The programme included high-level political meetings with the Minister for Economy, Planning and Cooperation and the Minister for Sport and Youth. I also met with the Institute Pasteur Dakar, a key vaccine research partner for Ireland’s National Institute for Bioprocessing Research and Training. I travelled to Goree Island, the first UNESCO designated World Heritage Site in Africa, where I met with the Mayor of Goree Island and members of the local community. I engaged with the small number of Irish diaspora in Senegal at an informal dinner arranged by the Embassy, in addition to the formal St. Patrick’s Day reception event where the Minister for Public Services, Labour and Public Service Reform and a number of key development partners also attended. I travelled to Abuja and Lagos in Nigeria, where a key part of the visit was the official opening of the new Chancery building in Abuja. The visit also provided an opportunity for me to meet a number of leading Nigerian political, business and cultural figures, including a meeting with Economic Community of West Africa States (EOCWAS) and the Minister of the Federal Capital Territory at the SPD reception in Abuja. I also had meetings with the senior leadership in Guinness Nigeria, the CEO of Air Peace, and an engagement organised by Bord Bia in their promotion of Irish produce in Nigeria. In addition to this I also visited the Kuchigoro Primary and Secondary School in Abuja where Irish Aid funding to Crystal Aid Response Foundation (CARF) funded a restock of the library at the primary school. In Lagos, I visited St. Finbarr’s College to launch their sports diplomacy project, an Ireland-Nigeria Sports Programme. I engaged with a members of the Irish-Nigerian community throughout my visit, including a notable historian who provided an exhibition for the opening of the Embassy in Abuja. To complement this, I visited the J. Randle Centre for Yoruba Culture and History and the Loving Lagos Centre. In Lagos, I spoke at a St Patrick’s Day business lunch organised by the Friends of Ireland in Nigeria for around 80 guests, in addition to participating in a roundtable discussion at the Lagos Chamber of Commerce. I participated in two St. Patrick’s Day reception events in Nigeria, the first in Abuja which included the opening of the Chancery building, and the second in Lagos hosted by the Honorary Consul. Both events were attended by Irish diaspora and key development partners. The theme for St. Patrick’s Day 2026 highlighted Ireland’s place in the world as an open trading economy. In concluding on my visit as part of the St. Patrick’s Day programme 2026, I would highlight that in 2025, Ireland’s goods exports to Senegal and Nigeria were worth €71 million and €203 million respectively. My colleague, Minister of State Frank Feighan, T.D., visited the Philippines and Singapore for St. Patrick’s Day 2026. The visit to the Philippines included political, economic and cultural meetings, including Secretary of the Department of Economy, Planning and Development, Undersecretary for Bilateral Affairs at the Department of Foreign Affairs, and Secretary of Department of Information and Communication Technology. Minister Feighan also met with a number of Irish community organisations in the Philippines, including the Chair of Manila GAA; Chair of the St Patrick's Society; Duyan Centre (Embassy-funded Centre for children with HIV). He also met with members of the Irish diaspora during the St. Patrick’s Day reception event at the official residence. As part of the wider trade, and economic meetings during the visit, Minister Feighan met with a number of businesses with Irish trading links, including, the European Chamber of Commerce and CEO of Bosch Philippines, Go Digital Philippines and the Association of Data Centres. The visit to Singapore focused on elements of the Minister’s specific portfolio and he met with a Minister of the Prime Minister’s Office and Second Minister for Finance, and Second Minister for National Development as well as the Chief of Government Procurement for Singapore. On the digital agenda, Minister Feighan had a bilateral meeting with Minister of State in the Ministry of Digital Development and Information, and in the Ministry of Health. On the broader bilateral relationship, Minister Feighan met with Minister of State in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and in the Ministry for Trade and Industry. He also met with Minister of State in the Ministry of Culture, Community and Youth & Ministry of Manpower who was Guest of Honour at the Embassy National Day reception. At the official reception in Singapore, Minister Feighan met with the leadership of each of the eleven main Irish community and diaspora groups in Singapore. In addition, he met with key partners to the Irish Embassy in Singapore, including the Irish Chamber of Commerce Singapore, Ireland Funds Singapore, St Patrick’s Society Singapore and Singapore Gaelic Lions Academy for their St Patrick’s Day Soccer Tournament. Minister Feighan also met with a number of trading partners to discuss strengthening the Ireland-Singapore trading relationship. These meetings included Horizon Quantum, Irish Duck Company, Siemens Digital Industries Software (Siemens ASEAN) and ICDL Foundation. In concluding on Minister of State Feighan’s visit as part of the St. Patrick’s Day programme 2026 and recalling again the focus on Ireland’s place in the world as an open trading economy, I would highlight that in 2025, Ireland’s goods exports to the Philippines and Singapore were worth €198 million and €785 million respectively. Finally, I have asked the Minister of State with special responsibility for the Office of Public Works, Kevin Boxer Moran, T.D., to reply to you directly in respect of his visit to Australia as part of the St. Patrick’s Day programme 2026.

question: 427. Deputy Ruth Coppinger asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment the status of a work permit renewal application (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [21608/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment I propose to take Questions Nos. 427 and 432 together. Ireland operates a managed employment permits system designed to address skills and labour shortages that cannot be met from within the domestic or EEA labour market. The employment permits system operates in line with the Employment Permits Act 2024 and associated Regulations, which set out the statutory framework for the granting, renewal and refusal of employment permits. Both applications referenced by the Deputy remain on hold due to the ongoing Workplace Relations Commission (WRC) inspection involving the employer. In accordance with standard procedure, applications linked to employers that are under WRC inspection are placed on hold pending the outcome of that review. Applicants seeking to renew their existing employment permit may continue to work while their renewal application is being processed, including where their current permit has expired. This ensures continuity for both employees and businesses. Processing of the applications will resume once the inspection has concluded and any necessary actions have been addressed. To support applicants and employers, the Department has introduced a Self-Service Portal which provides real-time updates on employment permit application status. A dedicated mailbox for Oireachtas members is also available at tdepqueries@enterprise.gov.ie.

question: 444. Deputy Eoghan Kenny asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment if he is aware that non-EU post-primary and secondary school teachers are unable to meet the criteria for a general employment permit, owing to the requirement for job advertisements to be posted on multiple platforms while teaching roles are advertised only on specific education recruitment platforms; the steps he will take to reduce this barrier,; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [22263/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment (Deputy Alan Dillon) I have been made aware of queries raised recently regarding the requirements for the grant of a General Employment Permit, specifically with regard to conducting the Labour Market Needs Test (LMNT). The employment permits system is grounded in legislation that sets clear and objective criteria for salary thresholds, qualifications, and the eligibility of occupations. These criteria ensure that permits are issued only where there is a demonstrable shortage and that the system remains fair, transparent, and responsive to Ireland’s labour market needs. The LMNT is a core safeguard within the system. It ensures that job vacancies are first made available to Irish and EEA nationals before an employer may recruit a non-EEA national. To fulfil the LMNT requirement, employers are required to undertake advertisement of their vacancy in two categories only. Firstly, they can advertise their vacancy on at least one online employment platform of their choosing. The second element in the LMNT legislation requires the advertisement be placed on the Department of Social Protection’s JobsIreland platform and the EU-wide EURES network for at least 28 days. These channels provide broad and accessible visibility for vacancies across the domestic and wider EEA labour markets. The LMNT allows employers, at their discretion, to advertise the role on multiple online employment platforms should they wish to do so in addition to the minimum requirement of JobsIreland/EURES plus one other online platform. The Employment Permits Act 2024 has introduced a number of modernisations including revising the LMNT to remove the outdated requirement for print-media advertising and to facilitate online advertising on appropriate platforms. There are currently no plans to amend the LMNT requirements for occupations for which it applies. My Department is not aware of any legislation or regulation that prohibits education-sector employers from advertising teaching roles on JobsIreland or EURES in addition to their sector-specific platforms. Employers remain free to advertise through their customary education-sector channels while also advertising the role on JobsIreland/EURES as well. Employment permits form part of a managed and strategic approach to addressing skills gaps while maintaining the protection of the domestic labour market and supporting opportunities for Irish and EEA jobseekers. While recognising the challenges raised by some stakeholders, the LMNT remains a key mechanism to ensure balanced, fair and sustainable recruitment practices.

In Bosnia Herzegovina, the Minister of State met with members of the diaspora community at the Sarajevo St Patrick’s Day reception. question: 534. Deputy Eoghan Kenny asked the Minister for Education and Youth if she is aware that non-EU post-primary and secondary school teachers are unable to meet the criteria for a general employment permit, owing to the requirement for job advertisements to be posted on multiple platforms while teaching roles are advertised only on specific education recruitment platforms; the steps she will take to reduce this barrier,; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [22261/26]
answer: Minister for Education and Youth The Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment is responsible for administering the employment permit system. The Department of Education and Youth engages with the Department of Trade and Employment on this matter. The EU Directive 2005/36/EC governs the recognition of professional qualifications. Applications from teachers who qualified outside the Republic of Ireland are processed in line with this Directive and are assessed under its general system in the same manner, regardless of whether the applicant qualified within or outside of the EU. The recruitment and appointment of teachers to fill teaching posts is a matter for the individual school authority, subject to procedures agreed under Section 24(3) of the Education Act 1988 (as amended by the Education (Amendment) Act 2012). Schools are required to employ appropriately qualified and registered teachers for the respective sector. The Teaching Council is the body with the statutory authority and responsibility for the registration and regulation of the teaching profession in Ireland. While it is acknowledged that shortages exist in some schools, sectors and locations, the number of unfilled teaching posts remains low with over 98% of teaching posts filled according to an analysis of payroll data from November 2025. The analysis showed there are 75,000 teachers employed in schools across the country, including 34,600 in the post-primary sector.
