question: 671. Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Social Protection the number of Irish diaspora groups, including but not limited to sporting and cultural organisations, as well as emigrant organisations he and Ministers of State in his Department met for the St. Patrick's Day engagements overseas this year. [21927/26]
answer: Minister for Social Protection I propose to take Questions Nos. 670, 671, 672 and 673 together. As part of the Government’s St. Patrick’s Day programme for 2026, I travelled to Canada to promote Ireland, Irish values, and Ireland’s interests across the world. Deepening Ireland’s political, cultural, economic and trade relationship with Canada remains a key priority for this Government. My programme took place over a week across Ottawa, Montreal, and Toronto. In terms of the value of the trade relationship with Canada, official statistics from the Central Statistics Office reports that some 51,299 tonnes of goods were exported from Ireland to Canada in 2025, with a value of €2.69 billion, while we imported over a million tonnes (1.07 million) of goods from Canada worth €1.59 billion in 2025. Figures for services are not yet available for 2025, but in 2024, some €4.03 billion in services were exported to Canada, and a further €2.97 billion worth of services were imported from Canada. My St Patrick’s Day programme was a unique and special moment to connect with Irish Canadian diaspora and celebrate Ireland’s close connection and partnership with Canada. Over the course of my visit to Toronto, I had the opportunity to engage with a wide range of Irish Community Organisations, many of which are supported by the Irish Government, including through the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade’s Emigrant Support Programme. These included: the Canada Ireland Foundation, the Canada Ireland Fund, the Irish Canadian Immigration Centre, the Ireland-Canada Chamber of Commerce, several Toronto-area GAA clubs and branches of Comhaltas Ceoltóirí Éireann, the Emerald Isle Seniors Society, the Irish Cultural Society of Toronto, the Pot of Gold Charity Lottery, the Rose of Tralee, the Toronto St. Patrick’s Day Parade Society, the Toronto Irish Players, the Irish Person of the Year Committee, the Benevolent Society of London and Area, the London Irish Canadian Cultural Society, the Toronto Bloomsday Festival, the Irish Club of Mississauga, The Toronto Irish Players, the One Little Goat Community theatre, local Gaeilgeoirí and participants in the Irish Canadian University Scholar (ICUF) Programme and Toronto-area Irish Community Radio. I also met with representatives of the Toronto Fire Service which, while not specifically a diaspora group, has a strong historic connection with the Irish community in Toronto. The elected officials that I meet during the Toronto leg of the trip included James Maloney MP and Chris Bittle MP. I also met with Her Honour the Honourable Edith Dumont, Lieutenant Governor of Ontario, the Honourable Donna Skelly, Speaker of the Legislative Assembly of Ontario, and several Members of the Executive Council of Ontario, including the Honourable Stan Cho, Ontario Minister of Tourism, Culture and Gaming; the Honourable Todd McCarthy, Ontario Minister of the Environment, Conservation and Parks and Acting Minister of Infrastructure; the Honourable Vic Fedeli, Ontario Minister of Economic Development, Job Creation and Trade; the Honourable Caroline Mulroney, President of the Treasury Board of Ontario and Ontario Minister of Francophone Affairs; and the Honourable Lisa Thompson, Ontario Minister for Rural Affairs; as well as other Members of the Legislative Assembly of Ontario, including Dawn Gallagher-Murphy MPP, Mary Margaret McMahon MPP, Sheref Sabawy MPP, and Terence Kernaghan MPP. I also met with the Mayor of Toronto, Olivia Chow, Deputy Mayor of Toronto for Scarborough Paul Ainslie, as well as mayors and other representatives of a number of towns and cities across Ontario, including Bradford, Hamilton, Niagara Falls, Niagara-on-the-Lake, London, Oakville, Peterborough, Uxbridge and Waterloo. The elected officials that I meet during the Ottawa & Montreal leg of the trip included: Prime Minister Mark Carney at the Official St. Patrick’s Day Reception; the Secretary of State for Rural Development Buckley Belanger; Minister of Canadian Identity and Culture and Minister responsible for Official Language, Marc Miller; Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister, Kody Blois; the Parliamentary Secretary for International Trade, Yasir Naqvi MP; Quebec Minister for International Relations, Christopher Skeete; and the Minister of Jobs and Families Patty Hadju. I also attended a flag-raising ceremony with Mayor Sutcliffe, and attended a Canada–Ireland Inter-parliamentary group Lunch. Looking at businesses, Canada is the 12th largest market globally for Irish companies. Enterprise Ireland have 315 client companies exporting €585m to Canada. I attended a Business Leaders' lunch in Ottawa and met with Tom Jenkins of Opentext. I also met with Accenture and Employment and Social Development Canada on Canada’s Benefits Delivery Modernisation. In Montreal, I attended a Business Breakfast hosted with the Montreal Ireland Chamber of Commerce and Enterprise Ireland and Invest Northern Ireland and met with Hubert Bolduc, President of Investissement Québec International and Kerry Group. In terms of Enterprise Ireland clients, I met with Kinvara Skincare & Purity Life, Osbourne Recruitment, Combilift, Xcentuate, Maya Data Privacy Limited, Capella, Morgan McKinley, CodeEast and Deerpark Knitwear. At the Ambassador's reception, I met Fineos, Aryza, and Wrksense. International State visits play a significant role in advancing both trade and tourism and provide a high-level platform for us to strengthen our diplomatic ties, while directly promoting economic co-operation. The trip helped to build long term economic partnership, build confidence among businesses, and promote Ireland as a destination for investment and tourism.

question: 679. Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the timeframe in which he intends to bring forward legislation in response to the Independent Review Group reports on the Offences Against the State Act; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [21380/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration In May 2025, following extensive consideration and analysis, I informed the Government that I proposed to accept, in principle, the recommendations of the majority report of the Independent Review Group which examined the Offences Against the State Acts. This set a clear direction for reform. The majority recommended the repeal of the Acts and their replacement with modern bespoke legislation. As part of its package of recommendations, it recommended the replacement of the Special Criminal Court with a permanent non-jury court, subject to certain safeguards. Other key recommendations in the majority report include a range of additional safeguards and transparency measures concerning the structure of the new court, the role of the DPP, the abolition of scheduled offences, the proscription of unlawful organisations, and the handling of evidence in relation to membership of such organisations. The Report also recommended that consideration be given to consolidation of all legislation dealing with terrorist offences. Given the importance of the Acts over many decades, detailed proposals for reform must be thoroughly considered and approached with the utmost care. That work will take some time to complete and I will return to Government with detailed proposals in due course.

question: 681. Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the Garda stations or regions that are currently using the investigation management system within An Garda Síochána. [21411/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Garda Commissioner is responsible for the management and administration of An Garda Síochána under section 33 of the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024, which includes all operational policing matters and the operation, maintenance and evaluation of all IT systems that support routine policing matters. I am advised by the Garda authorities that the purpose of the Investigation Management System (IMS) is to digitise and standardise the management of investigations across An Garda Síochána. The system was designed to provide a consistent, statutory-compliant framework for managing investigation files. The system ensures investigations are conducted to the highest of standards across all incident types and allows management the capability to audit and monitor the standard of investigations. The system also provides for case management across a Division, Section or Region. I am informed by An Garda Síochána that all Divisions in the Eastern and North Western Region are using the IMS and that in the Southern Region, the Clare/Tipperary Division is using the IMS. Garda authorities also advise that the IMS will be deployed across a further 13 Divisions by the end of the second quarter of 2026 and that plans are in place to commence training in the Dublin Metropolitan Region (DMR) in the first quarter of 2027. At that juncture the IMS will have been deployed across the full organisation.

[21519/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 684, 685 and 686 together. The Garda Commissioner is responsible for the management and administration of An Garda Síochána under Section 33 of the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024. This includes determining the manner in which members of Garda personnel are to be distributed and stationed throughout the State. The Commissioner is independent in his functions under Section 34 of the Act and I, as Minister, have no role in these matters. An Garda Síochána police the country on a divisional basis and not a station basis, viewing their station buildings as locations within communities where the public can attend, and where resources are based. question: 688. Deputy Gary Gannon asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to provide the assumptions and framework on which the output of his Department's online child maintenance calculator is based; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [21549/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 688 and 728 together. The development of the Child Maintenance Guidelines was a key recommendation of the 2024 Review of the Enforcement of Child Maintenance Orders. An interdepartmental group (“The Child Maintenance Guidelines Committee”) was established in February 2024 to develop the child maintenance guidelines for use by all parties, on a voluntary basis, when putting child maintenance arrangements in place. The Committee was Chaired by my Department and its membership included representatives from the Department of Social Protection, Department of Children, Disability and Equality, Legal Aid Board, Courts Service and Tusla. Development of the guidelines was informed by a comprehensive comparative review covering England and Wales, Scotland, Northern Ireland, United States, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Germany, Austria, Denmark and the Netherlands. It was also critically important to listen to the views of parents who have been involved in making child maintenance arrangements. For this reason, in April 2025, the Committee conducted a survey-based consultation to get the public's views on important aspects of the guidelines. The published guidelines along with a comparative review of guidelines in other jurisdictions and a public consultation report can be accessed at the following link: www.gov.ie/en/department-of-justice-home-affairs-and-migration/publications/child-maintenance-guidelines-for-ireland/ The Guidelines are compatible with Irish legislation on child maintenance and can be used by the courts. However, the courts are not obliged to consider the guidelines when making child maintenance orders. The objectives of the Guidelines include: • to establish fair, consistent and predictable amounts of maintenance for children whose parents are not together. • to increase transparency, consistency and predictability for those seeking and paying child maintenance. • to reduce conflict and tension between parents by making the calculation of child maintenance more objective. • to reduce the number of child maintenance applications made to the courts by giving parents guidance in setting the levels of child maintenance and by encouraging private maintenance agreements. • to ensure consistent treatment of parents and children who are in similar circumstances. • to promote a culture of payment of child maintenance. The child maintenance calculator was launched on 26 February 2026, following publication of the Child Maintenance Guidelines on 19 January. The guidelines and accompanying calculator are a first for Ireland and a significant step forward to improving fairness, consistency and transparency when parents are making child maintenance arrangements. The child maintenance calculator is intended as a voluntary support tool to help parents begin the process of working out an appropriate amount of child maintenance for their child or children. The estimate provided by the calculator is not legally binding or enforceable, nor will it change an existing court order. It is a guide only. Child maintenance is calculated by looking at: each parent’s gross annual income; share of parenting time; the age/number of the children; and, the age/number of other dependent children each parent has. Significant costs related to disability, childcare, education or medical needs are not included in the child maintenance estimate. The variation in costs of this nature due to individual circumstances mean that they are not suited to inclusion in guidelines and a calculator such as this. These types of expenses are typically handled outside the standard way of calculating maintenance. This is in line with best practises observed internationally, where these costs are typically adjudicated outside the guidance framework. Costs of these expenses are typically shared equally between parents. Furthermore, given that the guidelines and calculator are formula based and rely on aggregate data to estimate average costs of children, they will not be appropriate in all cases. Particular circumstances where they may not be appropriate in estimating reasonable child maintenance payments include: • either parent has significant financial or other assets including property; • where non-parent carers, like grandparents, who may be involved in a child’s care are seeking maintenance; • a parent is paying child maintenance for more than one child where the children are from different relationships; • there are dependants with significant earnings, property or other financial resources; and • there are significant costs related to disability, childcare, education or medical needs. However, it may still help users to identify a potential rate of child maintenance or a starting point for discussion with the other parent. In summary, the key principles in the guidelines and calculator include: • shared financial responsibility – Both parents are expected to contribute to the cost of raising their child based on their means; • income shares model – Maintenance is based on the combined income of both parents, with each parent contributing a proportion that reflects their share of that income; • recognition of parenting time – The amount of time a child spends with each parent is considered, as share of parenting time directly influences the costs each parent has; • continuity of expenditure – Children should, as far as possible, continue to benefit from the standard of living they would have enjoyed if their parents were living together; and • protection of basic personal needs – A self-support amount, set at the level of the ‘at risk-of-poverty’ threshold, is included to ensure parents retain sufficient income for basic personal needs. Together, these principles aim to place the child at the centre of maintenance decisions. The calculator’s key parameters will be regularly updated, to take account of annual movements in the Consumer Price Index and the Central Statistics Office’s annual Survey on Income and Living Conditions. Such updates will include the costs per child by gross household income decile; the minimum rates; household income deciles, and the self-support allowance. Regular updating and indexation of key parameters will help ensure the model and calculator remain grounded in real-world data and reflect evolving expenditure patterns. Information will also be updated on the website www.childmaintenancecalculator.ie to ensure the purpose, benefits and limitations of the online calculator are clearly outlined and available.

question: 690. Deputy Fionntán Ó Súilleabháin asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he is prepared to follow the example of countries such as Sweden, and publish anonymised annual statistics on the nationality and immigration status of persons convicted of sexual-related offences in Ireland, in the interests of transparency, objectivity and better-informed policy discussions; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [21640/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Under the Policing, Security, and Community Safety Act 2024 the Garda Commissioner is responsible for the management and administration of Garda business, including the management of the PULSE system. I am advised by the Garda authorities that when information on a person's nationality is known, it is generally recorded as part of their PULSE record. I am further informed that An Garda Síochána is aligned with the practice of the Central Statistical Office (CSO) of not publishing or compiling crime statistics based on nationality, ethnicity or citizenship. Furthermore, the CSO is Ireland's national statistical agency is responsible for the compilation and publication of all crime statistics based on data recorded on An Garda Síochána’s PULSE system. The CSO is not a body under my aegis as Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration, and I have no role in the CSO's operations, functions, oversight or governance. However, the Deputy may be interested to know that the Programme for Government commits to the introduction of a common identification number for individuals in the criminal justice system. My Department is currently considering the legislative and technological updates required to introduce a unique identifier. The development of a single unique identifier will support a more joined-up, efficient and transparent criminal justice system. It will be particularly beneficial in the areas of data accuracy, enhanced data management and integrity, allowing more seamless information sharing and enhanced data collection. This will ultimately support research and help to inform both policy and service development.

question: 691. question: 696. Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the estimated full year cost if 1,400 new Gardaí were recruited; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [21855/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 696 and 705 together. Under section 33 of the Policing Security and Community Safety Act 2025, the Garda Commissioner is responsible for the administration and management of An Garda Síochána. This includes the recruitment, training and appointment of members of Garda personnel. The Commissioner is independent in his functions under section 34 of the Act. I am advised by the Garda authorities that the first year estimated payroll and fixed subsistence cost of recruiting 1,400 Garda is in the region of €45.8 million and to recruit 1,200 new Gardaí is approximately €39.3 million. This sum includes a basic training allowance for 35 weeks along with 17 weeks of post attestation salary in year 1 of employment, and an estimation of certain fixed allowances and variable unsocial hours’ allowances, employer’s PRSI and an estimate of subsistence paid during the trainees’ deployment to an operational station. Other costs, including the cost of equipment, training and accommodation are not included as these are covered and facilitated by the Garda college. It should also be noted that the estimated figures do not take account of potential overtime costs in excess of estimated briefing time payments or potential future pension costs. These figures are based on that assumption that the recruits commenced training on 1 January 2026.

question: 699. Deputy Louise O'Reilly asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of mandatory alcohol testing checkpoints run by An Garda Síochána during Christmas week 2025; and the number of detections of drink driving uncovered at these checkpoints, in tabular form. [21890/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Garda Commissioner is responsible for the management and administration of An Garda Síochána under Section 33 of the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024, which includes all operational policing matters. I play no role in these independent functions. Road traffic legislation is enforced as part of the day-to-day duties of members of An Garda Síochána, as well as through a programme of high-visibility road safety and enforcement operations carried out in partnership with other state agencies, in order to make our roads safer for all. An Garda Síochána carried out a dedicated road traffic enforcement operation throughout the 2025 Christmas period which began on Monday, 1 December 2025 and continued until Monday, 5 January 2026. During the course of the operation, An Garda Síochána carried out nearly 10,000 checkpoints, both statutory Mandatory Intoxicant Testing (MIT) and regular, high-visibility policing checkpoints. 765 people were arrested during this period for driving under the influence of an intoxicant (either alcohol and/or drugs). The Deputy may also be interested to note that An Garda Síochána publishes quarterly Road Policing statistics at the following link: https://www.garda.ie/en/roads-policing/statistics/roads%20policing%20offences%20by%20region%20and%20division/

question: 701. Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of heads of government, heads of state, ministers, governors, mayors or other senior elected officials he and Ministers of State in his Department met for the St. Patrick's Day engagements overseas this year. [21906/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 701, 702 and 703 together. St. Patrick’s Day provides an unparalleled opportunity to showcase Ireland on the global stage and to engage at the highest levels with political, business, civil society, cultural and diaspora leaders. As part of this year’s St. Patrick’s Day programme, I visited Greece. While it had been planned to also visit Cyprus as part of this visit, I did not, regrettably, travel to Nicosia as was scheduled. This was due to ongoing travel disruptions in the region, and consideration of the decision taken by the Cyprus Presidency to cancel all meetings in Cyprus during March. During my time abroad I met with my Greek counterparts, Minister for Justice, Giorgos Floridis, Minister of Citizen Protection, Michalis Chrysochoidis, Minister for Migration and Asylum, Athanasios Plevris and Minister of the Interior, Minister Theodoros Livanios. On 7 March, I met with representatives of the Irish diaspora in Greece when attending the St. Patrick’s Day Ball, hosted by the Greek Irish Society. The Greek Irish Society was founded in 1977 with that aim of developing social and cultural relations between the people of Ireland and of Greece. This ball brought together 300 guests from the diaspora, business, diplomatic and cultural communities. I did not formally meet on a bilateral basis any business representative organisations during St. Patrick’s Day travel in Greece. However, there were 25 individual business contacts in attendance at a reception event hosted by the Ambassador. My Colleague, Minister of State Colm Brophy TD travelled to Austria and Czechia as part of this year’s programme. During his time in Vienna, Minister Brophy met with the Austrian Minister for the Interior, Gerhard Karner. In Prague, Minister Brophy met with 1st Deputy Minister of the Interior, Lukáš Klucka, Chair of the Senate Committee on Foreign Affairs, Defence and Security, Senator Pavel Fischer, Deputy Minister for Justice Adam Šimice, Deputy Foreign Minister, Marie Chatardová and Lord Mayor of Prague, Bohuslav Svoboda. Minister Brophy also met with three members of the Subcommittee on Migration and Asylum in the Chamber of Deputies. This included Deputies Tomáš Helebrant, Denis Doksanský and Irena Fercíková Konecná. In both Vienna and Prague, Minister Brophy attended reception events hosted by the respective Ambassadors. These events were attended by Irish diaspora groups, such as the Vienna Gaels, the Austro-Irish Association and the Irish Ball committee. One of the groups met by Minister Brophy in Prague was a business representative organisation. In addition, there were 15 individual business contacts in attendance at the reception in Vienna and 9 in attendance at the reception in Prague. My colleague Minister of State Niall Collins TD did not travel for St. Patrick's Day this year.

question: 708. Deputy Peter 'Chap' Cleere asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of reported burglaries in Carlow and Kilkenny in 2023, 2024 and 2025; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [22037/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Central Statistics Office (CSO), as the national statistical agency, is responsible for the compilation and publication of all crime statistics. The CSO produces these statistics using data recorded on An Garda Síochána’s PULSE system and makes regular releases in relation to various crime statistics. The requested statistics can be found, by station, at the following link: https://data.cso.ie/table/CJA07 Alternatively, recorded crime statistics are published by the CSO at Garda Division level (including the Kildare/Carlow and Waterford/Kilkenny Divisions) quarterly for the Q1 2003 to Q3 2025 period: https://data.cso.ie/table/CJQ06 All reported incidents of burglary and theft are investigated by An Garda Síochána. As part of Budget 2026, Government provided an unprecedented €2.74 billion to An Garda Síochána to support them in preventing crime and keeping our communities safe. In recent years, an Garda Síochána have had unprecedented success in reducing and preventing burglaries through Operation Thor. In the 10 years since Operation Thor began, burglary and related offences have declined overall. The level of residential burglaries during the winter months, October to March, has fallen by a remarkable 75% since it started in 2015. Under Operation Thor, the Garda National Drugs and Organised Crime Bureau co-ordinates and supports Divisional resources with intelligence led-interventions that target organised crime gangs and repeat offenders, particularly involved in rural burglaries and crimes. Gardaí conduct high-visibility patrols and check-points at specific times of day in known ‘hot-spots’ to reduce the movement of burglars, gathering intelligence on known offenders and regularly communicating with the public about crime prevention measures. An Garda Síochána also provide the public with information and guidance on steps that can be taken by home owners to secure property and deter crime. The local Garda Crime Prevention Officers provide practical guidance to a range of people and businesses on deterring crime including burglary and theft.

question: 709. Deputy Peter 'Chap' Cleere asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of young persons referred to diversion programmes in Carlow and Kilkenny in 2025; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [22041/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Government’s focus on youth diversion and interventions is a keystone in the Youth Justice Strategy 2021-2027. The strategy emphasises early intervention, prevention, family support and community engagement. It is aimed at promoting positive behavioural change and targeting this behaviour so that we can break the cycle of offending by young people. The budget allocation for Youth Justice measures has increased by 144% from 2020 to 2026 with a significant allocation of €7.3 million in additional core exchequer funding for Youth Justice measures announced as part of Budget 2026 amounting to a total of €43 million. Part 4 of the Children Act 2001 (as amended) provides the statutory basis for the Garda Youth Diversion Programme. The intention of this programme is to divert children, aged 12-17 years old, who have engaged in criminal or anti-social behaviour away from the Criminal Justice system and towards more positive pro-social behaviour and life choices. Children who commit criminal offences are considered for admission to the Garda Diversion Programme, as provided in the Children Act 2001. Each such case is assessed and the Director of the Garda Diversion Programme (Garda Superintendent) decides if the case is suitable, or not, for inclusion in the Programme. The operation of the programme includes informal and formal Garda warnings, delivered in the presence of parents or guardians, as well as provision for supervision by a Garda Juvenile Liaison Officer. Young people deemed suitable by the Director of the Garda Youth Diversion Programme may be referred to local Youth Diversion Projects (YDPs), where in collaboration with a Garda Juvenile Liaison Officer these Projects provide supports to children to address their behaviour and engage in positive self-development and engagement in their communities. YDPs are community based, multi-agency youth crime prevention initiatives which primarily seek to divert young people who have been, or are at risk of becoming, involved in anti-social and/or criminal behaviour. There are currently two 2 YDPs in Carlow and Kilkenny, COMPASS YDP and HUB YDP, which my Department funds to a combined sum of €451,475. With these funds, the YDPs employ dedicated Youth Justice Workers who respond to the needs of young people in Carlow and Kilkenny. As per the last available records, in 2024, 72 young people engaged with COMPASS YDP and HUB YDP in that calendar year. Every young person in Carlow and Kilkenny, and across the country, now has access to a YDP service. Participant numbers for 2025 are expected to be available in quarter two of 2026.

question: 710. Deputy Thomas Gould asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the stages of a citizenship application; and the average processing time for each stage. [22096/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration My Department does not collate processing times for each individual stage of the naturalisation process and, as such, it is not possible to provide a breakdown of timelines by stage as requested. My Department does track the overall processing time for naturalisation applications. The median processing time for a decision on an application in 2024 and 2025 has been approximately 8 months. This is a significant improvement from the median processing time of 15 months in 2023, 19 months in 2022, and 24 months in 2021. Despite a substantial increase in applications received in recent years, the fact that processing times have significantly reduced is a huge credit to the work of my Department. While no two naturalisation applications are the same and some take longer than others to process, I expect that, going forward, most applicants will receive a decision within one year, although this cannot be guaranteed in the case of every individual application.

question: 711. Deputy Alan Kelly asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration his plans to improve An Garda Síochána resources in the mid-west. [22126/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Garda Commissioner is responsible for the management and allocation of Garda resources. I am assured by the Commissioner that when allocating Garda resources, consideration is given to commitments and undertakings outlined in the Annual Policing Plan. The requirements of all Garda Divisions nationwide are also taken into account, which include: • Local and national crime trends and workloads • Policing arrangements and operational strategies • Local population and trends, geographical area and size • Transfer applications, including welfare, personnel issues and concerns. Under Budget 2026, I secured record funding of €2.74 billion for An Garda Síochána to support recruitment and staffing. This will support recruitment of up to 1,000 Gardai, 200 more Garda staff and additional members of the Garda Reserve. At the end of January 2026, the latest date for which figures are available, the total Garda workforce stood at over 18,000, which included 14,397 Gardaí, 3,527 Garda Staff, and 308 Garda Reserves. Significant initiatives have been taken to boost recruitment and as reflected in the number of applications received to join An Garda Síochána, we are already seeing the impact of these changes. Just under 800 trainees entered the Garda College in 2025, the highest number since 2018. Recruitment into An Garda Síochána is now gathering real momentum and with a strong pipeline in place, I am looking forward to seeing large numbers attesting from the Garda college throughout 2026. In 2025, there were 54 probationer Gardaí assigned to the Limerick, Clare and Tipperary Divisions, and 15 assigned to date in 2026. In addition it should be noted that the recruitment and attestation of more Gardai supports and facilitates the allocation and transfer of Gardaí to all parts of the country and I am confident that as overall numbers rise more Gardaí will be available for deployment in all areas.

question: 712. Deputy Alan Kelly asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the actions he is taking to improve recruitment and retention of Gardaí. [22127/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration At the end of January 2026, the latest date for which figures are available, the total Garda workforce stood at over 18,000, which included 14,397 Gardaí, 3,527 Garda Staff, and 308 Garda Reserves. Under Budget 2026, I secured record funding of €2.74 billion for An Garda Síochána to support recruitment and staffing. Significant initiatives have been taken to boost recruitment including increasing the Garda trainee allowance to €354 per week; increasing the maximum age of entry from 35 to 50; and increasing the mandatory retirement age to 62. Recruitment timeframes have also been shortened, the physical competency test has been reformed and two recruitment competitions were held in 2025. As reflected in the number of applications received to join An Garda Síochána we are already seeing the impact of these changes. Last year, 619 Gardaí attested from the Garda College to take up positions in communities across the country as they began a career of service to their communities and to the people of Ireland. Just under 800 trainees entered the Garda College in 2025, the highest number since 2018. Recruitment into An Garda Síochána is now gathering real momentum and with a strong pipeline in place, I am looking forward to seeing large numbers attesting from the Garda college throughout 2026. I am also pleased to say that the level of resignation from An Garda Síochána is low in comparison to other employments in the public and private sectors and when compared to police services internationally. While very low, in order to better understand any resignations, and to inform measures which could aid retention, Garda management have introduced an exit interview process. The increase in the retirement age to 62 has resulted in some Gardaí remaining in service for longer and I have also approved applications for extensions beyond 62, where recommended by the Garda Commissioner. The high level of applications to join An Garda Síochána received in 2025 demonstrates that there is a strong and sustained interest in a career as a Garda amongst the public. A further recruitment competition will be run this year to ensure that there is a steady pipeline of new recruits ready to enter the Garda College. I want to commend the Garda Commissioner and his team who have worked with publicjobs and my own Department to transform the recruitment process. I am satisfied that the work done over recent years has ensured that the huge interest in a career in An Garda Síochána translates into more Gardaí on our streets and in our communities.

question: 719. Deputy Colm Burke asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the status of an application (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [22161/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The naturalisation application referred to by the Deputy continues to be processed by my Department. I understand that extended wait times can be frustrating for applicants. I want to assure anyone who has an application for naturalisation submitted that the Citizenship Division of my Department is doing everything possible to progress applications as quickly as possible. It is important to note, however, that no two naturalisation applications are the same and some take longer than others to process. Given the importance of citizenship, robust and comprehensive checks must take place on each application. Unfortunately, some checks, such as international checks, can take a considerable amount of time and these are largely outside of the control of the Immigration Service. For that reason, while, I expect that going forward, that most applicants will receive a decision within one year, this cannot be guaranteed in the case of applications made in any specific year. Citizenship Division have taken a significant number of steps to improve up the process for applicants. These included introducing an online digital application, online payments, and the introduction of eVetting. I am pleased to inform the Deputy that these changes are reducing processing times. Applicants can now directly check the status of their immigration application on the Immigration Service’s Customer Service Portal. They can register for, or log in to their existing account, at: https://portal.irishimmigration.ie/en/ As an Oireachtas member, you can also request the status of individual immigration cases by e-mail, using the Oireachtas Mail facility at: IMoireachtasmail@justice.ie, which has been specifically established for this purpose. This service enables up to date information on such cases to be obtained without the need to seek information by way of the Parliamentary Question process.

question: 720. An Garda Síochána publishes figures in relation to the allocation of Garda personnel nationally. This includes a breakdown of Gardaí by rank and Division from 2009 to the end of January 2026, the latest date for which figures are available. This information can be found at the following links: 2014-2025 https://www.garda.ie/en/about-us/our-departments/human-resources-and-people-development/garda-hr-directorate/garda-strength-breakdown-2025/garda-strength-breakdown-2025.html 2026 https://www.garda.ie/en/about-us/our-departments/human-resources-and-people-development/garda-hr-directorate/garda-strength-breakdown-2026/january-2026.html The Deputy should select the current month and access the file titled “ Garda Members by Division District Station ” for a breakdown of total Garda numbers by rank and Division. I am assured that policing for an area is delivered using all the resources in a particular Community Engagement Area, supported by both divisional and national resources and units, as appropriate.

question: 721. Deputy Máire Devine asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the preparatory work that is underway to transpose the EU Directive on Combating Violence against Women and Domestic Violence, particularly provisions relating to technology-facilitated violence. [21630/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The EU Directive on combatting violence against women and domestic violence was adopted in May 2024, and will enter into force in June 2027. The purpose of the Violence Against Women Directive is to provide a comprehensive framework to effectively prevent and combat violence against women and domestic violence throughout the European Union. The measures under the Directive are designed to address the specific needs of women and girls, given that, as confirmed by data and studies, they are disproportionately affected by the forms of violence covered by this Directive. Combatting all forms of domestic, sexual and gender-based violence (DSGBV) is an absolute priority for this government. Last year Government approved the drafting of the Sexual Offences, Domestic Violence and International Instruments Bill 2025. Among other things, the provisions in this Bill will remove dual criminality in respect of certain offences, including female genital mutilation (FGM) and forced marriage, which is a requirement under the Directive. The General Scheme of this Bill underwent pre-legislative scrutiny by the Joint Committee on Justice, Home Affairs and Migration on 20 January 2026. The recommendations of the Committee will be carefully considered once received, with drafting of the Bill prioritised. Many of the provisions contained in the Directive are already provided for under existing Irish legislation or in the aforementioned Bill. However, work is underway to determine what further legislative reforms may be required to fully transpose the Directive. In relation to the technology facilitated violence provisions, several of these provisions are already transposed by the Harassment, Harmful Communications and Related Offences Act 2020 (Coco’s Law) and the Non-Fatal Offences Against the Person Act 1997. However, my Department is consulting with the Attorney General’s Office to identify any additional legislative amendments which may be required in order to ensure that Ireland is fully compliant with the Directive.

question: 722. Deputy Gary Gannon asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the reason the proposals in the general scheme of the Civil Reform Bill 2025 concerning judicial review go beyond the judicial review recommendations of the Review of the Administration of Civil Justice and the Law Reform Commission; the reason his Department has not yet published an explanatory memorandum in relation to the heads of the general scheme; whether his Department will publish an explanatory memorandum in relation to the heads of the general scheme; whether it will publish an evidence-based policy rationale for each of the changes proposed; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [22176/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration (Deputy Jim O'Callaghan) I propose to take Questions Nos. 722 to 727, inclusive, together. On 16 December 2025, the Government approved the General Scheme of the Civil Reform Bill 2025. The General Scheme has been submitted for pre legislative scrutiny, and I understand the Justice Committee is consider the general scheme on Tuesday 24 March. Subject to drafting, it is intended to publish the Bill in Quarter 3 2026 and, in line with commitments in the Accelerating Infrastructure Report and Action Plan , and subject to Oireachtas approval, have the Bill enacted no later than Quarter 2 2027. An explanatory memorandum will be published to accompany the Bill. The Civil Reform Bill is the legislative implementation vehicle for the Kelly Report recommendations. As part of the Kelly Review process, stakeholder consultation was undertaken through an open call for submissions. The Irish Human Rights and Equality Commission furnished a submission to the Review. The General Scheme was the subject of a presentation and discussion at the legal costs module of the Cost of Business Advisory Forum, chaired by Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment. It is intended to conduct further stakeholder engagement in advance of publication of the Bill. The Review process also considered Courts Service data available relating to caseloads in various areas of litigation including judicial review. Further review of more recent caseload data available relating to judicial review and other areas has been undertaken as the General Scheme was developed. In certain areas the scheme goes beyond the Kelly Report recommendations, taking into account the time passed since the recommendations were reported in 2020 and the evolving requirements for reform of civil procedures, court jurisdiction and of judicial review, particularly in the context of accelerating infrastructure measures and forthcoming changes relating to asylum and migration. The Department is compliant with its obligations under section 42 of the Irish Human Rights and Equality Commission Act 2014. Amongst a range of improvements to civil law procedures, the Bill will codify the existing law on judicial review, placing it on a statutory basis. Key reforms should ensure that the system cannot be misused on purely technical grounds, costs are reduced where possible and litigants have sufficient standing to properly challenge decisions. Given the significant challenges currently facing our State in terms of housing shortages, energy deficits, inadequate water supplies and climate changes, all of which are exacerbated by the demands of a rising population, we can no longer delay on reform of the judicial review system. I am confident that the Civil Reform Bill will remove weaknesses in the current Judicial Review regime, eliminate impediments to progress and deliver reform for the public benefit. I am also confident that measures in the Bill preserve the right of the citizen to ensure that public bodies act lawfully and are accountable for their decisions. Another major area of reform in the Bill is in relation to Discovery, which will be replaced with a system of Production of Documents focused on those documents which parties intend to, or are reasonably likely to, rely on at trial. The Kelly Report found that economically stronger parties frequently weaponised the current discovery regime to effectively impede the less well-resourced party in the conduct of proceedings. The reforms I am introducing should minimise both delay and cost in the conduct of civil litigation in the State and achieve greater equality between parties . The proposed Bill, in implementing the recommendations of the Kelly Report, will also provide for a suite of civil reform measures including the creation of case conduct principles, a presumption against granting of adjournments, limiting the term of a Lis Pendens; deemed discontinuance of civil actions and a requirement for plaintiffs in personal injuries actions to distinguish between pre-existing injuries and those which are the subject of the claim. Further, the Bill will amend the general monetary jurisdiction of the District Court from €15,000 to €20,000, the Circuit Court generally from €75,000 to €100,000 and for Personal Injuries proceedings from €60,000 to €100,000. These changes will result in more non-complex cases being heard in lower courts, in particular Personal Injuries cases, and should reduce legal costs.

The reforms I am introducing should minimise both delay and cost in the conduct of civil litigation in the State and achieve greater equality between parties . The proposed Bill, in implementing the recommendations of the Kelly Report, will also provide for a suite of civil reform measures including the creation of case conduct principles, a presumption against granting of adjournments, limiting the term of a Lis Pendens; deemed discontinuance of civil actions and a requirement for plaintiffs in personal injuries actions to distinguish between pre-existing injuries and those which are the subject of the claim. Further, the Bill will amend the general monetary jurisdiction of the District Court from €15,000 to €20,000, the Circuit Court generally from €75,000 to €100,000 and for Personal Injuries proceedings from €60,000 to €100,000. These changes will result in more non-complex cases being heard in lower courts, in particular Personal Injuries cases, and should reduce legal costs.

question: 726. Deputy Gary Gannon asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the intended timeline for the finalisation, introduction to the Houses of the Oireachtas and enactment of the Civil Reform Bill 2025; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [22180/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration (Deputy Jim O'Callaghan) I propose to take Questions Nos. 722 to 727, inclusive, together. On 16 December 2025, the Government approved the General Scheme of the Civil Reform Bill 2025. The General Scheme has been submitted for pre legislative scrutiny, and I understand the Justice Committee is consider the general scheme on Tuesday 24 March. Subject to drafting, it is intended to publish the Bill in Quarter 3 2026 and, in line with commitments in the Accelerating Infrastructure Report and Action Plan , and subject to Oireachtas approval, have the Bill enacted no later than Quarter 2 2027. An explanatory memorandum will be published to accompany the Bill. The Civil Reform Bill is the legislative implementation vehicle for the Kelly Report recommendations. As part of the Kelly Review process, stakeholder consultation was undertaken through an open call for submissions. The Irish Human Rights and Equality Commission furnished a submission to the Review. The General Scheme was the subject of a presentation and discussion at the legal costs module of the Cost of Business Advisory Forum, chaired by Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment. It is intended to conduct further stakeholder engagement in advance of publication of the Bill. The Review process also considered Courts Service data available relating to caseloads in various areas of litigation including judicial review. Further review of more recent caseload data available relating to judicial review and other areas has been undertaken as the General Scheme was developed. In certain areas the scheme goes beyond the Kelly Report recommendations, taking into account the time passed since the recommendations were reported in 2020 and the evolving requirements for reform of civil procedures, court jurisdiction and of judicial review, particularly in the context of accelerating infrastructure measures and forthcoming changes relating to asylum and migration. The Department is compliant with its obligations under section 42 of the Irish Human Rights and Equality Commission Act 2014. Amongst a range of improvements to civil law procedures, the Bill will codify the existing law on judicial review, placing it on a statutory basis. Key reforms should ensure that the system cannot be misused on purely technical grounds, costs are reduced where possible and litigants have sufficient standing to properly challenge decisions. Given the significant challenges currently facing our State in terms of housing shortages, energy deficits, inadequate water supplies and climate changes, all of which are exacerbated by the demands of a rising population, we can no longer delay on reform of the judicial review system. I am confident that the Civil Reform Bill will remove weaknesses in the current Judicial Review regime, eliminate impediments to progress and deliver reform for the public benefit. I am also confident that measures in the Bill preserve the right of the citizen to ensure that public bodies act lawfully and are accountable for their decisions. Another major area of reform in the Bill is in relation to Discovery, which will be replaced with a system of Production of Documents focused on those documents which parties intend to, or are reasonably likely to, rely on at trial. The Kelly Report found that economically stronger parties frequently weaponised the current discovery regime to effectively impede the less well-resourced party in the conduct of proceedings. The reforms I am introducing should minimise both delay and cost in the conduct of civil litigation in the State and achieve greater equality between parties . The proposed Bill, in implementing the recommendations of the Kelly Report, will also provide for a suite of civil reform measures including the creation of case conduct principles, a presumption against granting of adjournments, limiting the term of a Lis Pendens; deemed discontinuance of civil actions and a requirement for plaintiffs in personal injuries actions to distinguish between pre-existing injuries and those which are the subject of the claim. Further, the Bill will amend the general monetary jurisdiction of the District Court from €15,000 to €20,000, the Circuit Court generally from €75,000 to €100,000 and for Personal Injuries proceedings from €60,000 to €100,000. These changes will result in more non-complex cases being heard in lower courts, in particular Personal Injuries cases, and should reduce legal costs.

question: 728. Deputy Liam Quaide asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration his plans to monitor the real-world implications of use of the child maintenance calculator to ensure it reflects the real cost of raising children; the role he intends the child maintenance calculator to play in judicial decision-making; if he plans for future iterations to include education, childcare, medical and disability related costs; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [22201/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 688 and 728 together. The development of the Child Maintenance Guidelines was a key recommendation of the 2024 Review of the Enforcement of Child Maintenance Orders. An interdepartmental group (“The Child Maintenance Guidelines Committee”) was established in February 2024 to develop the child maintenance guidelines for use by all parties, on a voluntary basis, when putting child maintenance arrangements in place. The Committee was Chaired by my Department and its membership included representatives from the Department of Social Protection, Department of Children, Disability and Equality, Legal Aid Board, Courts Service and Tusla. Development of the guidelines was informed by a comprehensive comparative review covering England and Wales, Scotland, Northern Ireland, United States, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Germany, Austria, Denmark and the Netherlands. It was also critically important to listen to the views of parents who have been involved in making child maintenance arrangements. For this reason, in April 2025, the Committee conducted a survey-based consultation to get the public's views on important aspects of the guidelines. The published guidelines along with a comparative review of guidelines in other jurisdictions and a public consultation report can be accessed at the following link: www.gov.ie/en/department-of-justice-home-affairs-and-migration/publications/child-maintenance-guidelines-for-ireland/ The Guidelines are compatible with Irish legislation on child maintenance and can be used by the courts. However, the courts are not obliged to consider the guidelines when making child maintenance orders. The objectives of the Guidelines include: • to establish fair, consistent and predictable amounts of maintenance for children whose parents are not together. • to increase transparency, consistency and predictability for those seeking and paying child maintenance. • to reduce conflict and tension between parents by making the calculation of child maintenance more objective. • to reduce the number of child maintenance applications made to the courts by giving parents guidance in setting the levels of child maintenance and by encouraging private maintenance agreements. • to ensure consistent treatment of parents and children who are in similar circumstances. • to promote a culture of payment of child maintenance. The child maintenance calculator was launched on 26 February 2026, following publication of the Child Maintenance Guidelines on 19 January. The guidelines and accompanying calculator are a first for Ireland and a significant step forward to improving fairness, consistency and transparency when parents are making child maintenance arrangements. The child maintenance calculator is intended as a voluntary support tool to help parents begin the process of working out an appropriate amount of child maintenance for their child or children. The estimate provided by the calculator is not legally binding or enforceable, nor will it change an existing court order. It is a guide only. Child maintenance is calculated by looking at: each parent’s gross annual income; share of parenting time; the age/number of the children; and, the age/number of other dependent children each parent has. Significant costs related to disability, childcare, education or medical needs are not included in the child maintenance estimate. The variation in costs of this nature due to individual circumstances mean that they are not suited to inclusion in guidelines and a calculator such as this. These types of expenses are typically handled outside the standard way of calculating maintenance. This is in line with best practises observed internationally, where these costs are typically adjudicated outside the guidance framework. Costs of these expenses are typically shared equally between parents. Furthermore, given that the guidelines and calculator are formula based and rely on aggregate data to estimate average costs of children, they will not be appropriate in all cases. Particular circumstances where they may not be appropriate in estimating reasonable child maintenance payments include: • either parent has significant financial or other assets including property; • where non-parent carers, like grandparents, who may be involved in a child’s care are seeking maintenance; • a parent is paying child maintenance for more than one child where the children are from different relationships; • there are dependants with significant earnings, property or other financial resources; and • there are significant costs related to disability, childcare, education or medical needs. However, it may still help users to identify a potential rate of child maintenance or a starting point for discussion with the other parent. In summary, the key principles in the guidelines and calculator include: • shared financial responsibility – Both parents are expected to contribute to the cost of raising their child based on their means; • income shares model – Maintenance is based on the combined income of both parents, with each parent contributing a proportion that reflects their share of that income; • recognition of parenting time – The amount of time a child spends with each parent is considered, as share of parenting time directly influences the costs each parent has; • continuity of expenditure – Children should, as far as possible, continue to benefit from the standard of living they would have enjoyed if their parents were living together; and • protection of basic personal needs – A self-support amount, set at the level of the ‘at risk-of-poverty’ threshold, is included to ensure parents retain sufficient income for basic personal needs. Together, these principles aim to place the child at the centre of maintenance decisions. The calculator’s key parameters will be regularly updated, to take account of annual movements in the Consumer Price Index and the Central Statistics Office’s annual Survey on Income and Living Conditions. Such updates will include the costs per child by gross household income decile; the minimum rates; household income deciles, and the self-support allowance. Regular updating and indexation of key parameters will help ensure the model and calculator remain grounded in real-world data and reflect evolving expenditure patterns. Information will also be updated on the website www.childmaintenancecalculator.ie to ensure the purpose, benefits and limitations of the online calculator are clearly outlined and available.

question: 729. Deputy Martin Kenny asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if a person (details supplied) who has encountered long delays with their citizenship application will be awarded this in the near future; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [22229/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The naturalisation application cited was returned to the person concerned on 3 March 2026 as it was incomplete. This may either mean that some documents are missing or some of the documents submitted are not satisfactory. I can advise the Deputy that in cases where incomplete naturalisation applications are received, the application is returned to the applicant with a request to provide the missing documentation within 28 days. A reminder is issued after 18 days if the required documentation has still not been provided. My Department has produced a comprehensive guidance document for all potential applicants, outlining all the documents required for an application. This document is published on my Department's Immigration website and is available here: https://www.irishimmigration.ie/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/Citizenship-Guidance-Document-April-2024.pdf Detailed information on how to apply for naturalisation and other resources is available here: https://www.irishimmigration.ie/how-to-become-a-citizen/. As an Oireachtas member, you can also request the status of individual immigration cases by e-mail, using the Oireachtas Mail facility at: IMoireachtasmail@justice.ie, which has been specifically established for this purpose. This service enables up to date information on such cases to be obtained without the need to seek information by way of the Parliamentary Question process.

question: 730. Deputy Conor D. McGuinness asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of marked and unmarked Garda vans attached to Waterford-Kilkenny Division as of 18 March 2026, in tabular form. [22290/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Garda Commissioner is responsible for the management and administration of An Garda Síochána under Section 33 of the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024. This includes all operational policing and responsibility for the allocation and deployment of resources and personnel available to him, including the Garda fleet. I am informed by the Garda authorities that, as of 28 February 2026, the latest date for which figures are available, there were 3,658 vehicles attached to the overall Garda fleet. Garda authorities have provided the below table which shows the number of marked and unmarked Garda vans attached to Waterford/Kilkenny Division. Waterford/Kilkenny Division Marked Unmarked Total 19 14 33 An Garda Síochána publishes detailed information on the Garda fleet from 2008 to date, including a Divisional/District monthly breakdown. Monthly Fleet reports are currently available from 2020 to February 2026. This is publicly available on their website at the following link: https://www.garda.ie/en/about-us/our-departments/finance-services/finance-fleet-management.html The purchase and allocation of vehicles by An Garda Síochána is made on the basis of identified operational demands, the availability of resources and is reviewed on a continual basis.

question: 731. Deputy Martin Daly asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of Gardaí assigned to the Roscommon-Galway constituency compared to the sanctioned strength, and any plans to increase Garda resources in the area. [22330/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration An Garda Síochána publishes information in relation to the allocation of Gardaí nationally. This includes a breakdown of Gardaí assigned by Garda Stations from 2009 to the end of January 2026, the latest date for which figures are available. Information for 2026 can be found at the following link: https://www.garda.ie/en/about-us/our-departments/human-resources-and-people-development/garda-hr-directorate/garda-strength-breakdown-2026/january-2026.html Information for previous years can be found at the following link: https://www.garda.ie/en/about-us/our-departments/human-resources-and-people-development/garda-hr-directorate/garda-strength-breakdown-2025/december-2025.html The Deputy should select the most recently available date and then select the file titled ‘Garda Members by Division, District, Station" to access a breakdown of members assigned. An Garda Síochána is not aligned operationally to Dáil Éireann Constituency boundaries but rather by Garda Divisions. As a result, figures by constituency are not available. The Garda Commissioner is responsible for the management and administration of An Garda Síochána under section 33 of the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024, which includes the distribution and stationing of Garda personnel throughout the State. While I regularly engage with the Commissioner, I cannot direct him on the allocation of Gardaí as this matter is reserved to him by law. I am assured by the Garda Commissioner that the allocation of Garda resources is kept under continued review to ensure their optimum use. Among the factors considered are crime trends, population statistics and operational policing demands. I am informed that when allocating resources, consideration is also given to commitments and undertakings outlined in the Annual Policing Plan. Under Budget 2026, I secured record funding of €2.74 billion for An Garda Síochána to support recruitment and staffing. Interest in a career as a Garda remains high, with over 11,000 applications received last year across two recruitment campaigns. Just under 800 trainees entered the Garda College in 2025, the highest number since 2018. Recruitment into An Garda Síochána is now gathering real momentum and with a strong pipeline in place, I am looking forward to seeing large numbers attesting from the Garda college throughout 2026 which will result in more Gardaí on our streets and in our communities.

question: 732. Deputy Martin Daly asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the average Garda response time to incidents in rural parts of the Roscommon–Galway constituency over the past 12 months, in tabular form. [22331/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I am informed by Garda authorities that data from the GardaSAFE computer aided dispatch system is not yet supported by An Garda Síochána’s Analysis Service and therefore the information requested cannot be supplied at this time. GardaSAFE was rolled out incrementally across the organisation in 2023. The initial focus has been on bedding in the new system and processes in the live operational environment in the Control Rooms to monitor call volumes etc. Work is now commencing on use of GardaSAFE data for statistical purposes. Garda authorities expect initial reports on call volumes to be available in Q3 2026, with the incremental development of other reports to follow. I am advised that An Garda Síochána operates a Regional Control Room strategy which ensures that Garda resources are available to respond to calls for service from the public, including situations where a local resource is not immediately available. Calls for service, whether received through a local Garda station or the 999 ECAS system, are routed through the Regional Control Rooms and prioritised for response. Higher priority calls will always take priority over lower priority calls. The Garda authorities inform me that An Garda Síochána aim is to answer 80% of 999 calls within 7 seconds and deploy resources immediately giving an estimated time of arrival. An Garda Síochána will take appropriate steps to deal with all incidents and ensure that emergency and life threatening calls receive priority. They will endeavour to get to callers within 15 minutes in urban locations and as soon as possible, given the distance to be travelled, in more rural areas.

question: 733. Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the name of the individual or individuals who chaired and were members of the Garda Vetting Review Group since its establishment in April 2021. [22366/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 733, 734 and 735 together. The primary purpose of vetting carried out by the Garda National Vetting Bureau is to ensure the safety of children and vulnerable adults. Clearly, this requires a robust Garda vetting process that reassures the public, and in particular parents, that appropriate checks are conducted on people taking on positions of trust. The Interdepartmental Vetting Review Group was chaired by my Department and comprised representatives of the following Departments and Agencies: • An Garda Síochána • Tusla • Public Appointments Service • Department of Education • Department of Children, Equality, Disability, Integration and Youth • Department of Housing, Planning and Local Government • Health Service Executive • Department of Foreign Affairs. The initial focus of the Group' work was the introduction of a system for re-vetting, as well as a review of the approach to vetting for specific employments, to streamline, as far as possible, the administrative arrangements, without compromising the safety of children and vulnerable adults. As the group moved ahead with its work, additional issues were raised and considered. The group took a careful and thorough approach, as was necessary in meeting its aim of ensuring that the vetting system remains robust and effective as a crucial safeguard for the most vulnerable members of society, that is children and vulnerable adults, while also improving the service to customers. Ultimately, the group did not agree a report, however I was provided with details of its work and it is clear that aspects of the current vetting system result in a highly-segmented process. I believe that the vetting system should be updated to ensure that the burden of seeking vetting disclosures, particularly on volunteers and organisations working in their communities, is minimised to the greatest extent possible, while maintaining the necessary high standards for this process. I have therefore directed that steps be taken to implement a number of key changes, specifically in relation to re-vetting and the portability of vetting. In practice, and subject to a general requirement that vetting be renewed every three years, it is envisaged that this will mean that when a person is vetted for the work they will be or are likely to be involved in as part of their employment or volunteering within identified risk categories, that individual would not be required to repeat the process if they were to move to another role within the same risk category. These changes will require amending legislation and updated technical systems to support the revised approach, to make the process more efficient for volunteers and organisations, without compromising the essential safeguards that protect those in our care. My Department continues to engage with the Garda National Vetting Bureau on the detailed work of developing the necessary legislative and technical steps to meet these goals in a way that is workable in practice. It is my objective to ensure that the vetting system is fit for purpose and, to the greatest extent possible, efficient and future-proofed to continue to protect our children and vulnerable adults.
