question: 736. Deputy Alan Kelly asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if his Department is aware of any occasions where any person or organisation has unlawfully intercepted communications that is contrary to the provisions of the Interception of Postal Packets and Telecommunications Messages (Regulation) Act 1993 since its enactment. [22425/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 736, 737 and 738 together. As the Deputy is aware, in Ireland, lawful interception is governed by the Interception of Postal Packets and Telecommunications Messages (Regulation) 1993. The Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration may authorise bodies designated under the Act to lawfully intercept communications for the purposes of investigating serious crime or safeguarding the security of the State. Under section 6 of the Act, an application for authorisation of interception may be made by the Garda Commissioner, the Chief of Staff of the Defence Forces, or the Police Ombudsman. Use of the 1993 Act is subject to a number of strict conditions including that investigations not involving interception have failed, or are likely to fail, to produce the necessary information or evidence; that the intelligence resulting from an interception would be of material assistance and that it is justified, notwithstanding the importance of preserving privacy. Section 12 of the 1993 Act restricts disclosure in respect of lawful interception authorisations and it places a requirement on the Minister to ensure that such arrangements are in place to limit to the minimum necessary for the purpose of the prevention or detection of serious offences or in the interests of the security of the State, the disclosure of the fact that an authorisation has been given, and the contents of any communication which has been intercepted pursuant to an authorisation. It is not the practice, and it would be contrary to the public interest, to disclose detail of any authorisations to intercept or indeed to comment on the specific details of any means that may be used by State agencies in exercising statutory lawful interception powers. The operation of the Act is overseen independently by the Independent Examiner of Security Legislation, the office for which was established by the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024. The Independent Examiner is to keep under review compliance by the competent authorities with the requirements of the Act and report annually to the Taoiseach. The Independent Examiner's reports are required to be laid before the Houses of the Oireachtas. Prior to the establishment of the Independent Examiner, this role was previously carried out by Judges of the High Court as Designated Judges for the purposes of the Act. There is also a statutory Complaints Referee who can receive and investigate any complaints made relating to lawful interception. In carrying out his functions, the Complaints Referee has, by law, full access to people and records he considers relevant to his investigations and my officials have a duty to cooperate with him. While still appropriate and in use today, the 1993 Act does not apply to modern digital communications. I recently announced that the Government had approved my proposals to draft a new Communications (Interception and Lawful Access) Bill which will update and replace the current Act. This is essential to ensure that the law in this area can yield the intelligence that is vital to combat serious and organised crime and threats to the security of the State, including terrorism. The new legislation will include further legal safeguards and will, for the first time, make provision for judicial authorisation of interception requests. There will also be a requirement that agencies requesting an interception will have to outline any issues with regard to privileged material.

question: 737. Deputy Alan Kelly asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he will ensure that no Member of the current Houses of the Oireachtas has had their phone calls or other forms of personal or business communications listened to, copied or intercepted; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [22426/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 736, 737 and 738 together. As the Deputy is aware, in Ireland, lawful interception is governed by the Interception of Postal Packets and Telecommunications Messages (Regulation) 1993. The Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration may authorise bodies designated under the Act to lawfully intercept communications for the purposes of investigating serious crime or safeguarding the security of the State. Under section 6 of the Act, an application for authorisation of interception may be made by the Garda Commissioner, the Chief of Staff of the Defence Forces, or the Police Ombudsman. Use of the 1993 Act is subject to a number of strict conditions including that investigations not involving interception have failed, or are likely to fail, to produce the necessary information or evidence; that the intelligence resulting from an interception would be of material assistance and that it is justified, notwithstanding the importance of preserving privacy. Section 12 of the 1993 Act restricts disclosure in respect of lawful interception authorisations and it places a requirement on the Minister to ensure that such arrangements are in place to limit to the minimum necessary for the purpose of the prevention or detection of serious offences or in the interests of the security of the State, the disclosure of the fact that an authorisation has been given, and the contents of any communication which has been intercepted pursuant to an authorisation. It is not the practice, and it would be contrary to the public interest, to disclose detail of any authorisations to intercept or indeed to comment on the specific details of any means that may be used by State agencies in exercising statutory lawful interception powers. The operation of the Act is overseen independently by the Independent Examiner of Security Legislation, the office for which was established by the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024. The Independent Examiner is to keep under review compliance by the competent authorities with the requirements of the Act and report annually to the Taoiseach. The Independent Examiner's reports are required to be laid before the Houses of the Oireachtas. Prior to the establishment of the Independent Examiner, this role was previously carried out by Judges of the High Court as Designated Judges for the purposes of the Act. There is also a statutory Complaints Referee who can receive and investigate any complaints made relating to lawful interception. In carrying out his functions, the Complaints Referee has, by law, full access to people and records he considers relevant to his investigations and my officials have a duty to cooperate with him. While still appropriate and in use today, the 1993 Act does not apply to modern digital communications. I recently announced that the Government had approved my proposals to draft a new Communications (Interception and Lawful Access) Bill which will update and replace the current Act. This is essential to ensure that the law in this area can yield the intelligence that is vital to combat serious and organised crime and threats to the security of the State, including terrorism. The new legislation will include further legal safeguards and will, for the first time, make provision for judicial authorisation of interception requests. There will also be a requirement that agencies requesting an interception will have to outline any issues with regard to privileged material.

question: 739. Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the Garda to population ratio in each county. [22453/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Garda Commissioner is responsible for the management and administration of An Garda Síochána under Section 33 of the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024, which includes the distribution and stationing of Garda personnel throughout the State. An Garda Síochána police on a Divisional basis, and not on the basis of population, using all resources in a Community Engagement area, supported by Divisional resources and units. This Operating Model has been designed to enable An Garda Síochána to meet the challenges of modern-day policing more consistently around the country by enabling specialisation in the delivery of key services and freeing up more Gardaí to focus on front line policing. Under this structure, each Division is organised into four Functional Areas: Community Engagement, Crime, Performance Assurance, and Business Services. The model, coupled with some realignment of responsibilities, is helping to deliver a consistent, community-focused policing service. This reflects best international practice and will ensure that each Division has the resources and skills to deliver a wider range of community policing and specialist services based on the demands in their area. The service provided to local communities remains 24/7. I regularly engage with the Garda Commissioner to ensure our Gardaí have the resources they need. I am informed that when allocating and transferring Garda members to and from any Division, consideration is given to commitments and undertakings outlined in the Annual Policing Plan and priorities as determined in delivering ‘A Policing Service for The Future’. The Deputy may be interested to note that Garda authorities advise that the requirements of all Garda Divisions nationwide are also taken into account, which include: • Local and national crime trends and workloads; • Policing arrangements and operational strategies; • Minimum establishment statistics; • Local population and trends, geographical area and size; • Transfer applications, including welfare, personnel issues and concerns. An Garda Síochána publishes information in relation to the allocation of Gardaí nationally. This includes a breakdown of Gardaí assigned by Garda Stations from 2009 to the end of January 2026, the latest date for which figures are available. Information for 2026 can be found at the following link: https://www.garda.ie/en/about-us/our-departments/human-resources-and-people-development/garda-hr-directorate/garda-strength-breakdown-2026/january-2026.html Information for previous years can be found at the following link: https://www.garda.ie/en/about-us/our-departments/human-resources-and-people-development/garda-hr-directorate/garda-strength-breakdown-2025/december-2025.html The Deputy should select the most recently available date and then select the file titled ‘Garda Members by Division" to access a breakdown of members assigned by Garda Division.

question: 740. Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of Gardaí who reported being assaulted while on active duty in County Mayo in each of the past ten years. [22454/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I have requested the information sought by the Deputy from the Garda authorities. Regrettably, the information is still not available. I will write to the Deputy once the information is to hand.

question: 741. Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of burglaries reported in County Mayo in each of the past ten years, in tabular form. [22455/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Central Statistics Office (CSO), as the national statistical agency, is responsible for the compilation and publication of all crime statistics. The CSO produces these statistics using data recorded on An Garda Síochána’s PULSE system and makes regular releases in relation to various crime statistics. The requested statistics can be found, by Garda Division, at the following link: https://data.cso.ie/table/CJQ06 In recent years, an Garda Síochána have had unprecedented success in reducing and preventing burglaries through Operation Thor.

question: 763. Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the number of Irish diaspora groups, including but not limited to sporting and cultural organisations, as well as emigrant organisations he and Ministers of State in his Department met for the St. Patrick's Day engagements overseas this year. [21912/26]
answer: Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine I propose to take Questions Nos. 762 to 765, inclusive, together. As part of my St Patrick's Day visit to the West Coast of the USA, I visited Seattle, San Francisco and Sacramento and attended a series of meetings and events which sought to build on the mutually beneficial trading relationship between Ireland and the United States. Bilateral trade in goods between Ireland and Washington State represented $1.45 billion in 2024, with this dominated by aerospace exports from Washington to Ireland. Bilateral trade in goods between Ireland and California was $4 billion in 2024, dominated by the pharma, electrical machinery and chemicals sectors. My visit included three political or senior official meetings or engagements, including a meeting with the Assistant Director of Farm and Food Systems Development in Seattle, the Californian Secretary of Food and Agriculture in Sacramento and an appearance at the California State Assembly. The visit also included eight meetings or engagements with the Irish diaspora which celebrated Irish diaspora in the area and recognised the contribution by the vibrant diaspora groups to the Ireland-US relationship over the years. Given the focus on the bilateral trading relationship with the United States during my visit, I had a total of nine separate business/trade focused meetings or engagements which included meeting with representatives from Boeing in Seattle. There was also a strong focus on agri-food trade through meetings with distributors of both Irish spirit drinks and meat products. I also attended promotional events for Irish dairy and drinks companies operating in the region. I met with agritech companies at the World Agritech Innovation Summit and Irish tech companies at the Irish Tech Summit in San Francisco. Research and innovation also featured prominently during my visit with three separate engagements, including a visit to UC Davis, where I formally announced the expansion of the research partnership between UC Davis and University College Dublin. Minister of State Grealish's St. Patrick's Day Visit As part of Minister Grealish’s St Patrick’s Day visit to New Zealand, he had three separate political engagements which included meetings with the Assistant Speaker of the House of Representatives and the Minister for Agriculture, Forestry, Trade and Investment. He also met a series of Mayors. In total, he had seven engagements with Ministers/Mayors/elected representatives. The visit also included ten separate diaspora events in Christchurch, Auckland and Wellington. Aligned with the ambition of the programme to advance research collaboration, particularly in climate and agriculture, Minister Grealish visited the New Zealand Bio economy Science institute and the Agriculture Emissions centre. Ireland and New Zealand have collaborated on a joint research programme since 2022 and Minister Grealish visited a number of the eleven collaborative research projects funded to date, where he met with a number of key stakeholders. In his bilateral meeting with the New Zealand Minister for Agriculture, Forestry, Trade and Investment, a joint statement was signed that commits to continuing this research partnership into a second phase. Minister Grealish also had eight separate business engagements, including a meeting with the Irish Business Network of New Zealand, which highlighted opportunities that exist for Irish businesses to enter and expand in the New Zealand market. In 2025, bilateral trade in goods between Ireland and New Zealand was valued at €194 million. Minister of State Healy-Rae's St. Patrick's Day Visit Minister of State Healy-Rae visited Estonia, Latvia, Finland and Lithuania as part of the St. Patrick's Day programme. During his visit to Estonia, Minister Healy Rae met with the Undersecretary for Biodiversity and Environmental Protection and the Head of the Forestry Department. In Finland, Minister Healy-Rae met with the Minister for Agriculture and Forestry and also met with a major Finnish forest industry group. In Latvia, the Minister met the Minister for Agriculture and undertook a site visit at Port of Riga with two Enterprise Ireland client companies. Minister Healy-Rae also met with the Chair of the Latvian-Ireland Parliamentary Friendship. In Finland, Minister Healy Rae attended a lunch with a group of buyers in the Finnish food industry with a view to growing Irish agri-food exports on the Finnish market. In Lithuania the Minister attended an Irish community lunch at the Embassy of Ireland in Vilnius and extended St. Patrick's Day greetings to the public gathered for the greening of the Vilnelé river as part of the celebrations. Minister met with Irish diaspora during the St. Patrick's Day celebrations in Estonia, Finland, Latvia and Lithuania. In 2025, bilateral trade in goods between Ireland and the countries visited by Minister Healy Rae was as follows: Estonia (€43 million); Latvia (€136 million); Finland (€561 million) and Lithuania (€270 million). Minister of State Dooley's St. Patrick's Day Visit Minister Dooley led a St. Patrick’s Day visit to Canada in his capacity as Minister of State at the Department of Climate, Energy and the Environment.

question: 809. Deputy Aisling Dempsey asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality if she has had discussions with Cabinet colleagues on adding childcare staff to the critical skills list; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [21590/26]
answer: Minister for Children, Disability and Equality The role of the early years educator and school-age childcare practitioner are valuable ones, and they play an important part in supporting children's development, learning and care. It is acknowledged that those working in the early learning and care and school-age childcare sector do not receive the recognition they deserve. In a very competitive labour market and with low levels of unemployment, recruitment and retention is a challenge for all employers. It is acknowledged many early learning and childcare services report recruitment and retention challenges. In general, these challenges are not caused by insufficient supply of staff, but by high levels of turnover which is significantly influenced by pay and conditions. The State’s general policy is to promote the sourcing of labour and skills needs from within the workforce of Ireland, the European Economic Area , the UK or Switzerland. Employment opportunities that arise in Ireland, should, in the main, be offered to suitably skilled Irish and other nationals from the European Economic Area, the UK or Switzerland. The Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment manages the employment permit process to allow non-EEA citizens to work in Ireland by operating a Critical Skills Occupations List and an Ineligible Occupations List. The lists are subject to regular evidence-based review and the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment carried out a public consultation during 2025 to ensure the employment permits system continues to reflect the needs of Ireland’s labour market. Officials in the Department of Children, Disability and Equality are aware that submissions were made both supporting and opposing the inclusion of early years educators on the Critical Skills List. Current data suggests there are sufficient numbers of suitably qualified people in Ireland and the EU to meet the demand for staff in the ELC and SAC sector and recent data from the Annual Early Years Sector Profile shows that the number of educators/practitioners working with children in the sector has increased by over 8% between 2024 and 2025 and has increased by over 33% since 2022. The Department continues to monitor the relevant indicators, engaging bilaterally with the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment and is keeping the matter under review.

Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the number of Irish diaspora groups, including but not limited to sporting and cultural organisations, as well as emigrant organisations she and Ministers of State in her Department met for the St. Patrick's Day engagements overseas this year. [21913/26]
answer: Minister for Children, Disability and Equality As part of the Government's St Patrick's Day Programme I travelled to Italy, including the Holy See. My programme was postponed until 16th March, returning to Dublin on the 18th March. I met with two diaspora groups during my Rome engagements: Pontifical Irish College + Broadford Youth Choir Irish nationals at FAO 1. Pontifical Irish College (Vespers + Youth Choir Recital) – evening of 17th March • The Pontifical Irish College is an Irish Catholic institution in Rome. • The event included: • Solemn Vespers • Recital by Broadford Youth Choir (an Irish youth cultural group) 2. Irish nationals working at Farm and Agriculture Organisation – 18th March • This was an event to facilitate engagement directly with the Irish diaspora employed in an international organisation. Minister of State for Disability, Emer Higgins TD, visited Copenhagen, Denmark from Sunday 15th March until Tuesday 17th March and Stockholm, Sweden from Tuesday 17th March until Wednesday 18th March. Minister Higgins met with one diaspora Group on her St Patrick's Day trip, although two different events were held with The Irish Culture Association of Denmark (ICAD) either in attendance or organising: The Irish Culture Association of Denmark (ICAD) – Parade and Festival • On Monday15th March Minister Higgins personally greeted over 200 Irish community members at St. Patrick's Day Community festival at Rådhuspladsen, organised by ICAD. • On Tuesday 16th March members of the Irish community and the Irish Culture Association of Denmark (ICAD) were in attendance at Irish Community reception at the official residence of the Irish Ambassador to Denmark Kyle O’Sullivan.

question: 868. Deputy Richard Boyd Barrett asked the Minister for Health if she will guarantee additional funding for all Drug and Alcohol Taskforce-funded community organisations to cover their mandatory contributions towards employee superannuation under the pension auto-enrolment scheme, in line with similar funding provided by the Department of Social Protection and Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration (details supplied).; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [21566/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Health (Deputy Jennifer Murnane O'Connor) Auto-enrolment is a universal pension scheme designed to benefit all workers, regardless of sector. Staff in HSE-funded organisations under section 39, including community-based drug services, will gain access to enhanced retirement savings, supported by employer and State contributions. This is a positive step for fairness and long-term security. These HSE-funded organisations are voluntary and not-for-profit bodies that deliver essential health and social care services. Staff in Section 39 funded organisations are not public servants but are critical to service delivery in areas such as drugs services and inclusion health. Many staff of voluntary bodies funded by the HSE under Section 39 are already part of occupational pension schemes or have in place a personal pension via payroll deductions. Auto-enrolment will not apply to those staff. Auto-enrolment only covers employees who are not already members of an occupational or personal pension via payroll deductions. The Department recognises that auto-enrolment will have cost implications for Section 39 funded organisations. In negotiating funding allocations with these organisations, the HSE will consider the impact of auto-enrolment costs to ensure services remain sustainable and staff are supported. The HSE has informed the Department that it will be gathering data from the Section 39 sector it funds over the coming months to establish what level of staff the auto-enrolment will apply to. This exercise will enable an assessment of the likely scale/materiality of any cost of the auto-enrolment scheme for HSE funded Section 39 employers. I have been assured that this assessment will inform consideration of the funding requirements associated with auto-enrolment for community-based drug services.

Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science the number of Irish diaspora groups, including but not limited to sporting and cultural organisations, as well as emigrant organisations he and Ministers of State in his Department met for the St. Patrick's Day engagements overseas this year. question: 1064. Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht the number of Irish diaspora groups, including but not limited to sporting and cultural organisations, as well as emigrant organisations he and Ministers of State in his Department met for the St. Patrick's Day engagements overseas this year. [21926/26]
answer: Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht I propose to take Questions Nos. 1063 to 1065, inclusive, together. As Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht, and Minister for Social Protection, I was privileged to represent the Irish Government in Ottawa, Montreal and Toronto, Canada this year as part of the St. Patrick's Day overseas programme. These trips are an important part of promoting Ireland, Irish values, and Ireland's interests across the world. Canada is the 12th largest market globally for Irish companies, and Enterprise Ireland have 315 client companies exporting to Canada, with those exports valued at €585 million. Helping to develop new markets for Irish companies is a key goal of the Government’s St. Patrick’s Day programme. Overall trade between our two countries is very significant, with the most recent CSO data showing it is valued at over €12 billion, with exports of goods and services valued at €8.1 billion and imports valued at €4.1 billion. While additional detail will be provided in answer to this question with a focus on my role as Minister for Social Protection, much activity related strongly to my role as Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht. A significant number of my meetings were with Irish language and community organisations, many of which are supported by the Irish Government. It is of note that Canada is home to the first and only officially designated Gaeltacht area outside of Ireland. Established in 2007, Gaeltacht an Oileáin Úir (the North American Gaeltacht) is located in Tamworth, Ontario and is a gathering place for Irish speakers. Engagements on the programme included, meeting with branches of Comhaltas Ceoltóirí Éireann; local Gaeilgeoirí and participants in the Irish Canadian University Scholar (ICUF) Programme; the Canada Ireland Foundation, the Irish Canadian Immigration Centre, Toronto-area Irish Community Radio, and several Toronto-area GAA clubs. While in Canada I also met with a large number of businesses and business representative organisations. For example, I attended a business leaders' lunch in Ottawa and met with Tom Jenkins of Opentext. In Montreal. I also attended a Business Breakfast hosted with the Montreal Ireland Chamber of Commerce and Enterprise Ireland and Invest Northern Ireland. Some of the elected officials that I met in Ottawa and Montreal included, Prime Minister Mark Carney at the Official St. Patrick’s Day Reception; the Secretary of State for Rural Development, Buckley Belanger and; the Minister responsible for Official Languages, Marc Miller. During the Toronto leg of the trip I met with the Mayor of Toronto, Olivia Chow. I also met with several Members of the Executive Council of Ontario, including the Honourable Lisa Thompson, Ontario Minister for Rural Affairs. Minister of State Buttimer represented the Irish Government in China, visiting Beijing, Shanghai and Hong Kong. China is Ireland's largest trading partner in Asia with the most recent CSO figures indicating there is over €40 billion in bilateral trade between both countries, with exports of goods and services valued at €22.8 billion and imports valued at €16.5 billion. This is a hugely important market for Irish companies and the Irish economy as a whole. There are also ever increasing cultural connections between Ireland and China with many people travelling between our countries for work, tourism and family visits. Minister of State Buttimer undertook an extensive programme of engagements in Beijing, Shanghai and Hong Kong. In total around 290 business or business representative organisations were engaged with during the programme. In addition, 20 Irish diaspora groups were engaged, including Beijing GAA, Ireland China Friendship Association, a number of third level alumni group, Irish Shanghai GAA, Suzhou GAA, Hong Kong St. Patricks Society and Hong Kong GAA. Significant political engagements also took place including meetings with the Vice Minister for Transport and Vice Minister for Foreign Affairs in Beijing, the Vice Mayor of the Shanghai Municipal Government and, in Hong Kong, the Acting Secretary of Transport and Logistics and the Justice Secretary of Hong Kong. Overall, I am confident that the level of engagement on both trips helped advance to goals of the overall overseas programme, promoting Ireland, Irish values, and Ireland's interests across the world.

question: 1072. Deputy Noel McCarthy asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht when he expects the next funding round of the Community Centre Investment Fund to open for applications; when applications approved under this round are then envisaged to be announced; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [22171/26]
answer: Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht I propose to take Questions Nos. 1072 and 1073 together. Since becoming Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht, I have prioritised investment in community infrastructure. As part of Budget 2026, I was delighted to announce increased funding for the programmes that are delivering on this priority. This includes an increase in the annual budget for the Community Centre Investment Fund (CCIF) by €3 million to €20 million. The CCIF was introduced to provide high quality, accessible, community spaces that are available to all groups in all communities in both rural and urban areas. Through the CCIF, some €111 million has been allocated since 2022 for the enhancement and refurbishment of existing community centres and the construction of new centres where such a need has been identified. All successful projects under previous rounds of the fund have now been announced. I am committed to delivering further iterations of the CCIF in the coming years in line with the commitment in the Programme for Government for this to become a permanent rolling fund. My officials are currently finalising the details of the next call for applications under the fund, which will focus on refurbishment to existing community centres. I expect to open this new round of funding very shortly, with successful projects being announced before the end of the year.

question: 1. Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of gardaí who attested in 2025; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20732/26]
answer: Deputy Matt Carthy For all the rhetoric, there has actually been very little progress made in tackling the Garda recruitment and retention crisis. There continues to be a severe over-dependence on overtime for routine Garda work. Considering the significant challenges gardaí will face this year, will the Minister inform the House of precisely how many gardaí attested in 2025? Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration (Deputy Jim O'Callaghan) The number of people we have in An Garda Síochána is extremely important from the point of view of enforcing the law. It is probably the most important part of the functions carried out by us, as Ministers, to ensure that the law we make in this House is enforced. At present, there is a workforce of approximately 18,000 in An Garda Síochána. This includes 14,397 attested members, 3,527 Garda staff and 308 Garda reserves. Last year, 619 gardaí attested from the Garda College, which, I am pleased to say, was the highest number in seven years. If the Deputy wants to look at this from the point of view of the year of the date of appointment of the Government in January 2025, he will note as well that there was an extra attestation in February of this year, which brought the number who attested up to 786. Recruitment is going in the right direction. The Deputy used the phrase "recruitment and retention crisis". There is no such crisis. In fact, even the representative associations do not now refer to a crisis. Resignations from An Garda Síochána are really low. Last year, 141 members of the force resigned. That is less than 1%. This is remarkably small when compared with nearby jurisdictions. I know recruitment is going in the right direction because in December, we took in 223 new recruits into Templemore. This is the highest it has been in years. If I can get up to 225 or 250 on each intake, we will get to where we want to be. Deputy Matt Carthy The Minister stated he wants to reach 5,000 attestations over the lifetime of the Government. It does not take much deduction to realise that 619 gardaí attesting in the calendar year of 2025 remains way below what is needed in order meet that goal. That number will come as a surprise to many people, especially when they have heard so much about the fact that over 11,000 people applied to join An Garda last year. That points to a crisis. It certainly points to a failure. Despite the welcome increase in the intakes into Templemore, there has to be a recognition the numbers are still nowhere near where they need to be. What is the Government going to do about this? What additional measures are going to be put in place? We have outlined proposals to increase both the training allowance and the number of training places and to encourage gardaí who have left the force to rejoin it. Has the Minister done any of those things? Deputy Jim O'Callaghan We can agree on one thing, namely that it is heading in the right direction. It is certainly improving. The fact that we have seen the highest number of gardaí attesting in seven years is a very positive story from the point of view of the Irish public. The Deputy is correct in stating that we ran two recruitment campaigns, in which there was huge interest, last year. We got 11,000 people expressing an interest in applying to join. We are processing those applications much faster. The fact that we got 223 new recruits into Templemore in December is a really positive story. If we can consistently get numbers like that, we will see attestations coming up to the figure of 1,000 and to more than that in the future. The reason we want to do this, as the Deputy will be aware, is because people want to see more gardaí on the streets. On a visit to Cork last week, I heard a very positive account of extra Garda visibility. The same applies in Limerick, as the Minister of State, Deputy Collins, will attest to. A huge amount of work is being done to get the numbers up. That work will continue. Deputy Matt Carthy Of course we want to see more gardaí across all the regions, but we also need to address the failure in terms of numbers. In that context, I am sure the Minister will accept that there is far to much reliance on overtime for routine police work. We have far too few community and roads policing gardaí. We are in what is probably an unprecedented year, with the EU Presidency and the upcoming Ireland-Israel UEFA Nations League game, which, unfortunately, is still going ahead. We still have the potential of a visit by Donald Trump in September. The Minister mentioned the representative organisations. My understanding is that the Garda Representative Association, GRA, has threatened to refuse voluntary overtime as part of its dispute. An Garda Síochána has classified more than 40 events that will need to be the subject of major security operations during the Presidency . If we are going to rely on overtime for those, it will invariably mean that there will not be enough Garda visibility in areas outside of Dublin. What assurance will the Minister provide to communities that these additional responsibilities for gardaí will not leave their areas under-policed when the events to which I refer are taking place? Deputy Jim O'Callaghan Overtime is always an integral part of the service provided by An Garda Síochána. Every year, there are major events that have to be policed. I have spoken extensively to the Commissioner about the commitments arising from the EU Presidency and the Ireland-Israel soccer match. Whatever happens, the Commissioner has informed me that there will be resources available to police these events. We want to get as many people as we can into An Garda Síochána. A number of significant changes made in recent times have had a really positive impact. I refer, in particular, to changing the recruitment cut-off age from 35 years to 50. We are now seeing people who are in their 40s and in sedentary careers wanting the excitement of a career in An Garda Síochána. These individuals are joining the force. Also, increasing the mandatory retirement age to 62 has had a very positive impact. I have a very good relationship with all of the associations. They are very co-operative. Like me and, I presume, the Deputy, they want to see what is best for An Garda Síochána and the Irish public.

question: 2. Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the position regarding all discussions he has held with British authorities on the implementation of the EU migration and asylum pact and its impact on the common travel area; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20733/26]
answer: Deputy Matt Carthy I was watching in for parts of the Seanad debate on the International Protection Bill. I was interested in, but not a bit surprised about, the failure, either in the Bill or in the EU migration and asylum pact, to have due consideration for the common travel area. The latter was a dominant part of the debate. What discussions has the Minister had with the British authorities regarding the pact's implementation and its impact on the common travel area? Deputy Jim O'Callaghan I thank the Deputy for his very opportune question. Last Friday, at the UK-Ireland Summit 2026 in Cork, I had a discussion with the Secretary of State for Northern Ireland, Hilary Benn, in respect of the common travel area, the new legislation that we are going to enact here and the need to ensure that there will be no abuse of the common travel area. Regrettably, we do see the latter between this jurisdiction and Northern Ireland. Last month, I had a discussion by way of a remote meeting with the Home Secretary, Shabana Mahmood. At that meeting, we had a very extensive discussion about issues relating to asylum, the common travel area and other matters of mutual interest. As the Deputy knows, the UK is not only not part of the EU asylum pact, it also decided to leave the EU and go it alone. It is fair to say, without being too critical of the UK, that this policy has not worked. In order to be able to combat abuse of the common travel area or asylum mechanisms, countries need to work harmoniously with each other. That is why working within the EU is the best approach from Ireland's point of view. The number of asylum applications in the EU last year were down by 20%. In Ireland, they were down by 30%. They were only down by 4% in the UK. At present, as the Deputy will be aware, the UK is designated by me a safe third country. Once the legislation commences on 12 June, it will again be designated as a safe third country. As I have repeatedly stated, movement in the common travel area between Northern Ireland and the Republic is not permitted for people who are not citizens. I have engaged with the British Home Secretary on the measures that will be introduced, such as data sharing and operational measures. As the Deputy knows, Operation Sonnet is ongoing. Deputy Matt Carthy We can have our opinions on Brexit. In fact, I am sure we would agree on many points. However, we would also need to agree on the fact that Brexit is a fact of life and that we find ourselves in a unique position. It is a fact that no other state which has signed up to the EU migration and asylum pact is also part of a common travel area with a state outside of the Union. The Minister has repeatedly made the claim, as have other Ministers, that the majority of international protection applicants enter the State via the common travel area. In fact the Minister's review of Protocol 21, which was published last year, acknowledged that the opt-outs we had to things like the migration pact were important in order to maintain the common travel area. The Minister referred to discussions he has had with British Ministers. Correct me if I am wrong, but I did not hear anything about either a fundamental change or a new bilateral agreement being on the cards. Does the Minister not accept that this is what is required between this Government and the British Government if we are to have an asylum process that works? Deputy Jim O'Callaghan The basis upon which we think the greatest number of those claiming asylum in Ireland are coming from the UK is the number arriving at the International Protection Office. This year, 90% of people who have claimed asylum in Ireland did so at the IPO. That leads us to believe they are coming across the Border with Northern Ireland. It is a huge challenge whether we are in the migration pact or not. The simplistic view sometimes put forward is that if we had not gone into the migration pact, we would not have this issue. We would have this issue because of our land border with the United Kingdom and the common travel area. We need to emphasise that people who are not citizens of Ireland, the UK or the Channel Islands are not allowed to travel back and forth across the Border on the island of Ireland. We also need to recognise that I have discussed the issue of data sharing with the British Home Secretary and will reach agreement with her on that. That is extremely important in resolving abuses of the common travel area, as are operational measures between An Garda Síochána, the Police Service of Northern Ireland and Border Force. As to getting a written agreement with the British, I cannot force the British Government to enter into an agreement to take back asylum applicants from the Republic. Deputy Matt Carthy You can try, Minister. That is what I am asking. What efforts have been made? I will touch on the designation of Britain as a safe third country. Let us assume the figures the Minister has given are accurate, although a lot of work needs to be done on the collection of data as to where IP applicants are coming from. Section 220 of the International Protection Bill 2026 requires the Minister to be satisfied that any proposed safe third country fully meets EU standards, particularly in relation to non-refoulement and access to a functional asylum system. Will the Minister outline the assessments that his Department has carried out as to the prospects of Britain meeting these criteria and how these will be assessed? Has analysis been carried out as to what happens if Britain does not meet statutory and EU requirements or if a legal challenge to such designation in the courts were to be successful? The Minister will agree that if the figures he has cited are anywhere close to the reality, this would create huge problems, which could potentially derail the entire system he intends to implement. Deputy Jim O'Callaghan At present, the UK is designated by me as a safe third country. That designation was done on the basis of an assessment. By 12 June, I will designate it as a safe third country under the new legislation, provided I get the assessment. There is no reason to think the assessment will change. Circumstances in Britain have not changed since I previously designated it as a safe third country. On the impact of this measure, under the legislation, certain applications from people who come from a safe third country will be inadmissible. It will also be possible to return people to a safe third country. As the Deputy will know, when it comes to the deportations that take place and that have taken place, I can only deport or remove people to countries that are prepared to receive them. I cannot just charter a flight, land it in the UK and say "Here you are". Co-operation with the UK is required. I have a very good relationship with the Home Secretary. There is recognition of the issues that arise in respect of the common travel area and there will be an agreed response from the Irish and UK Governments. It is a difficult challenge. Can the Deputy come up with a simple response to it? I am not being facetious but the only way to stop it is to put a hard border on the island and we do not want to do that.

question: 3. Deputy Gary Gannon asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he will respond to reports that women prisoners are being held in degrading and overcrowded conditions in the Dóchas Centre; and whether the Government accepts that continuing to rely on incarceration without sufficient investment in alternatives to custody, risks simply warehousing vulnerable women in the prison system. [20842/26]
answer: Deputy Gary Gannon Will the Minister respond to reports that women prisoners are being held in degrading and overcrowded conditions in the Dóchas Centre? Does the Government accept that continuing to rely on incarceration without sufficient investment in alternatives to custody risks simply warehousing vulnerable women in the prison system? The phrase "warehousing vulnerable women" is not something I have concocted myself. It was used in a report presented to the Minister's Department, which has yet to be released. Deputy Jim O'Callaghan I thank Deputy Gannon very much for his question. I am concerned about overcrowding in the Dóchas Centre, the female prison in Mountjoy. To make the House aware of some statistics regarding the centre, as of yesterday, there were 223 women in custody in Mountjoy, 29 of whom were on mattresses. The centre's bed capacity is 146. I am concerned about this. I previously said that I do not have the same level of concern in respect of the women's prison in Limerick, which I know the Deputy has visited. That is true because, as I am sure the Deputy will appreciate, that is a very modern prison. What is the solution to this? Part of the solution has to be creating more spaces within the Dóchas Centre. I am not saying that is the only solution but it must be part of it. There are plans to build another 65 spaces across the prison system in 2026, 26 of which will be new spaces for the Dóchas Centre. That will increase capacity to 172. As I have indicated previously, I have got approval from Government to develop further prison spaces between 2026 and 2030. The projects that I have got approval for include an extension to Rowan House at the Dóchas Centre that is expected to accommodate 50 female prisoners. There has to be some recognition that more spaces are required. That is my response in respect of that. An awful lot of work is also being done to ensure that services are provided to facilitate women in availing of supervised temporary release. A scheme is being run by the Irish Prison Service to support the needs of women who are transitioning from prison to the community. The pilot is located in Limerick women’s prison and I am advised that, to date, over 50 women have accessed the scheme, with approximately 25 successful completions. An evaluation of the programme is under way. I will give the Deputy further information on my proposals when I respond to him again. Deputy Gary Gannon I thank the Minister for his response. The figures are fairly stark. Last night, the Dóchas Centre was at 153% of its capacity and 29 women were sleeping on the floor. Can the Minister imagine what that does to a person's capacity for rehabilitation and sense of place in the world? I understand these people have committed crimes and that there are consequences to that but the consequences of placing people in these conditions go well beyond what is appropriate to the crime, impacting their families and their children. I appreciate the Minister has said that 26 extra spaces will be provided at the Dóchas Centre during his term but that same report that has not been released yet also highlighted the fact that the Garda National Immigration Bureau is showing up at overcrowded prisons to place people into them without any consultation with the prison guards. That is extraordinary and it is happening on the Minister's watch. These 26 extra spaces will not fix this. We need something far more radical and different. Deputy Jim O'Callaghan To deal with the issue of the report, that report will be published this week. I only got to look at it in the past ten days or so. I have approved it and it will be published this week. On the other measures that can be put in place, I do not believe prisons are the solution to all of the ills of society. We obviously need a combined approach in respect of these issues. The Probation Service plays a very important role. This year, it is providing over €21 million in funding to 60 community organisations to cover the costs of providing services and programmes. Probation obviously plays a big role. When this House enacts the miscellaneous provisions Bill, it will provide for the greater use of community sanctions and community service orders. With regard to what the Deputy has said about deportations, I recognise the pressures this puts on the prison system. Perhaps we need a separate place where people who are going to be subject to enforced deportation can be detained. That is something I will look at. Deputy Gary Gannon I would definitely like to hear a lot more about these separate places because we still have not ratified the Optional Protocol to the Convention against Torture, OPCAT, on the prevention of torture. Today, I am here talking about the Dóchas Centre. A couple of weeks ago, I was talking about the women's prison in Limerick. The conditions in the men's prisons are extraordinary. We had the Inspector of Prisons before the committee a couple of months ago and his contribution was jaw-dropping. He spoke about conditions in our prison system being tantamount to torture. We know recidivism rates are nearly seven out of ten in this country. Is it time to be more radical? What would a citizens' assembly on prisons and incarceration in this country look like? We should begin a full exploration of our prison system. What is working and what is very clearly not working? What do we need to do differently and what can we do differently? Do we really need to imprison women whose children will have to visit them and be traumatised by that prospect? There are a lot of things we can do if we had a vision for something very different. Clearly, what we have is not only not working, it has been described as being tantamount to torture. Deputy Jim O'Callaghan I do not agree that it is tantamount to torture. Like the Deputy, I have visited the majority of prisons. I have visited seven, and I will be visiting another one very shortly that I have not visited already. There is a lot of excellent work going on in prisons. Many people who come out of prison do not go on to offend again. That is particularly the case in respect of serious offences. I am well aware that there are people in prison who, because of addiction issues or chaotic lives, do go on to commit further offences. That is a challenge in terms of how it can be responded to. I engaged with the Inspector of Prisons, Mr. Kelly, and had a good conversation with him in respect of this issue. At present, we have about 5,800 people in prison. We have a population of 5.5 million. Ours is not a society that is at the higher echelons of incarceration, either in Europe or across the wider world. We have a moderate view in terms of who needs to be incarcerated. As the Deputy knows, however, there are debates in this House on a variety of issues, including that of victims saying that they want justice, and justice sometimes requires incarceration.

question: 4. Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he will establish a historical investigations unit, as proposed by the Irish Council for Civil Liberties and the Committee on the Administration of Justice, to allow for independent police investigations into unresolved deaths and incidents of torture or ill-treatment; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20734/26]
answer: Deputy Matt Carthy I am sure the Minister's office is even more inundated than mine in respect of this matter. Anybody who has ever been a member of the justice committee will have dealt with a huge number of outstanding legacy issues relating to the ongoing legacy of the Garda heavy gang, unresolved cases relating to the conflict and other historical investigative failures. How we have dealt with those matters has been a matter of much debate. The Irish Council for Civil Liberties and the Committee for the Administration of Justice proposed the establishment of a historical inquiries unit. That proposal merits consideration. Is the Minister considering the establishment of such a unit? Deputy Jim O'Callaghan We need to be balanced about this matter. Obviously, there are legacy issues arising from the Troubles in Northern Ireland. The Deputy mentioned the Garda heavy gang. We also have to acknowledge that murders carried out by the Provisional IRA give rise to legacy issues that need to be resolved. One of the inadequacies of the Good Friday Agreement is that it does not really deal with legacy issues at all. Governments have been grappling with this matter since then. Regrettably, and this applies in many instances, legacy is being used as a political tool. However, we do have to try to deal with legacy issues. Where there are historical offences, it is important that we try to resolve them. It is important to say that there is no de facto moratorium or amnesty in this jurisdiction in respect of any murders or serious criminal activities that took place during the Troubles in Northern Ireland. That does not happen. There are many serious events that occurred that have still not been resolved. People have not got justice in respect of them. From speaking to An Garda Síochána and officials within my Department, I know that the relevant files remain open. There has been progress recently. The framework agreement between the two Governments has given rise to a commitment that there a statutory regime to deal with Troubles-related killings, as they are referred to, or incidents will be put in place. That legislation, as the Deputy knows, is going through the Houses of Parliament in the UK. In May, I will bring forward a general scheme to Government in respect of corresponding inquiries here. The Garda Commissioner established a Troubles legacy liaison unit at the beginning of the year. That is an important development. Deputy Matt Carthy Of course, there are a range of historical cases. I am talking about cases in this State in respect of which justice and accountability have not been delivered. There are well-known cases of collusion and cases relating to the legacy of the conflict. The actions of the Garda heavy gang need to be addressed, particularly as those involved were central to a number of miscarriages of justice. The 50th anniversary of the Sallins case is approaching. There was no accountability for the actions of the gardaí involved in those events. The Kerry babies case is an outstanding area of concern. Little or nothing has been done regarding a number of conflict-related events, including the killing of Eddie Fullerton, the Dublin Airport bombing, the Dublin-Monaghan bombings and the case of John Francis Green in my constituency. All of these cases cast a shadow in terms accountability and give rise to an ongoing burden for the families involved. The Irish Government has supported the establishment of an historical inquiries unit in the North. Why will it not do the same in this State? Deputy Jim O'Callaghan The Deputy has fallen into the trap that I identified earlier. It is difficult not to do that. He stated that the actions of the Garda heavy gang need to be addressed. The murders carried out by the Provisional IRA also need to be addressed. The Deputy referred to Eddie Fullerton, a Sinn Féin councillor who was brutally murdered. The murder of Billy Fox, a Member of these Houses, needs to be addressed. The murder of Robert Bradford needs to be addressed. We cannot be selective about which atrocity we want to focus upon. That is why the legacy framework that has been agreed to by both Governments is welcome. The Deputy mentioned the Sallins train robbery. I have already given a response on that matter. I am not going to have a public inquiry in respect of it. If it comes within the parameters of the legacy issues in due course, so be it. The issue in that regard relates to a robbery occurred 50 years ago. Two people had their convictions overturned in 1980. A presidential pardon was given to a third person in 1992. Financial settlements were subsequently made. I want to focus on where justice has not been delivered. Deputy Matt Carthy That answer speaks volumes. Let me be clear: every family that lost a loved one deserves truth and justice. I say that without equivocating or engaging in whataboutery. Let us deal with the Sallins case. Anyone looking at the detail of that matter can see that the investigation was rotten from start to finish. People's confessions were coerced, and that undermined the justice system. The problem is that, under the current framework, the Minister can just say that he does not think there should be a public inquiry. It should not be up to him, me or any other politician to decide which families are entitled to truth and justice. We should have a stand-alone mechanism for people, regardless of their background, the amount of money they have or their level of political influence. If individuals are entitled to the truth, they should have recourse to get it. Otherwise, how do we not create a scenario whereby there is the potential for political favouritism and a feeling that some people are entitled to truth and justice and others are not? That is why the proposal from the Irish Council for Civil Liberties and the Committee for the Administration of Justice warrants consideration. Deputy Jim O'Callaghan I am going to conclude on a point of harmony. The Deputy makes a valid point. We do not want people to be selecting individual atrocities for the purpose of investigation. That is what the legacy framework is about. It will predominantly deal with Troubles-related killings. Those are the ones that have to be prioritised in the context of families that have not got justice yet and where there have been no prosecutions let alone convictions. There has been political agreement, but I would like to see legislative co-ordination between both jurisdictions to allow Troubles-related killings to be inquired into. Inquiries would focus on killings that happened during certain periods, and we would not have to decide who would get a public inquiry. The call from the Irish Council for Civil Liberties related to an inquiry in respect of Sallins. I am not going to do that. I hear the point the Deputy is making. We will benefit from having enacted legislation in both jurisdictions that allows for an independent quasi-judicial inquiry into and investigation of Troubles-related killings.

question: 5. Deputy Joe Cooney asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of contracts issued to hotels and-or guest houses to accommodate Ukrainian people, including the total number of beds, by county, at end of both February 2025 and February 2026, in tabular form; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20884/26]
answer: Deputy Joe Cooney County Clare has welcomed significant numbers of Ukrainian people fleeing the war, just as it did with Hungarian and Kosovan refugees in the past. Our communities opened their schools, organisations and workplaces to them. Now, four years on, many Ukrainians are moving on from emergency accommodation and hotel contracts are ending. Will the Minister of State confirm how many contracts have been concluded and how many beds may return to their original purpose? Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration (Deputy Colm Brophy) As the Deputy knows, Ireland remains steadfast in its support for Ukraine. My Department continues to work as part of a whole-of-government response to the war in Ukraine with a focus on providing access to emergency, but temporary, accommodation to those fleeing the conflict. For new arrivals, State-contracted accommodation is provided for 30 days in designated centres, together with supports to assist them in making independent living arrangements for those who wish to remain for the duration of temporary protection. As of 13 March 2026, over 125,700 people have fled Ukraine and received temporary protection here. Of those, over 94,300 have requested and been provided with access to State-supported accommodation. Almost 19,200 people are currently in State-contracted accommodation. This is a significant and welcome reduction from a peak of, believe it or not, 60,000 people in November 2023. All accommodation contracts by my Department are temporary in nature. Persons with temporary protection are advised of that when requesting access to be assigned to temporary accommodation. Approximately 531 contracts are in operation. Our current contracted accommodation capacity is approximately 22,450 beds. It includes hotels, guesthouses and bed and breakfasts. In sourcing and securing accommodation, the central consideration is the safety and security of the displaced people fleeing the war in Ukraine. In 2024 and 2025, approximately 420 and 195 contracts, respectively, were able to be terminated in terms of changes that we are making in the reduction in numbers. So far in 2026, 25 contracts have been terminated and we have received three notices from providers for termination of contracts. In relation to County Clare, as of the end of February 2025, there were 31 contracts, which was equivalent to 2,610 beds. To give the Deputy an indication, as of the end of February 2026, there were only 18 contracts, with 1,041 beds, representing a very significant return of beds from this area. Additional information not given on the floor of the House With this reply, I am providing the Deputy as requested with a table that shows the number of contracts and beds by county at the end of February 2025 and end February 2026. February 2025 February 2026 County No. of contracts No. of beds No. of contracts No. of beds Carlow 8 281 7 200 Cavan 19 687 13 221 Clare 31 2610 18 1041 Cork 67 4248 50 2121 Donegal 56 2504 41 719 Dublin* 69 4486 64 3536 Galway 43 2348 36 1225 Kerry 111 5867 102 3449 Kildare 7 1822 6 1049 Kilkenny 13 942 13 720 Laois 6 202 6 165 Leitrim 12 450 10 258 Limerick 23 1967 14 1197 Longford 6 167 5 140 Louth 16 912 11 761 Mayo 29 1823 21 924 Meath 15 1369 9 613 Monaghan 6 250 6 115 Offaly 18 1172 16 791 Roscommon 8 465 6 186 Sligo 28 1355 20 431 Tipperary 26 918 17 541 Waterford 13 918 10 643 Westmeath 16 1234 11 463 Wexford 32 1665 22 920 Wicklow 16 1339 14 988 TOTAL 694 42,001 548 23,417 *Please note that the figure for Dublin includes Citywest with 1,704 beds. Deputy Joe Cooney I thank the Minister of State for the reply and welcome the reduction in the hotel contracts. This is a positive step, showing that many people are moving on from emergency accommodation by finding homes, entering work and moving elsewhere. We should recognise the support of Clare communities and the contribution many Ukrainians have made in return. Hotels returning to serving visitors is an important opportunity for tourism and the hospitality sector. It will support local businesses, boost occupancy and protect jobs, which is important. Will the Minister of State provide data on how many businesses have exited contracts and are now operating again as tourist accommodation? Deputy Colm Brophy I have supplied the Deputy as part of my answer to him a table in tabular form with all the information for every county. I have outlined the total figures to him. It is important to recognise that, as part of an ongoing process, we are moving toward a reduction and eventual elimination of this accommodation situation. There will be a motion coming forward in the Dáil next week regarding the extension of the accommodation recognition payment, ARP. Temporary protection is something that was brought in by the European Commission across Europe, and we wanted to support it in that. As we look to the future and changes in that area, though, we want to see businesses going back to what they were doing originally and having the ability to put beds and accommodation back into local communities for the benefit of those local communities and areas. Deputy Joe Cooney Clare has lost thousands of tourist bed nights each month over the past four years, with the vast majority in north and west Clare, where tourism is a key part of the local economy. While I understand that tourism is not directly within the Minister of State's brief, the return of this bed stock is both vital and important. It must be managed to ensure that it delivers the maximum benefit quickly. Will the Minister of State outline whether there is any engagement with local authorities, Fáilte Ireland or Tourism Ireland to make the most of this capacity returning to the market? Are any targeted promotional campaigns planned to boost visitor numbers, where returning to our capacity will make a real and welcome difference? Deputy Colm Brophy Obviously, that is not within my area. That would be more within the area of the Minister with responsibility on the tourism side. From our point of view as a Department, what we want to do is facilitate the return of beds to the sector so that they are there and available. Like the Deputy, I would like to see, particularly in a wonderful county like Clare, that those beds would go back into the accommodation, tourism and hospitality sectors. Hospitality and tourism are key drivers for economics in a whole host of counties in our country and are very important. Therefore, as an initial stage, what we are doing here is making the beds available again by terminating the contracts and moving out of this area. I would hope, therefore, that in conjunction with the local authorities, the necessary tourism boards would put in place a process to ensure that those beds go back into hospitality.

question: 6. Deputy Noel McCarthy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the measures being considered by his Department to ensure the quicker processing of naturalisation applications; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20206/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I am delighted to say that my Department is holding a number of citizenship ceremonies in Killarney next month. I look forward to having the opportunity to meet and congratulate approximately 5,000 of our new Irish citizens. These ceremonies are a truly special occasion and it is an honour to be there to celebrate this special moment in people's lives. Despite a substantial increase in applications received in recent years, the fact that processing times have significantly reduced is a huge credit to the work of my Department. The median processing time for a decision on an application in 2024 and 2025 has been approximately 8 months. This is a significant improvement from the median processing time of 15 months in 2023, 19 months in 2022, and 24 months in 2021. My Department has taken a significant number of steps to speed up the process for applicants. These included introducing an online digital application, online payments, and the introduction of eVetting. This digitisation has facilitated a record number of citizenship decisions made last year. In just over two years, my Department has gone from processing around 12,000 applications a year, to processing over 20,000 applications in 2023, and approximately 31,000 decisions in both 2024 and 2025.

question: 7. Deputy Joe Cooney asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration for the number of properties in receipt of the ARP, by county, at end of February 2025 and 2026, in tabular form; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20885/26]
answer: Deputy Joe Cooney I believe that a lot of people in County Clare have been housed through the accommodation recognition payment scheme. From what I can see, it is working well and I have not heard of any major issues from house owners or tenants. It is important that we have a clear picture of how many people are supported under this scheme nationwide. With that in mind, will the Minister of State provide an overall number and county-by-county breakdown of the properties receiving the accommodation recognition payment? Deputy Colm Brophy I thank the Deputy. The accommodation recognition payment was introduced to recognise the generosity of people who opened their homes to provide accommodation to beneficiaries of temporary protection in Ireland who fled the war in Ukraine. The ARP scheme is provided in Part 2 of the Civil Law (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2022 and is administered by the Department of Social Protection on behalf of our Department. The scheme involves a monthly payment of €600 to a host in respect of providing accommodation in accordance with the rules of the scheme. The ARP is not rent and is not payable where there is a rental agreement in place. The scheme currently extends to March 2026 but it may be extended by ministerial order - as I mentioned earlier, a motion will be before the Dáil next week in relation to that - in accordance with the legislation. The Deputy may be aware that motions are to be considered in this House and in the Seanad next week that will extend the scheme to March 2027 in line with the current application of the EU temporary protection directive. By the end of February, the ARP scheme had supported over 42,000 temporary protection beneficiaries accommodated in over 23,500 properties at a monthly cost of approximately €14.5 million. I am providing in tabular form with this response the information sought by the Deputy. Awarded Claims – Property Distribution by County County February 2025 February 2026 Carlow 442 538 Cavan 359 442 Clare 562 633 Cork 1504 1791 Donegal 1812 2177 Dublin 3071 3399 Galway 989 1120 Kerry 1182 1443 Kildare 656 816 Kilkenny 242 300 Laois 300 376 Leitrim 372 471 Limerick 861 1037 Longford 339 402 Louth 612 730 Mayo 1297 1542 Meath 528 635 Monaghan 275 305 Offaly 437 537 Roscommon 112 134 Sligo 501 619 Tipperary 820 1014 Waterford 753 886 Westmeath 612 730 Wexford 883 1052 Wicklow 429 477 Totals 19950 23606 Deputy Joe Cooney I believe this scheme shows that trust, along with fair financial support, can bring thousands of homes into the rental market. Over 42,000 people are currently housed in more than 20,000 properties, mostly without formal inspection or registration. That is a lot of people willing to rent out their properties under the right circumstances. I am not against proper oversight, but this scheme clearly shows that a system that is simple, fair and works for both sides can be effective. There also appear to be very few complaints about conditions or arrangements. Is there any data that gives way to this? Deputy Colm Brophy The scheme has worked, but the time for the scheme should come to an orderly conclusion. Like all temporary schemes, I believe you must look, introduce where needed and phase out where it is no longer appropriate. It is therefore my view that we will be extending the scheme as indicated for 12 months. This will be part of a phasing out process of the ARP. It will also be the intention to reduce the payment from €600 to €400 as part of that phasing out of ARP. That will enable us to have a gradual winding down of the scheme. Ukrainians who have enjoyed temporary protection in Ireland are a welcome part of our community. There are many opportunities for them to avail of housing in their own right and many Ukrainians are doing so at the moment. We will work to a process of making it very clear the ARP scheme will be coming to an end and will have a phase out on it. I want to make that clear to the Deputy. Deputy Joe Cooney The difference between this scheme and the current private rental market is something we should look at closely. The private rental sector sees a lot of RTB disputes, complaints and at times poor relationships between landlords and tenants. The ARP scheme shows a different way of doing things. When property owners are offered a fair, simple and worthwhile arrangement, they respond well. Over 20,000 have already done this. There are lessons here that could bring more homes into use, ease pressures on rents and improve things for many people who depend on the rental market. It would be a very positive outcome from this programme. Has there been any discussion between the Department of justice and others on how a model like this could be expanded? Deputy Colm Brophy I acknowledge what the Deputy is saying but we have to remember how the process of temporary protection came about. It was a temporary process in reaction to accommodation being made available to provide for Ukrainians who had fled from a war. It was designed and put in place as a very particular measure and to facilitate people welcoming people into their homes. It is something for which its time and place is naturally coming to a conclusion. There is a better and fairer way to do it, which allows everyone to have the same access rights to accommodation. The longer term position for Ukrainians who either will or will not return home at the end of the war is that we are putting in place a situation where access to accommodation will be equal and fair with everybody else. While I acknowledge what the Deputy is saying about the scheme and some of its benefits in freeing up accommodation, at this point the best way to deal with it is the orderly wind down we are proposing and moving to the next stage.

question: 8. Deputy Naoise Ó Cearúil asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to outline the criteria used by Cuan in identifying priority locations for new refuge units; if counties with established DSGBV services, such as Kildare, may be considered for inclusion in future phases of refuge development; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20827/26]
answer: Deputy Naoise Ó Cearúil I had the opportunity to visit Teach Tearmainn women’s refuge in Kildare recently where I met Lorraine Rowan, the CEO, and her team who are carrying out incredible work. A lot of questions arose from that meeting, particularly the need to outline the criteria being used by Cuan in identifying priority locations for new refuge units and if counties with established domestic, sexual and gender based violence services, such as Kildare, may be considered for inclusion in future phases of refuge development. Deputy Jim O'Callaghan I thank Deputy Ó Cearúil for his question. I have also visited Teach Tearmainn. It is a wonderful refuge in County Kildare but, like very many of the refuges that have been established, it is obviously under pressure in terms of meeting the demand for its services, unfortunately. Cuan is instrumentally part of funding to ensure that we can provide refuges and safe homes for predominantly women who are fleeing domestic violence. We are now increasing funding for Cuan, which is within my Department, up to €80 million per year. It is a very important function that is carried out within my Department. Obviously, there is collaboration between Cuan and a series of stakeholders, whether local authorities, the Department of housing and housing agencies. Between them the objective is to try to identify and ensure there are refuges or, indeed, safe homes, which are of use also, around the country to ensure there is sufficient refuge space and safe home space for people fleeing domestic violence. The Deputy’s specific question was around whether another location in Kildare could be identified. While Kildare has not been identified as a priority location for new refuge construction in the current phase, Cuan is considering it as a location for consideration in future refuge development programmes and is supportive of ensuring Kildare is on the priority list for phase 2 development. A lot of work is being done around ensuring new refuge spaces are established. A lot were established last year. The number increased by 13, with four in Louth and nine in Dublin, bringing the total number to 172 refuges. Additionally, another nine units have been developed in Dublin 22 and further units are being developed. I will liaise with Cuan in respect of ensuring Kildare is adequately serviced. Deputy Naoise Ó Cearúil I welcome the Minister saying that Cuan is considering Kildare for phase 2 development. That is welcome news. Teach Tearmainn is in Kildare town, which is quite a considerable distance from the north of the county, from the likes of Maynooth, Leixlip, Celbridge, Kilcock and Clane, and it is technically in the Kildare South constituency. However, it caters for women not only across Kildare but also across the midlands. The work it does is truly outstanding. One thing that has arisen for Teach Tearmainn is the amount of court-based related work it has been carrying out in Naas. There is need for a refuge centre in Naas, although I should say it has safe houses there. When will phase 2 be considered so that the likes of Teach Tearmainn can plan for the future? Deputy Jim O'Callaghan We need to take a broad look at the work Cuan is doing. It is working towards having a minimum of 50 new refuge units under construction across multiple sites this year. Last year the number of safe homes increased by eight which increased the total safe-home capacity to 60. It is working to increase that capacity to 94. That means that by the end of 2026, we aim to increase the number of safe accommodation spaces, refuges and safe homes to 287. I will come back to the Deputy on the priority phase 2 development issue he raised in terms of timelines.
