A number of new court rules have been completed including, but not limited to: • rules allowing defendants to make or increase a lodgement or tender without leave of the court in personal injury cases where a medical report is lodged; • rules encouraging greater compliance with time limits for hearing and determination of pre-trial (interlocutory) motions; • rules allowing the raising of particulars and Section 11 Notices under the Civil Liability and Courts Act 2004 by way of a single composite notice; and • digital Rules enabling e-filing, e-service, and e-issuing of court orders and documents were enacted in the first half of 2025 for all court jurisdictions. A simplified version of application forms has also been developed in support of the Assisted Decision-Making (Capacity) Act 2015, which commenced in April 2023. In addition, an informal consolidation of Superior Court Rules and Circuit Court Rules is now available on the Courts Service website. On 16 December 2025, the Government approved the General Scheme of the Civil Reform Bill 2025. Amongst a range of improvements to civil law procedures, the Bill will codify the existing law on judicial review, placing it on a statutory basis. Key reforms should ensure that the system cannot be misused on purely technical grounds, costs are reduced where possible and litigants have sufficient standing to properly challenge decisions. Given the significant challenges currently facing our State in terms of housing shortages, energy deficits, inadequate water supplies and climate changes, all of which are exacerbated by the demands of a rising population, we can no longer delay on reform of the judicial review system. I am confident that the Civil Reform Bill will remove weaknesses in the current Judicial Review regime, eliminate impediments to progress and deliver reform for the public benefit. I am also confident that measures in the Bill preserve the right of the citizen to ensure that public bodies act lawfully and are accountable for their decisions. Another major area of reform in the Bill is in relation to Discovery, which will be replaced with a system of Production of Documents focused on those documents which parties intend to, or are reasonably likely to, rely on at trial. The Kelly Report found that economically stronger parties frequently weaponised the current discovery regime to effectively impede the less well-resourced party in the conduct of proceedings. The reforms I am introducing should minimise both delay and cost in the conduct of civil litigation in the State and achieve greater equality between parties. The proposed Bill, in implementing the recommendations of the Kelly Report, will also provide for a suite of civil reform measures including the creation of case conduct principles, a presumption against granting of adjournments, limiting the term of a Lis Pendens; deemed discontinuance of civil actions and a requirement for plaintiffs in personal injuries actions to distinguish between pre-existing injuries and those which are the subject of the claim. Further, the Bill will amend the general monetary jurisdiction of the District Court from €15,000 to €20,000, the Circuit Court generally from €75,000 to €100,000 and for Personal Injuries proceedings from €60,000 to €100,000. These changes will result in more non-complex cases being heard in lower courts, in particularly Personal Injuries Cases, and should reduce legal costs.

question: 55. Deputy David Maxwell asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if a proposed date has been set for the next Garda Reserve recruitment campaign; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [11574/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Programme for Government commits to examining a range of further measures to enable An Garda Síochána to increase the personnel in the organisation, including recruiting 5,000 new Garda members in the lifetime of the Government and increasing the Garda Reserve. The Garda Vote in Budget 2026 includes unprecedented funding of €2.74 billion which will support the recruitment of up to 1,000 new Gardaí, 200 more Garda staff and a doubling of the Garda Reserve to over 600. Following the introduction of new regulations governing recruitment, training and deployment of the Reserve, a competition to recruit Garda Reserves opened in June 2024 and received over 1,800 applications. In addition, to help support the work of Reserves, the maximum stipend a Reserve member receives for voluntary service in a given year has been increased from €1,000 to €3,000. The first cohort of 19 successful candidates entered Templemore in 2025 and 17 of these attested in November 2025. A further class of Garda Reserves are currently in training and further intakes will commence training during 2026. I also understand that An Garda Síochána are engaging with Publicjobs in relation to the possible scheduling of the next recruitment competition for those interested in applying to join the Garda Reserve.

question: 56. Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of Gardaí in County Meath; if he is aware that County Meath has, for years, had the lowest number of gardaí per population in the State; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19697/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration This Government is committed to ensuring that An Garda Síochána has the resources it needs to fight crime and a strengthened, well-resourced Garda organisation is central to this policy. The Garda Vote in Budget 2026 has unprecedented funding of over €2.74 billion and will support recruitment training and staffing. I am informed that, as of January 2026 the latest date for which figures are available, the total Garda workforce is over 18,000, the highest ever level. As of January 2026, there are 554 Garda members assigned to the Meath/Westmeath Division. This includes 24 Community Gardaí, 33 members assigned to Roads Policing and 32 probationer Gardaí assigned to the division since January 2025. Additionally there are 78 Garda staff assigned to the Meath/Westmeath Division. The Garda Commissioner and his senior management team keep the distribution of resources under ongoing review and I understand that, when allocating and transferring Garda members to and from any Division, consideration is given to commitments and undertakings outlined in the Annual Policing Plan. In deciding on the allocation of resources, An Garda Síochána takes into account a number of factors, including: • Local and national crime trends and workloads; • Policing arrangements and operational strategies; • Minimum establishment statistics; • Local population and trends, geographical area and size; • Transfer applications, including welfare, personnel issues and concerns.

question: 57. Deputy Louise O'Reilly asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether future revisions of the child maintenance calculator will incorporate cost-of-living and necessary expenditure considerations; whether the formula of the child maintenance calculator will be benchmarked to inflation; whether international best practice models are being reviewed as part of this reform; the consultation that took place with single parents and family law practitioners prior to implementation; how his Department plans to monitor outcomes for children affected by this model; if he is aware of the disproportionate rates of poverty and material deprivation affecting children in single parent households; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20908/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 38 and 57 together. The development of the Child Maintenance Guidelines was a key recommendation of the 2024 Review of the Enforcement of Child Maintenance Orders. An interdepartmental group (“The Child Maintenance Guidelines Committee”) was established in February 2024 to develop the child maintenance guidelines for use by all parties, on a voluntary basis, when putting child maintenance arrangements in place. The Committee was Chaired by my Department and its membership included representatives from the Department of Social Protection, Department of Children, Disability and Equality, Legal Aid Board, Courts Service and Tusla. Development of the guidelines was informed by a comprehensive comparative review covering England and Wales, Scotland, Northern Ireland, United States, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Germany, Austria, Denmark and the Netherlands. It was also critically important to listen to the views of parents who have been involved in making child maintenance arrangements. For this reason, in April 2025, the Committee conducted a survey-based consultation to get the public's views on important aspects of the guidelines. The published guidelines along with a comparative review of guidelines in other jurisdictions and a public consultation report can be accessed at the following link: [ www.gov.ie/en/department-of-justice-home-affairs-and-migration/publications/child-maintenance-guidelines-for-ireland/ ] The Guidelines are compatible with Irish legislation on child maintenance and can be used by the courts. However, the courts are not obliged to consider the guidelines when making child maintenance orders. The objectives of the Guidelines include: • To establish fair, consistent and predictable amounts of maintenance for children whose parents are not together. • To increase transparency, consistency and predictability for those seeking and paying child maintenance. • To reduce conflict and tension between parents by making the calculation of child maintenance more objective. • To reduce the number of child maintenance applications made to the courts by giving parents guidance in setting the levels of child maintenance and by encouraging private maintenance agreements. • To ensure consistent treatment of parents and children who are in similar circumstances. • To promote a culture of payment of child maintenance. • Once the Guidelines were finalised an accompanying online calculator was developed to make the guidelines more accessible. The child maintenance calculator was launched on 26 February 2026, following publication of the Child Maintenance Guidelines on 19 January. The guidelines and accompanying calculator are a first for Ireland and a significant step forward to improving fairness, consistency and transparency when parents are making child maintenance arrangements. The child maintenance calculator is intended as a voluntary support tool to help parents begin the process of working out an appropriate amount of child maintenance for their child or children. The estimate provided by the calculator is not legally binding or enforceable, nor will it change an existing court order. It is a guide only. Child maintenance is calculated by looking at: each parent’s gross annual income; share of parenting time; the age/number of the children; and, the age/number of other dependent children each parent has. Significant costs related to disability, childcare, education or medical needs are not included in the child maintenance estimate. The variation in costs of this nature due to individual circumstances mean that they are not suited to inclusion in guidelines and a calculator such as this. These types of expenses are typically handled outside the standard way of calculating maintenance. This is in line with best practises observed internationally, where these costs are typically adjudicated outside the guidance framework. Costs of these expenses are typically shared equally between parents. Furthermore, given that the guidelines and calculator are formula based and rely on aggregate data to estimate average costs of children, they will not be appropriate in all cases. Particular circumstances where they may not be appropriate in estimating reasonable child maintenance payments include: • either parent has significant financial or other assets including property; • where non-parent carers, like grandparents, who may be involved in a child’s care are seeking maintenance; • a parent is paying child maintenance for more than one child where the children are from different relationships; • there are dependants with significant earnings, property or other financial resources; and • there are significant costs related to disability, childcare, education or medical needs. However, it may still help users to identify a potential rate of child maintenance or a starting point for discussion with the other parent. In summary, the key principles in the guidelines and calculator include: • Shared financial responsibility – Both parents are expected to contribute to the cost of raising their child based on their means; • Income shares model – Maintenance is based on the combined income of both parents, with each parent contributing a proportion that reflects their share of that income; • Recognition of parenting time – The amount of time a child spends with each parent is considered, as share of parenting time directly influences the costs each parent has; • Continuity of expenditure – Children should, as far as possible, continue to benefit from the standard of living they would have enjoyed if their parents were living together; and • Protection of basic personal needs – A self-support amount, set at the level of the ‘at risk-of-poverty’ threshold, is included to ensure parents retain sufficient income for basic personal needs. Together, these principles aim to place the child at the centre of maintenance decisions. The calculator’s key parameters will be regularly updated, to take account of annual movements in the Consumer Price Index and the Central Statistics Office’s annual Survey on Income and Living Conditions. Such updates will include the costs per child by gross household income decile; the minimum rates; household income deciles, and the self-support allowance. Regular updating and indexation of key parameters will help ensure the model and calculator remain grounded in real-world data and reflect evolving expenditure patterns. Information will also be updated on the website www.childmaintenancecalculator.ie to ensure the purpose, benefits and limitations of the online calculator are clearly outlined and available.

question: 58. Deputy Ruairí Ó Murchú asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether, in the course of his Department's review of 350,000 court cases from 2022 and 2023, further issues were identified; if so, what these issues were; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20825/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration As part of a programme of reform of criminal legal aid , my Department reviewed more than 350,000 District Court cases which took place during 2022 and 2023. As the Deputy is aware, while criminal case volumes in the District Court have decreased, expenditure on criminal legal aid in the District Court has nearly doubled, from €19 million in 2015 to €37 million in 2024. The review identified specific structural issues in the administration of criminal legal aid, namely: • Payment per appearance which incentivises additional adjournments • Multiple certificates granted for related cases increase costs and complexity • Multiple solicitors assigned in the same firm for related charges • A highly complex payment processing system creating a significant administrative burden. The proposed reform of the criminal legal aid fee structure in the District Court is aimed at addressing these structural issues. My Department has been engaging extensively with relevant stakeholders, including legal professionals and their representative bodies, on the proposed changes to the scheme. Officials from my Department met with the Bar Council and Law Society in May, July and October 2025, and again this month to discuss these reforms. My Department will continue this engagement in advance of the introduction of the new fee structure on 1 July.

question: 59. Deputy Naoise Ó Muirí asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the measures his Department is taking to ensure courthouses and facilities are suitable for victims of domestic, sexual and gender-based violence. [20957/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I am acutely conscious that coming forward to report sexual and/or domestic violence can be a deeply traumatic experience for victims and I am determined to do everything in my power to ensure that the criminal justice system empowers victims to have the confidence to report an offence, knowing they will be supported, informed, and treated respectfully and professionally for the entirety of the difficult journey they have to face. Victims and survivors of domestic, sexual and gender-based violence (DSGBV) can access a range of supports during court proceedings, including court accompaniment, information supports and referral pathways to specialist services, depending on individual circumstances and location. A key national support is Victim Support at Court (V-SAC), which provides free, independent court accompaniment and support, including practical information and support to help victims navigate the court process. V-SAC is supported through funding provided by my department under the Victims of Crime Fund. In addition, victims/survivors may be supported by specialist domestic violence and sexual violence support organisations, which can provide information, advocacy and referral supports linked to engagement with the criminal justice system. This work is complemented by wider criminal justice reforms aimed at strengthening the victim-centred response, including measures under Supporting a Victim’s Journey, the implementation plan developed to progress recommendations arising from the O’Malley Review, such as actions to support the use of intermediaries for vulnerable witnesses and improved access to information for victims through the Victims Charter website. The introduction of preliminary trial hearings under the Criminal Procedure Act 2021, is another recommendation of Supporting a Victims Journey that has been implemented. Their use improves the trial processes for a range of offences, including sexual offence cases by helping the trial process run more smoothly and reducing the potential for further trauma for victims. They also allow for certain technical and sensitive matters to be addressed in advance of the trial itself starting. In addition, the Criminal Evidence Act 1992 provides for a range of measures to assist vulnerable witnesses, including victims of DSGVB, during their testimony. This includes the utilisation of screens to shield the victim, providing evidence through a live television link, the use of intermediaries in giving testimony as part of the trial process and in limited cases, the use of pre-recorded video as evidence. These are measures to limit, as much as possible, stress, emotional and psychological detriment, and the re-traumatisation of the victim. When allocating special measures, the court is required to be cognisant of the need to protect the victim from secondary victimisation, intimidation, or retaliation. The court is required to consider the nature and circumstances of each case and the nature and circumstances of each victim, including any specific vulnerabilities or complexities relating to the case or the victim. The Courts Service is progressing its 10-year Modernisation Programme to deliver digitally enabled services designed around the user. Last year, as part of this programme, new district court forms, including those for domestic violence, were introduced. These have received very positive feedback from staff, legal practitioners, NGOs/advocacy groups and members of the public. Additionally, the rollout of a new appointment booking service allows court users to attend a court office at a time that suits them, thereby reducing waiting times. Furthermore, as part of the Modernisation Programme, the Courts Service is also developing and commencing rollout of trauma-informed practice training, tailored to the needs of the organisation and its users, for Courts Service staff.

question: 60. Deputy Pa Daly asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the date at which reckonable residence will commence for persons who are applying for citizenship or naturalisation; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20113/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I understand that the Deputy has clarified that this is a general question relating to all citizenship applicants. Applications for a certificate of naturalisation are assessed individually in accordance with the provisions of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956, as amended. In general, applicants are required to have 5 years of reckonable residence in the State before making an application. In the case of spouses of Irish nationals, the requirement is 3 years. In all cases, the final 12 months prior to an application must be continuous residence in the State. However, applicants may be absent from the State for up to 70 days during that period to allow travel for business, family or holiday purposes. Information on which immigration permissions qualify as reckonable residence, and a helpful residency calculator, are available on my Department's Immigration Service Delivery web site at: www.irishimmigration.ie/naturalisation-residency-calculator/.

question: 61. Deputy Tom Brabazon asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the actions his Department are taking to address domestic violence, including supports available for victims; and if the position regarding the implementation of the Third National Strategy on Domestic, Sexual and Gender Based Violence 2022-2026. [20111/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 61 and 69 together. This Government has taken unprecedented actions to tackle the scourge of domestic and sexual violence. These actions include an increase in funding under Budget 2026, to support Cuan and services working to tackle domestic and sexual abuse, and the implementation of the Zero Tolerance Strategy. The total funding of €80 million represents an increased investment of €12 million year-on-year. Last June, I published a targeted implementation plan for the final phase of Zero Tolerance, the Third National Strategy on domestic, sexual and general based violence. It contains 95 actions across the Strategy’s four pillars of Protection, Prevention, Prosecution and Policy Co-ordination, with a strong focus on delivery and collective action. Priority areas include continuing national leadership and cross government alignment, expanding refuge accommodation, delivering a comprehensive national emergency domestic violence accommodation plan, and advancing legislative reform. The legislative change includes measures: • to allow perpetrators of domestic violence to be included on a new register of domestic violence judgments; • to restrict disclosure of counselling records in sexual offence trials; • to reform sexual consent laws; • to criminalise offering or advertising rent in exchange for sex; and • to allow for the removal of guardianship rights of a person who has been convicted of killing their intimate partner. Other areas of note include the expansion of services for children and young people experiencing domestic or sexual violence, and the reform of the education curriculum, to empower students with the skills to nurture healthy relationships. I will shortly be bringing the Progress Report on implementation of the Zero Tolerance Strategy to Cabinet, which focuses on the progress of implementation in 2025. Specialised support services for victims/survivors of DSGBV include refuge and safe home services, national helplines such as Women’s Aid, Dublin Rape Crisis Centre, Men's Development Network and organisations such as Men's Aid MOVE, Pavee Point, Ruhama, and Akidwa. Nationwide helplines for victims of domestic, sexual, and gender-based violence, including two 24/7 Freephone helplines, are operated through Cuan-funded services. A third national helpline is focused on male victims of DSGBV. These helplines are confidential, offer information and advice, and increasingly provide online support. A comprehensive list of all state services, national helplines and support services (both national and by county) can be found on [ alwayshere.ie ] Cuan has committed to lead the development and fund the delivery of high quality and effective services and supports that are accessible to all individuals affected by or at risk of domestic, sexual and gender-based violence. Cuan is leading the development of safe accommodation for victims of domestic violence. Refuge units and Safe Homes are available nationwide and Cuan is working closely with stakeholders to ensure further development of emergency accommodation, which is a priority under the Zero Tolerance Strategy. An Garda Síochána and my Department are continuing to work hard to strengthen trust and confidence in the system, so that victims will feel confident in coming forward to report what has happened to them and get justice. An Garda Síochána prioritise and proactively respond to incidents of domestic abuse. The nationwide roll out of Divisional Protective Service Units ensures that when victims of crimes such as domestic abuse and sexual violence present to Gardaí, they are met with a consistently high standard of specialist, sensitive, professional and expert assistance. I can advise the Deputy that there is now a DPSU in every Garda Division. Among the key roles the government plays in tackling DSGBV, is to continue to raise awareness of the issue itself, the supports available to victims and survivors and to change problematic behaviours and attitudes that persist in our society that allow such violence and abuse to continue. There are a number of awareness campaigns, including on signposting domestic violence supports, and encouraging victims of violence to tell their stories – Always Here and Hardest Stories. The Government is delivering on the commitments in the Zero Tolerance Strategy to achieve a society where domestic violence, and the toxic attitudes that fuel it, are not accepted.

question: 62. Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to outline his Department’s policy in relation to the use of “electronic tagging” of prisoners, specifically with reference to the acute overcrowding of prisons we are facing; if the number of electronic tags in circulation could be provided for each of the years since the inception of tagging, in tabular form; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20541/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 37 and 62 together. The Programme for Government commits to implement electronic tagging for appropriate categories of prisoner. Existing legislation, including the Bail Act 1997 (as amended), the Criminal Justice Act 2006 (as amended), and the Sex Offenders Act 2001 (as amended), provides for the use of electronic monitoring (EM) in specific circumstances, including: • Individuals who have been charged with a serious offence or are appealing a District Court sentence and admitted to bail under certain conditions, such as curfew or exclusion zones (Bail Act 1997, as amended). • Persons on Temporary Release who are subject to movement restrictions or those who are subject to Restriction on Movement Orders as an alternative to a custodial sentence. (Criminal Justice Act 2006, as amended). • Convicted sex offenders subject to a post-release supervision order or a sex offender order that that includes a prohibition on going to, being in or leaving a specific place (Sex Offenders Act 2001, as amended). My Department is leading a cross-agency project to introduce EM for specific categories of individuals, as committed to in the Programme for Government, and in line with existing legal provisions. A steering group is in place, made up of sectoral representatives, who will be involved in the delivery of electronic tagging and comprises of representatives from the Department and relevant bodies including An Garda Síochána, the Courts Service, the Irish Prison Service, the Probation Service, the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions, and the Parole Board. Work is underway involving representatives from the various agencies, to prepare to operationalise electronic monitoring. This includes consideration of technology, data protection, procurement, implementation, and operating model design. My Department is tendering for an EM service provider for a 12-month pilot phase, which will focus on individuals on temporary release (TR) nationally and those admitted to bail in a pilot area. The pilot approach will allow for processes and procedures to be tested before a wider scale national rollout, while also supporting the agencies involved to build capability and knowledge of the EM system. Insights from the pilot will inform any future national rollout and procurement. Under Budget 2026 funding of €2.1m was allocated for the project to allow for staffing, procurement, and other set up costs. The tender for electronic monitoring was published on 4 December 2025 and closed at 5pm on 6 February without any compliant responses being received, therefore, the competition was cancelled. The Department has made a small number of changes to the technical specification and has now re-issued the RFT. Details are available on the eTenders site: www.etenders.gov.ie.

question: 63. Deputy Paul Murphy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether he agrees with the recommendation of a report commissioned by him called An Assessment of the Efficacy of Bail Laws in Ireland, which states that "the responsibility for the prosecution of offences should be removed from the Gardaí and all future Court proceedings should be conducted by legal professionals" (details supplied); his views on same; and if he will bring forward legislation to implement this recommendation. [19188/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The report completed by Mr Lorcan Staines SC ‘An Assessment of the Efficacy of Bail Laws in Ireland’ was published by my Department in November 2025. I would again like to express my thanks to Lorcan Staines for his work in compiling this comprehensive report. This examination of our bail laws and subsequent proposals underlines the need for additional actions to be considered, to ensure the criminal justice system effectively mitigates against risks that may be associated with individuals on bail. A number of the recommendations are under active consideration, or already in the process of being implemented, across my Department. The report recommended that the responsibility for the prosecution of offences be removed from the Gardaí and all future Court proceedings should be conducted by legal professionals. This was previously recommended by the Commission on the Future of Policing in Ireland and this was accepted in principle by the then Government, subject to a further evaluation of the implications, including resources. That subsequent operational evaluation, which was undertaken by a High-Level Review Group, concluded that the change was not appropriate and recommended instead the implementation of what has been termed the Reform Model. While the Reform Model deviates from the specific recommendation, it captures its intent. The model acknowledges shortcomings and considered the Commission’s central finding that the system must be strengthened significantly to meet existing challenges, and to address future demands. The key elements of the Reform Model include the following recommendations: • That An Garda Síochána retain responsibility for prosecution decisions in respect of many minor offences on behalf of the Director of Public Prosecutions. Rules around who in An Garda Síochána may make prosecution decisions would be clarified, to ensure the requisite level of authority, accountability and experience. • That An Garda Síochána retains responsibility for the presentation of prosecutions at court, to be supported by enhanced oversight and training from the office of the Director of Public Prosecutions (ODPP). • That the ODPP oversight of the exercise of prosecutions functions by Gardaí in its name be enhanced. This could include mandatory case sampling, record keeping, statistic gathering and publication, and regular structured auditing. It was intended that the Reform Model would be built on ongoing developments in An Garda Síochána in relation to oversight generally, in particular the development and roll out of the Operating Model, and the new Divisional Court Management Office structures. The use of the Divisional Court Management Office structure is expected to deliver many benefits including consistent delivery of court management services across all the Divisions, dedicated points of contact for court management related matters in each Division, an enhanced quality assurance by dedicated skilled personnel and the introduction of new national standardised/optimised processes designed to support the Divisional court management functions. A Summary Prosecution Reform Steering Committee, including representatives from my Department, the Department of the Taoiseach, the Director of Public Prosecutions, An Garda Síochána, the Courts Service, and the Government Chief Information Officer, has been established and will continue to work to drive forward the detailed design and implementation of the Reform Model.

question: 64. Deputy Shane Moynihan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of Garda patrols carried out in the Lucan/Clondalkin District between January 2025 and February 2026; and to provide a month-by-month breakdown; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20781/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Under the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024, the Garda Commissioner is responsible for the distribution and stationing of Garda personnel throughout the State. While I am unable to direct the Commissioner in these matters, I am assured that the resourcing of each Garda Division is fully considered within the overall context of the needs and requirements of Garda Divisions throughout the country. I am informed that a 'patrol' can be defined as any time Gardaí leave a station, whether on foot, by bicycle/motorbike, car or in another vehicle. I am advised by Garda Authorities that GardaSAFE, which manages and monitors emergency calls and dispatch resources, has been rolled out nationwide with initial statistical reports on call volumes expected in Q3 2026, with the incremental development of other reports to follow.
