question: 1287. Deputy John Paul O'Shea asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the current number of Garda members assigned to Roads Policing Units; the way in which this compares with the number assigned in 2014; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18972/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 1232, 1287, 1327 and 1331 together. An Garda Síochána play a vital role in enforcing road traffic law and in making our roads safer for all road users, including vulnerable road users. Road traffic laws are enforced by Gardaí assigned to Roads Policing and as part of the day-to-day duties of uniformed Gardaí nationwide. This includes a programme of high-visibility road safety and enforcement operations carried out in partnership with other state agencies. In this regard it should be noted that around 65% of drug-driving and drink-driving checks are carried out by regular Gardaí. The Garda Commissioner is responsible for the management and administration of An Garda Síochána under section 33 of the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024, which includes the distribution and stationing of Gardaí throughout the State and Garda policies. I am fully committed to ensuring that An Garda Síochána has the resources it needs, with Budget 2026 providing unprecedented funding of €2.74 billion to support recruitment, training and staffing. Recruitment into An Garda Síochána is now gathering real momentum and just under 800 trainees entered the Garda College in 2025, the highest number since 2018. As Garda recruitment continues and accelerates, additional Gardaí will become available to be deployed to priority areas. An Garda Síochána publishes figures in relation to the allocation of Gardaí nationally. This includes a breakdown of Gardaí assigned to Roads Policing by Garda Division from 2014 to the end of January 2026, the latest date for which figures are available. This can be found at the following links: 2014-2025 www.garda.ie/en/about-us/our-departments/human-resources-and-people-development/garda-hr-directorate/garda-strength-breakdown-2025/garda-strength-breakdown-2025.html 2026 www.garda.ie/en/about-us/our-departments/human-resources-and-people-development/garda-hr-directorate/garda-strength-breakdown-2026/january-2026.html The Deputy should select the most recent date and then select the file titled ‘Roads Policing by division 2014 to the most recent date" to access a breakdown of Gardaí assigned by Division. The Deputy may also be interested to note that An Garda Síochána publishes figures relating to Roads Policing Offences on a quarterly basis. This includes Fixed Charge Notices (FCNs) for offences relating to Speeding Overall as well as broken down into Intercept (Garda issued) and Non-Intercept (Speed Camera Van Operator). This can be found at the following link: www.garda.ie/en/roads-policing/statistics/roads%20policing%20offences%20by%20region%20and%20division/ The Deputy can select the “Roads Policing” file for the time period required.

question: 1288. Deputy Ged Nash asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to confirm that the recently launched child maintenance calculator is intended as guidance only; that it is not intended to influence judicial decision-making in the area; the frequency with which the calculator will be reviewed to reflect changes in the rate of inflation; if international best practice informed the development of the tool; the consultation which took place in the development of the calculators; if outcomes for children will be a feature of operational reviews of the calculator; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19003/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 1288, 1335, 1339, 1340, 1341, 1342, 1343, 1406 and 1407 together. The development of the Child Maintenance Guidelines was a key recommendation of the 2024 Review of the Enforcement of Child Maintenance Orders. An interdepartmental group (“The Child Maintenance Guidelines Committee”) was established in February 2024 to develop the child maintenance guidelines for use by all parties, on a voluntary basis, when putting child maintenance arrangements in place. The Committee was Chaired by my Department and its membership included representatives from the Department of Social Protection, Department of Children, Disability and Equality, Legal Aid Board, Courts Service and Tusla. Development of the guidelines was informed by a comprehensive comparative review covering England and Wales, Scotland, Northern Ireland, United States, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Germany, Austria, Denmark and the Netherlands. It was also critically important to listen to the views of parents who have been involved in making child maintenance arrangements. For this reason, in April 2025, the Committee conducted a survey-based consultation to get the public's views on important aspects of the guidelines. The published guidelines along with a comparative review of guidelines in other jurisdictions and a public consultation report can be accessed at the following link: www.gov.ie/en/department-of-justice-home-affairs-and-migration/publications/child-maintenance-guidelines-for-ireland/ The Guidelines are compatible with Irish legislation on child maintenance and can be used by the courts. However, the courts are not obliged to consider the guidelines when making child maintenance orders. The objectives of the Guidelines include: • To establish fair, consistent and predictable amounts of maintenance for children whose parents are not together. • To increase transparency, consistency and predictability for those seeking and paying child maintenance. • To reduce conflict and tension between parents by making the calculation of child maintenance more objective. • To reduce the number of child maintenance applications made to the courts by giving parents guidance in setting the levels of child maintenance and by encouraging private maintenance agreements. • To ensure consistent treatment of parents and children who are in similar circumstances. • To promote a culture of payment of child maintenance. • Once the Guidelines were finalised an accompanying online calculator was developed to make the guidelines more accessible. The child maintenance calculator was launched on 26 February 2026, following publication of the Child Maintenance Guidelines on 19 January. The guidelines and accompanying calculator are a first for Ireland and a significant step forward to improving fairness, consistency and transparency when parents are making child maintenance arrangements. The child maintenance calculator is intended as a voluntary support tool to help parents begin the process of working out an appropriate amount of child maintenance for their child or children. The estimate provided by the calculator is not legally binding or enforceable, nor will it change an existing court order. It is a guide only. Child maintenance is calculated by looking at: each parent’s gross annual income; share of parenting time; the age/number of the children; and the age/number of other dependent children each parent has. Significant costs related to disability, childcare, education or medical needs are not included in the child maintenance estimate. The variation in costs of this nature due to individual circumstances mean that they are not suited to inclusion in guidelines and a calculator such as this. These types of expenses are typically handled outside the standard way of calculating maintenance. This is in line with best practises observed internationally, where these costs are typically adjudicated outside the guidance framework. Costs of these expenses are typically shared equally between parents. Furthermore, given that the guidelines and calculator are formula based and rely on aggregate data to estimate average costs of children, they will not be appropriate in all cases. Particular circumstances where they may not be appropriate in estimating reasonable child maintenance payments include: • either parent has significant financial or other assets including property; • where non-parent carers, like grandparents, who may be involved in a child’s care are seeking maintenance; • a parent is paying child maintenance for more than one child where the children are from different relationships; • there are dependants with significant earnings, property or other financial resources; and • there are significant costs related to disability, childcare, education or medical needs. However, it may still help users to identify a potential rate of child maintenance or a starting point for discussion with the other parent. In summary, the key principles in the guidelines and calculator include: • Shared financial responsibility – Both parents are expected to contribute to the cost of raising their child based on their means; • Income shares model – Maintenance is based on the combined income of both parents, with each parent contributing a proportion that reflects their share of that income; • Recognition of parenting time – The amount of time a child spends with each parent is considered, as share of parenting time directly influences the costs each parent has; • Continuity of expenditure – Children should, as far as possible, continue to benefit from the standard of living they would have enjoyed if their parents were living together; and • Protection of basic personal needs – A self-support amount, set at the level of the ‘at risk-of-poverty’ threshold, is included to ensure parents retain sufficient income for basic personal needs. Together, these principles aim to place the child at the centre of maintenance decisions. The calculator’s key parameters will be regularly updated, to take account of annual movements in the Consumer Price Index and the Central Statistics Office’s annual Survey on Income and Living Conditions. Such updates will include the costs per child by gross household income decile; the minimum rates; household income deciles, and the self-support allowance. Regular updating and indexation of key parameters will help ensure the model and calculator remain grounded in real-world data and reflect evolving expenditure patterns. Information will also be updated on the website www.childmaintenancecalculator.ie to ensure the purpose, benefits and limitations of the online calculator are clearly outlined and available.

question: 1289. Deputy William Aird asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the position regarding the provision of a women's refuge in County Laois; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19014/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Combatting all forms of domestic, sexual and gender-based violence (DSGBV) and ensuring that victims and survivors receive the support and care they need are absolute priorities for me. This Government has taken unprecedented actions to tackle DSGBV, including by increasing funding to almost €80 million under Budget 2026 to support Cuan, the DSGBV Agency, as well as services working to implement the 'Zero Tolerance' Strategy. Cuan is committed to providing safe and accessible accommodation and support services for victims and survivors, wherever they are in Ireland. Cuan is currently collaborating with Laois Domestic Abuse Services, Laois County Council, the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage, and the Housing Agency to deliver a capital project for an eight-unit refuge in Laois. I am advised that a site has been secured for this refuge. Cuan is taking the lead on identifying an Approved Housing Body (AHB) through an expression of interest (EOI) process, with Laois Domestic Abuse Services reaffirming its role as the domestic violence service provider for this project. The EOI will seek eligible AHBs capable of accessing Capital Assistance Scheme funding and interested in partnering with Laois Domestic Abuse Services, who play a crucial role in delivering services locally.

question: 1290. Deputy William Aird asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he intends to overhaul the free legal aid system currently in place; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19015/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 1297, 1290, 1291, 1295, 1296, 1387, 1388 and 1389 together. The Legal Aid Board is the statutory, independent body responsible for the provision of civil legal aid and advice to qualifying individuals. The civil legal aid scheme has two parts: a legal advice element and a legal representation element. Eligibility for the scheme is determined by reference to a financial assessment and the merits of the case being taken. In accordance with the provisions of the Civil Legal Aid Act 1995 (as amended) and associated Regulations, the Legal Aid Board calculates financial eligibility with reference to the applicant’s disposable income and disposable assets after certain allowances are applied to both. Currently, the disposable income threshold is €18,000, while the disposable asset threshold is €100,000. The applicant must also meet the merits and other criteria under the Act. The primary merits criteria are that: • a reasonably prudent person, whose means were such that the cost of seeking such services at his or her own expense, while representing a financial obstacle to him or her would not be such as to impose undue hardship upon him or her, would be likely to seek such services in such circumstances at his or her own expense, and • a solicitor or barrister acting reasonably would be likely to advise him or her to obtain such services at his or her own expense. Furthermore, section 29(2)(b) of the Civil Legal Aid Act 1995 provides that the Legal Aid Board may waive any contribution payable from an applicant or accept a lower contribution if failure to do so would cause undue hardship to the applicant. The Legal Aid Board also engages private solicitors to supplement its services in certain areas of law on a case-by-case basis. A priority service is provided by the Board in certain cases, including cases involving domestic violence. The Family Law Legal Aid panels include a District Court Private Family Law Panel covering matters in the District Court and on appeal to the Circuit Court under the Domestic Violence Act 2018. In its over forty years of operation, the Civil Legal Aid Scheme has been a significant and beneficial public service, providing legal aid and advice to people of limited means in civil disputes, including family law. However, since the Scheme was set up, Irish society has changed, and the demands of the service have grown. In June 2022, a Civil Legal Aid Review Group under the chairmanship of former Chief Justice Frank Clarke SC, was established to review the current operation of the Civil Legal Aid Scheme. The outputs of the review were published in July 2025 and contained recommendations relating to eligibility for the Scheme including the income threshold, allowances and other aspects of the Scheme. Since the overall available income eligibility threshold is influenced by the level of deductible allowances, any changes must be considered in the round and the potential implications that such changes might have on the operation of the Scheme. While the Review highlights the need for comprehensive legal aid reform, it also recognises that the current legal aid system must function effectively in the meantime. A critical aspect of any implementation will therefore be the careful sequencing of reforms. Many of them would need to work in parallel with other ongoing reforms in the civil justice system. Having a civil legal aid scheme and a Legal Aid Board which is equipped to meet the changing needs of society is critical to ensuring access to justice, particularly for those who have very modest means. I was pleased to announce, as part of Budget 2026 measures for the justice sector, and as outlined in the Revised Estimates for Public Services 2026, additional funding of €8.97 million will be made available for the Legal Aid Board in 2026 bring its total allocation for the year to €73.08 million. This increase of 14% in funding will support a programme of modernisation and increased access to justice for clients of the Board. The recommendations will also have to be considered with due regard to the findings from Ireland’s first legal needs survey, recently completed with the support of the European Commission and the OECD. This survey will provide invaluable insights into the extent of legal need in Ireland. While preliminary results of the survey have been released on gov.ie, further analysis will be required before the full results are published. I have asked my officials to examine the recommendations, particularly in light of these developments. I will revert to Government in due course with proposals to reform the Scheme.

question: 1292. Deputy William Aird asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the position regarding the additional block extension at Midlands prison; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19017/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration On conclusion of the NDP Review in July 2025, I secured a total investment of €527 million from 2026 to 2030 for the IPS. €495 million is to be invested in infrastructural projects and, in line with the Programme for Government, includes an overall target of delivering over 1,500 spaces by 2031. This will be the largest ever building programme in the prison estate and includes a large extension to the existing Cork Prison on the site of the old, decommissioned Cork Prison, a new block in Wheatfield, an additional block extension at Midlands prison, and additional spaces at Castlerea, Mountjoy, Cloverhill, Portlaoise, Limerick and the Dóchas centre. Since 2024, 232 spaces have been constructed across the Prison Estate, with 126 constructed in 2024 and 106 constructed in 2025. The majority of these spaces are in use, with the remainder coming on stream very soon. There are plans to build another 65 spaces in 2026. The block extension at Midlands prison has started the tender process for the technical design consultancy.

question: 1293. Deputy William Aird asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration when the next recruitment campaign for prison officers will open; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19018/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The 2026 Recruit Prison Officer recruitment campaign is provisionally scheduled to open, in conjunction with Public Jobs, in September this year. I am advised that the Irish Prison Service continually monitors the staffing requirements and vacancies that arise, coupled with routine reviews of the resource requirements across the estate based on the prisoner cohort and the overall prison population. In 2025, a total of 304 Recruit Prison Officers were recruited.

question: 1294. Deputy John Brady asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration for an update on the tendering process related to the operation of the contribution charging model for IPAS residents in employment or self-employment; the expected cost; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19044/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The 2025 Programme for Government included a commitment to introducing a contribution model for people in international protection accommodation. A proposal for working international protection applicants to contribute to the cost of their IPAS accommodation was considered by Government in November 2025 and is now being progressed by the Department. IPAS Accommodation is provided for in EU regulations and transposed into Irish law. Statutory Instrument No 230/2018, European Communities (Reception Conditions) Regulations 2018, provides that all IP applicants are entitled to Material Reception Conditions. The Regulations further provide that where a resident is in receipt of an income above a certain level, they may be required to make a contribution to the cost of providing reception condition services. The contribution rates are set out in a Schedule to the Regulations and are proportionate to the amount that people earn. The contribution to cost scheme will be implemented within a planned 12-month period, allowing for the development of systems and resources to assess eligibility, share data securely and collect and process payments. The implementation process, which is underway, will include procurement of an appropriate third-party provider service, and this procurement process will involve further detailed analysis as the scheme comes into operation including determining the implementation cost. The introduction of this contribution for international protection applicants who are working and earning and income is aligned with processes already in place in other EU member states. The scheme will have a review and appeals process incorporated into the process as it is developed for implementation, expected by the end of 2026.

question: 1295. Deputy Donna McGettigan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the timeline and action plan for reform of the scheme of civil legal aid and advice; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19046/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 1297, 1290, 1291, 1295, 1296, 1387, 1388 and 1389 together. The Legal Aid Board is the statutory, independent body responsible for the provision of civil legal aid and advice to qualifying individuals. The civil legal aid scheme has two parts: a legal advice element and a legal representation element. Eligibility for the scheme is determined by reference to a financial assessment and the merits of the case being taken. In accordance with the provisions of the Civil Legal Aid Act 1995 (as amended) and associated Regulations, the Legal Aid Board calculates financial eligibility with reference to the applicant’s disposable income and disposable assets after certain allowances are applied to both. Currently, the disposable income threshold is €18,000, while the disposable asset threshold is €100,000. The applicant must also meet the merits and other criteria under the Act. The primary merits criteria are that: • a reasonably prudent person, whose means were such that the cost of seeking such services at his or her own expense, while representing a financial obstacle to him or her would not be such as to impose undue hardship upon him or her, would be likely to seek such services in such circumstances at his or her own expense, and • a solicitor or barrister acting reasonably would be likely to advise him or her to obtain such services at his or her own expense. Furthermore, section 29(2)(b) of the Civil Legal Aid Act 1995 provides that the Legal Aid Board may waive any contribution payable from an applicant or accept a lower contribution if failure to do so would cause undue hardship to the applicant. The Legal Aid Board also engages private solicitors to supplement its services in certain areas of law on a case-by-case basis. A priority service is provided by the Board in certain cases, including cases involving domestic violence. The Family Law Legal Aid panels include a District Court Private Family Law Panel covering matters in the District Court and on appeal to the Circuit Court under the Domestic Violence Act 2018. In its over forty years of operation, the Civil Legal Aid Scheme has been a significant and beneficial public service, providing legal aid and advice to people of limited means in civil disputes, including family law. However, since the Scheme was set up, Irish society has changed, and the demands of the service have grown. In June 2022, a Civil Legal Aid Review Group under the chairmanship of former Chief Justice Frank Clarke SC, was established to review the current operation of the Civil Legal Aid Scheme. The outputs of the review were published in July 2025 and contained recommendations relating to eligibility for the Scheme including the income threshold, allowances and other aspects of the Scheme. Since the overall available income eligibility threshold is influenced by the level of deductible allowances, any changes must be considered in the round and the potential implications that such changes might have on the operation of the Scheme. While the Review highlights the need for comprehensive legal aid reform, it also recognises that the current legal aid system must function effectively in the meantime. A critical aspect of any implementation will therefore be the careful sequencing of reforms. Many of them would need to work in parallel with other ongoing reforms in the civil justice system. Having a civil legal aid scheme and a Legal Aid Board which is equipped to meet the changing needs of society is critical to ensuring access to justice, particularly for those who have very modest means. I was pleased to announce, as part of Budget 2026 measures for the justice sector, and as outlined in the Revised Estimates for Public Services 2026, additional funding of €8.97 million will be made available for the Legal Aid Board in 2026 bring its total allocation for the year to €73.08 million. This increase of 14% in funding will support a programme of modernisation and increased access to justice for clients of the Board. The recommendations will also have to be considered with due regard to the findings from Ireland’s first legal needs survey, recently completed with the support of the European Commission and the OECD. This survey will provide invaluable insights into the extent of legal need in Ireland. While preliminary results of the survey have been released on gov.ie, further analysis will be required before the full results are published. I have asked my officials to examine the recommendations, particularly in light of these developments. I will revert to Government in due course with proposals to reform the Scheme.

question: 1298. Deputy Donna McGettigan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the plans to introduce a properly resourced national legal information and advice service for women, including victims of domestic violence; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19049/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration My Department seeks to ensure that individuals, including women and victims of domestic violence, are aware of and can access the range of supports available to them, including legal information and advice services. The Department continues to progress a number of initiatives to ensure that victims of domestic, sexual and gender-based violence (DSGBV) know where to access support organisations. Cuan, the statutory agency responsible for coordinating services relating to DSGBV run public awareness campaigns such as Always Here, which highlight DSGBV and promotes the supports available to victims. More broadly, my Department supports victims of crime through initiatives such as the Know Your Rights campaign, which aims to raise awareness of the victims’ rights and the services available to them. There are a range of statutory and independent bodies that provide legal information and advice across relevant areas. The Citizen's information Board is the statutory body that provides independent information, advice and advocacy on a wide range of public and social services, through its website and nationwide network of Citizens Information Services and Citizens Information Phone Service. The Legal Aid Board is an independent statutory body responsible for the provision of civil legal aid and advice to qualifying individuals. It offers both legal advice and legal representation, covering family law, childcare, and other civil matters. In Budget 2026, I was pleased to announce an increase in funding for the Board was increased of 8 million, a 12.5% increase, to support modernisation and improve access to justice. Free Legal Advice Centres (FLAC) have received grant-in-aid funding from my department since 1992, supporting the delivery of information, advice, and advocacy services. Its telephone information and referral line provides first-stop legal information. Funding for FLAC has increased from €500,000 in 2025 to €750,000 in 2026, enabling enhancements to the service. This includes prioritising callers with the greatest need, including victims of domestic violence, and developing a more effective and comprehensive legal assistance service. In addition, the Civil Legal Aid Review Group, chaired by former Chief Justice Frank Clark SC, published its report in July 2025. My Department is examining its recommendations alongside Ireland’s first Legal Needs Survey and I will revert to Government with proposals for reform in due course.

question: 1299. Deputy Paul Murphy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if turning off recommender algorithms by default and banning them completely for under-18s was considered by his Department as a tool for countering the emerging threat of nihilistic extremism in the context of the EU Internet Forum attended by the Minister of State with special responsibility for international law, law reform and youth justice; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19108/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I recently attended the Ministerial EU Internet Forum (EUIF) meeting at which countering the emerging threat of nihilistic extremism was one of the agenda items. The Ministerial EUIF brings together relevant EU Ministers, technology companies and experts to discuss and advance responses to terrorism, violent extremism and illegal content online. The Department of Culture, Communications and Sport is the lead Department for online safety and the associated regulation and oversight of online platforms. The Online Safety and Media Regulation (OSMR) Act 2022 established a new online safety and media regulator regulator, Coimisiún na Meán, putting it at the heart of Ireland’s emergency online safety framework, which consists of the Online Safety Code, the EU Digital Services Act (DSA) under which An Coimisiún is Ireland’s Digital Services Coordinator, and the Terrorist Content Online Regulation (TCOR) for which An Coimisiún is a competent authority. Under the framework, online platforms are required to put in place appropriate and proportionate measures to ensure a high level of privacy, safety, and security of minors, on their service. An Coimisiún is independent in the exercise of its functions. Failure to adequately fulfil these obligations can lead to significant financial sanctions and continued non-compliance can lead to criminal sanctions for senior management under the OSMR. The Digital Services Act, which is under the remit of the Department of Enterprise, Tourism & Employment, addresses issues around recommender systems. Article 27 of the EU Digital Services Act requires that platforms explain, in understandable language, the main parameters their systems use to suggest content, as well as providing options for users to change or influence these parameters. Articles 34 and 35 require platforms to assess and mitigate risks that their recommender systems may present, including to the protection of minors. Very Large Online Platforms and Very Large Online Search Engines that use recommender systems must allow users, including minors, the option to use recommender systems that do not rely on profiling. The obligation to focus on protecting minors is set out in the guidance produced by the European Commission, under Article 28 of the EU Digital Services Act (DSA). Progress is being made in addressing the risks of recommender systems. In February, the European Commission, which is the lead regulator for the very large online platforms and search engines under the Digital Services Act, issued preliminary findings in its investigation that TikTok was in breach of the DSA in respect of its recommender systems, amongst other things. TikTok must now address those issues. The European Commission is investigating a number of other platforms in respect of recommender systems as well. Designated video sharing platforms are also subject to the DSA which ensures consistency across the European Union, and which is a maximum harmonising piece of digital services legislation across the European Union.

This letter has outlined the options available to the person cited. As an Oireachtas member, the Deputy can also request the status of individual immigration cases by e-mail, using the Oireachtas Mail facility at: IMoireachtasmail@justice.ie, which has been specifically established for this purpose. question: 1302. Deputy Ivana Bacik asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration his views on plans to pay a researcher €270,000 to write a history of his Department; in particular if the appointed researcher will be given privileged access to an archive that is closed to all other researchers; if he is satisfied that academic independence and ethics can be upheld in such circumstances; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19228/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration My Department has entered into a partnership with Research Ireland to appoint a suitable researcher to write the history of the Department’s first 50 years, 1918-1968. This early period of the Department’s history has not been examined in detail and has the potential to make a unique contribution to our shared understanding of the new State’s early years, the establishment of the justice system in the newly independent Ireland and the functioning of the civil service in the new State. The expenditure over a three-year term to be covered by the proposed contract could amount to up to €270,000. The Department intends to appoint an experienced academic to fully examine the substantial collection of primary source material. The primary cost associated with this proposed contract is the annual salary of the researcher, which will be in line with Research Ireland’s Research Fellow grade. It is considered that a three-year contract is necessary to ensure that a substantial history of this period can be accurately produced with a view to publication in book form. Clear requirements have been outlined in the tender to ensure a quality output which delivers value for money and upholds the academic’s independence. The proposed arrangement mirrors a successful project undertaken by the Department of Finance, which partnered with the Irish Research Council in 2019 and appointed a researcher for a similar three-year term. The successful researcher will be afforded the independence to research and write a rigorous evaluation of the Department’s role in the early years of the new Irish State. Research Ireland will oversee the selection of an experienced researcher, underlying the commitment to academic independence and delivery of a high-quality output. Additionally, an external advisory group will be appointed to oversee the project, ensuring academic rigour is maintained at all stages. In terms of access to archives, a Records Management Unit was created in my Department in 2023, to modernise the management of archives and records of the Department, and to transfer larger volumes of records to the National Archives. Since then, approximately 9,000 records have been catalogued, prepared, and transferred to the National Archives by the Department. A further 13,915 files have been catalogued, prepared and will be transferred to the National Archives this summer when that organisation is in a position to accept further transfers. This work continues to be a priority. My Department is committed to ensuring access to its archives for researchers. To facilitate access to records which have not yet been transferred to the National Archives, the Records Management Unit of my Department regularly accommodates academics and researchers in Department offices to facilitate research projects requiring access to Department records. The same arrangements will apply to the appointed researcher.

question: 1303. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he has been furnished with a copy of the protocol for the taser pilot in an Garda Síochána; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19258/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 1303, 1313 and 1355 together. The Garda Commissioner is responsible for the management and administration of An Garda Síochána under Section 33 of the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024, which includes all operational policing policies and training for Garda personnel. The Commissioner is independent in his functions under Section 34 of the Act. An Garda Síochána's human rights based approach to policing provides guidance to Gardaí on how human rights are to be observed in the course of their work. An Garda Síochána's response to any incident involves a graduated policing response considering relevant legislation and public safety, with enforcement as a last resort. In carrying out their duties Gardaí, as far as practicable, consider non-physical means before resorting to the use of force in the resolution of incidents that they respond to. Conductive Energy Devices (CEDs) are issued to specialist firearms and protection units, and the use of these devices is covered by an existing internal policy document. An Garda Síochána have also commenced a CED pilot on the 18 December 2025 for a limited number of frontline uniform Gardaí in Dublin City and Waterford, where body worn cameras have already been deployed. I am advised that the current CED policy has been updated to allow for the uniformed members involved in the pilot to carry these devices. I am also advised by the Garda authorities that, as of 13 March, there have been no discharges of a CED during the course of this pilot. A CED has been drawn and successfully used as a de-escalation tool on four occasions, in DMR South Central and Waterford during January 2026, and again in DMR South Central and Waterford during February 2026. I am assured by the Garda Commissioner that eligible Gardaí are trained in the lawful use of CEDs, or "tasers" as they are commonly known. Each member in the pilot that is equipped with a CED has undertaken a comprehensive 3-day training course in the use of the CEDs before being authorised to carry these devices on operational duties. They have also completed an additional half day human rights awareness briefing. The 3-day Taser Training Course is grounded in Irish Constitutional and European Convention on Human Rights principles and Garda policy, Garda Decision Making Model, Garda Code of Ethics in addition to practical training and assessments. The fundamental principle underpinning the policy for use of CEDs is that any action taken which requires a member of An Garda Síochána to use a CED must comply with the fundamental principles of legality, necessity, proportionality and accountability. These tactical options are available to Gardaí when faced with violence or the threat of violence when it is reasonable to believe that such violence or threat of violence may result in injury to themselves or others, including self-harm by an individual. In order to ensure appropriate oversight any use of a taser will be referred to Fiosrú, the Office of the Police Ombudsman. The CED pilot will aim to evaluate the operational, ethical, human rights, and community impacts of deploying CEDs as an additional tactical option within a graduated use of force framework, in order to prevent harm to Garda personnel and members of the public. The Deputy may also be interested to note that a new overarching Use of Force Policy is being developed currently and is at an advanced stage. Once complete this will be made available on the Garda website. The sub-Procedure documents relating to this policy will be restricted documents and will only be available internally. These would include guidelines as to the use of tasers. This is in line with internal Garda policy procedures. Information on Garda use of force including the use of CEDs are published on the Garda website and in the Commissioner's monthly report to the Policing and Community Safety Authority. An Garda Síochána's Use of Force statistics can be found at the following link: www.garda.ie/en/information-centre/statistics/ While the Garda Commissioner's monthly reports to the PCSA can be found here: www.garda.ie/en/about-us/publications/general-reports/commissioner-s-monthly-reports-to-policing-and-community-safety-authority/[ ]

question: 1304. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if his attention has been drawn to the way in which the equivalent to the Garda vetting process is carried out in the UK, which includes a single live register, where individuals are continuously monitored and relevant organisations can check status in real time; if a similar system could be implemented in Ireland; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19262/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 1304 and 1328 together. The primary purpose of vetting carried out by the Garda National Vetting Bureau (GNVB) is to ensure the safety of children and vulnerable adults. This requires a robust Garda vetting process that reassures the public, and in particular parents, that appropriate checks are conducted on people taking on positions of trust. However, the Government is aware that concerns have been raised regarding certain aspects of the vetting process and I have listened carefully to the views of the sectors affected. In this regard I'm conscious that aspects of the current vetting system result in a highly-segmented process. Furthermore, I believe that the vetting system should be updated to ensure that the burden of seeking vetting disclosures, particularly on volunteers and organisations working in their communities, is minimised to the greatest extent possible, while maintaining the present high standards. Further to the work carried out by the Garda Vetting Review Group, steps are now being taken to implement a number of key changes to the vetting process that will ensure it remains robust and effective while improving the service to customers. It is my objective to ensure the vetting system is fit for purpose and, to the greatest extent possible, efficient and future-proofed to continue to protect our children. In practice, and subject to a general requirement that vetting be renewed every three years, it is envisaged that this will mean that when a person is vetted for the work they will be or are likely to be involved in as part of their employment or volunteering within identified risk categories, the person would not be required to repeat the process if they were to move to another role within the same risk category. These changes will require amending legislation and updated technical systems to support the revised approach and will make the process more efficient for volunteers and organisations, without compromising the essential safeguards that protect those in our care. The Garda National Vetting Bureau received 633,563 applications for vetting disclosures in 2025. The current processing time for 85% of vetting applications is 8/9 working days.

answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 1308 and 1309 together. This will support recruitment of up to 1,000 Gardai, 200 more Garda staff and additional members of the Garda Reserve. Over 11,000 people applied to join An Garda Síochána in 2025, approximately 6,300 in 2024, over 4,900 in 2023 and just over 11,000 in 2022. The Garda trainee recruitment process encompasses multiple stages across application, selection and appointment. The application and selection stages of the process are undertaken by publicjobs on behalf of the Garda Commissioner, the final element of which is the interview stage. Significant changes have been introduced over the past number of years that have improved the efficiency of these processes which have reduced timelines considerably. In 2024, it took 42 weeks from the closing date of the campaign for all candidates to complete the interview process. For the 2025 competition, this was reduced to 22 weeks for the vast majority of candidates. Candidates then enter the An Garda Síochána recruitment stages which consist of vetting, medical, physical competency test and substance misuse testing, all of which need to be undertaken before a candidate is offered a place to commence training in the Garda College. All candidates deemed successful are offered a contract to commence training at the next available intake. I am advised by the Garda authorities that the number of candidates deemed unsuitable per year were: Year No. of candidates deemed unsuitable 2022 37 2023 30 2024 and 2025 fewer than 5 The Garda Commissioner is responsible for the management and administration of An Garda Síochána under Section 33 of the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024, which includes all operational policing matters such as the recruitment and training of trainee Gardaí. Under Section 34(1) of the Policing Security and Community Safety Act 2024, the Garda Commissioner is independent in the performance of his functions. As Minister, I have no role in these independent functions.

question: 1310. Deputy Eoin Hayes asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the measures his Department is taking to ensure international protection applicants are provided with accommodation so they are not forced to sleep rough, especially if deportation orders have been granted or deportation is pending and appeals are ongoing; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19300/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Ireland is currently accommodating over 33,000 people in approximately 310 International Protection Accommodation Service (IPAS) centres around the country. Extensive challenges have been posed to the State in sourcing international protection accommodation over recent years, particularly during an unprecedented surge in applications from 2022 onward. Many of the impacts of this surge period remain in place at this time, though significant change is underway. From the end of 2023, accommodation shortages meant that not all applicants could be offered an accommodation place. From that period on, IPAS prioritised women, children and those who were most vulnerable for the limited accommodation available. IPAS remains unable to make an offer to all single male applicants for international protection due to accommodation shortages for this applicant group. People who are not offered accommodation are given a weekly allowance of €113.80 per week, an increase of €75 from the standard weekly allowance for asylum-seekers. Certain applicants do make their own accommodation arrangements and therefore are not rough-sleeping. IPAS has arrangements in place with a range of NGO partners to provide drop-in day services so people can access facilities including hot showers, meals and laundry services. IPAS teams do seek to make offers of accommodation to any applicant who is rough-sleeping, identified through outreach that is organised seven days a week. The limited number of available beds for this group are kept available as contingency for those who are most vulnerable on arrival, and for those who cannot source alternative accommodation. This means that since March 2025, IPAS has been able to review the cases of people who are awaiting an offer of accommodation and make offers to those who have been waiting longest, using the information they have provided to the International Protection Office (IPO). Through various actions taken since I have taken office, the number of people unaccommodated has reduced from over 3,500 to 649 currently. IPAS teams continue to work on a daily basis to make best use of the limited accommodation available, conduct reviews and outreach, and arrange offers of accommodation for those who are most vulnerable. Currently, there are approximately 600 people subject to deportation orders residing in IPAS accommodation. This number fluctuates regularly as people leave Ireland under the relevant return pathways, and as new orders are made. Some people subject to deportation orders may have the enforcement of their order suspended due to legal proceedings or due to personal circumstances such as health grounds. Others will be in the process of arranging to leave the State as directed. My Department works closely with the Garda National Immigration Bureau to arrange for the removal of persons subject to deportation orders.

question: 1311. Deputy Eoin Hayes asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of reported car thefts in the Dublin metropolitan region, per district; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19303/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Central Statistics Office (CSO), as the national statistical agency, is responsible for the compilation and publication of all crime statistics. The CSO produces these statistics using data recorded on An Garda Síochána’s PULSE system and makes regular releases in relation to various crime statistics. The requested statistics can be found, by station, at the following link: data.cso.ie/table/CJA07 Alternatively, recorded crime statistics are published by the CSO at Garda Division level (including the DMR) quarterly for the Q1 2003 to Q3 2025 period: data.cso.ie/table/CJQ06 All reported incidents of burglary and vehicle theft are investigated by An Garda Síochána. I am advised that local operations targeting vehicle theft are supported by specialist Garda units, including Roads Policing, Crime Task Forces, and the Garda Stolen Motor Vehicle Investigation Unit, as needed. The Garda Stolen Motor Vehicle Investigation Unit continually monitors offenders for all crime types related to the unauthorised taking of vehicles. This Unit supports local Garda Divisions in the investigation of vehicle crime and identification of stolen vehicles nationally. It should also be noted that, with the completion of the roll-out of the Garda Operating Model, Divisions no longer operate on a District model and are now organised into Functional Areas. Under this model an Garda Síochána do not police on a station basis, but rather on a Divisional basis and see stations as locations within communities for people to attend, and for resources to be accommodated. Policing for an area will be delivered using all resources in a Community Engagement Area and supported by Divisional resources and units.

question: 1312. Deputy Conor D. McGuinness asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the Garda numbers per capita in each county, in tabular form. [19328/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration An Garda Síochána publishes information in relation to the allocation of Gardaí nationally. This includes a breakdown of Gardaí assigned by Garda Stations from 2009 to the end of January 2026, the latest date for which figures are available. This can be found at the following link: www.garda.ie/en/about-us/our-departments/human-resources-and-people-development/garda-hr-directorate/garda-strength-breakdown-2026/garda-strength-breakdown-2026.html The Deputy should select the most recently available date and then select the file titled ‘Garda Members by Division District Station to the most recent date" to access a breakdown of Garda members assigned by Division. The Deputy should note that An Garda Síochána is not structured or aligned operationally to county boundaries and, as a result, figures by county are not available. I am also informed that when allocating Gardaí to and from any Division or station, consideration is given to commitments and undertakings outlined in the Annual Service Plan. The requirements of all Garda Divisions nationwide are also taken into account, which include: • Local and national crime trends and workloads; • Policing arrangements and operational strategies; • Minimum establishment statistics; • Local population and trends, geographical area and size; • Transfer applications, including welfare, personnel issues and concerns. It should also be noted that, with the completion of the roll-out of the Garda Operating Model, Divisions no longer operate on a District model and are now organised into Functional Areas. Under this model, An Garda Síochána do not police on a station basis, but rather on a Divisional basis and see stations as locations within communities for people to attend, and for resources to be accommodated. question: 1313. Deputy Richard Boyd Barrett asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he has been furnished with a copy of the protocol for the taser pilot in an Garda Síochána; if he can confirm that protocol obliges that the pilot will be subject to an independent assessment and evaluate the impact of tasers on public trust, particularly among over-policed communities; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19372/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 1303, 1313 and 1355 together. The Garda Commissioner is responsible for the management and administration of An Garda Síochána under Section 33 of the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024, which includes all operational policing policies and training for Garda personnel. The Commissioner is independent in his functions under Section 34 of the Act. An Garda Síochána's human rights based approach to policing provides guidance to Gardaí on how human rights are to be observed in the course of their work. An Garda Síochána's response to any incident involves a graduated policing response considering relevant legislation and public safety, with enforcement as a last resort. In carrying out their duties Gardaí, as far as practicable, consider non-physical means before resorting to the use of force in the resolution of incidents that they respond to. Conductive Energy Devices (CEDs) are issued to specialist firearms and protection units, and the use of these devices is covered by an existing internal policy document. An Garda Síochána have also commenced a CED pilot on the 18 December 2025 for a limited number of frontline uniform Gardaí in Dublin City and Waterford, where body worn cameras have already been deployed. I am advised that the current CED policy has been updated to allow for the uniformed members involved in the pilot to carry these devices. I am also advised by the Garda authorities that, as of 13 March, there have been no discharges of a CED during the course of this pilot. A CED has been drawn and successfully used as a de-escalation tool on four occasions, in DMR South Central and Waterford during January 2026, and again in DMR South Central and Waterford during February 2026. I am assured by the Garda Commissioner that eligible Gardaí are trained in the lawful use of CEDs, or "tasers" as they are commonly known. Each member in the pilot that is equipped with a CED has undertaken a comprehensive 3-day training course in the use of the CEDs before being authorised to carry these devices on operational duties. They have also completed an additional half day human rights awareness briefing. The 3-day Taser Training Course is grounded in Irish Constitutional and European Convention on Human Rights principles and Garda policy, Garda Decision Making Model, Garda Code of Ethics in addition to practical training and assessments. The fundamental principle underpinning the policy for use of CEDs is that any action taken which requires a member of An Garda Síochána to use a CED must comply with the fundamental principles of legality, necessity, proportionality and accountability. These tactical options are available to Gardaí when faced with violence or the threat of violence when it is reasonable to believe that such violence or threat of violence may result in injury to themselves or others, including self-harm by an individual. In order to ensure appropriate oversight any use of a taser will be referred to Fiosrú, the Office of the Police Ombudsman. The CED pilot will aim to evaluate the operational, ethical, human rights, and community impacts of deploying CEDs as an additional tactical option within a graduated use of force framework, in order to prevent harm to Garda personnel and members of the public. The Deputy may also be interested to note that a new overarching Use of Force Policy is being developed currently and is at an advanced stage. Once complete this will be made available on the Garda website. The sub-Procedure documents relating to this policy will be restricted documents and will only be available internally. These would include guidelines as to the use of tasers. This is in line with internal Garda policy procedures. Information on Garda use of force including the use of CEDs are published on the Garda website and in the Commissioner's monthly report to the Policing and Community Safety Authority. An Garda Síochána's Use of Force statistics can be found at the following link: www.garda.ie/en/information-centre/statistics/ While the Garda Commissioner's monthly reports to the PCSA can be found here: www.garda.ie/en/about-us/publications/general-reports/commissioner-s-monthly-reports-to-policing-and-community-safety-authority/[ ]

question: 1314. Deputy Eoghan Kenny asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to outline the current delays in immigration processing for international students in Ireland, the measures being taken to address the delays; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19409/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I understand the Deputy has clarified that his question relates to both Extension of Student Conditions (ESTC) applicants and students who have applied to renew their immigration permission online. For international students who have submitted an application to renew their immigration permission using my Department’s online platform, and as is the case with all other types of renewals, they are processed in order of date submitted. This is to ensure a fair and equitable service for all applicants. Customers may also submit their renewal applications up to 12 weeks prior to expiry of permission, to allow sufficient time for an application to be reached and processed prior to a current permission expiring. The Registration Office of my Department is currently experiencing an exceptionally high demand for immigration permission renewal applications and provide a live processing date, which is updated every Monday, and is available at the following link: www.irishimmigration.ie/registering-your-immigration-permission/how-to-renew-your-current-permission/renewing-your-registration-permission-if-you-live-in-the-republic-of-ireland/#processing They are currently processing applications submitted from 22 December 2025. If an application is approved, it may take up to a further 15 business days to receive the new Irish Residence Permit (IRP) card by post. I understand that the extended wait times can be frustrating for applicants. I can assure the Deputy that my Department is doing everything possible to facilitate as many customers as possible. Further measures to reduce processing times are currently being implemented with additional staff being assigned to this work. I expect that this will address the delays currently being experienced. The Registration Office has also issued a notice to employers regarding the legality of employing someone awaiting renewal. This notice can be found here: www.irishimmigration.ie/notice-to-employers-regarding-employees-awaiting-renewal-of-their-irp-card/ In relation to ESTC applications, I can inform the Deputy that there has been a significant increase in such applications in recent months. These are being dealt with as expeditiously as possible but it is only in exceptional circumstances that such an application will be considered. To be fair to all applicants, ESTC applications are dealt with in chronological order by date received. My Department endeavours to process applications as quickly as possible. However, processing times may vary due to a number of factors, such as the number of applications on hand, individual circumstances, the complexity of applications, whether further information is required, and the resources available. Applicants can now directly check the status of their immigration application on the Immigration Service’s Customer Service Portal. They can register for, or log in to their existing account, at: portal.irishimmigration.ie/en/

question: 1315. Deputy Martin Daly asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the expected processing time for a family reunification application (details supplied) submitted on 31 March 2025, in circumstances where the sponsor is an Irish citizen; and if, in light of the significant child welfare concerns associated with this case, the Minister will ensure that the application is examined as a matter of urgency. [19426/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I can advise the Deputy that the Join Family visa application referred to was created on 20 March 2025. The application and supporting documentation was received by the Dublin Visa Office on 31 March 2025 where it awaits examination and processing. My Department’s business target for join family visa applications is 12 months. It must be made clear that these are business targets for the immigration service. The business target reflects the detailed and often complex assessment that is required to be carried out in relation to applications for family reunification. While I acknowledge the personal difficulties an applicant might be experiencing; it is not possible to give a definitive date as to when this application will be finalised. All applications are processed in chronological order, based on date order of receipt. While every effort is made to process applications as soon as possible, processing times will vary having regard to the volume and complexity of applications, the possible need for the Immigration Service Delivery function of my Department to investigate, inquire into, or seek further information, and the resources available. The Dublin Visa Office have established a dedicated “South Africa desk” to process applications from residents of South Africa. Target processing times and weekly decision reports, for this desk, are available at the following link: www.irishimmigration.ie/south-africa-visa-desk/ I am acutely aware that join family applications are very important for the people impacted. I understand that people are eager to have their families join them in Ireland, and I am committed to improving the service my Department provides. The person concerned can now directly check the status of their visa application on the Immigration Service’s Customer Service Portal. They can register for, or log in to their existing account, at: [ portal.irishimmigration.ie/en/ ] As an Oireachtas member, you can also request the status of individual immigration cases by e-mail, using the Oireachtas Mail facility at: IMoireachtasmail@justice.ie, which has been specifically established for this purpose. This service enables up to date information on such cases to be obtained without the need to seek information by way of the Parliamentary Question process.

question: 1319. Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to outline the current legal status of so-called “non-crime hate incidents” in Ireland and any recent changes made to policy in this regard; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19584/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Non-crime hate incidents are reports made by members of the public to An Garda Síochána, which do not relate to a specific criminal offence but where there is a hate motive reported. An Garda Síochána defines a non-crime hate incident as "Any Non-Crime Incident which is perceived by any person to, in whole or in part, be motivated by hostility or prejudice, based on actual or perceived age, disability, race, colour, nationality, ethnicity, religion, sexual orientation or gender." An Garda Síochána keeps a record of all non-crime hate incidents reported. As such, this is an operational matter for An Garda Síochána. The Garda Commissioner is responsible for the management and administration of An Garda Síochána under section 33 of the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024. This includes all operational policing. Furthermore, under section 34(1) of the Policing Security and Community Safety Act 2024, the Garda Commissioner is independent in the performance of his functions. As Minister, I have no role in these independent functions

question: 1320. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether his Department has undertaken any review of the adequacy of the current legal and regulatory framework governing the use by private sector organisations of facial biometric processing technologies for identification, verification, authentication, or database matching purposes; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19598/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 1320, 1321, 1322 and 1323 together. The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) governs the processing of personal data including biometric data. Biometric data is categorised as ‘special category’ data under the GDPR and the processing of such data is subject to more stringent conditions given its sensitivity and potential impact on fundamental rights. Processing of special category data is prohibited, unless it comes within scope of one of the ten exemptions set out in GDPR Article 9(2). The GDPR does not distinguish between public bodies or private sector organisations who seek to use biometric data, with all data controllers having to comply with the requirements of the GDPR. Where an organisation seeks to process biometric data it should ensure that there is a clear legal basis for doing so and that one of the specific exemptions for processing such data, as set out in the legislation, are met. The operation of the GDPR is kept under review in accordance with Article 97. The most recent Art 97 review was published in 2024. GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018, which gives further effect to the GDPR, provide for complaints and redress mechanisms. The Data Protection Commission (DPC) is Ireland’s independent supervisory authority under the GDPR. Under the Data Protection Act 2018, the Commission is statutorily independent of the Government in the performance of its responsibilities and functions, as required by the GDPR. Where there is a concern that there has been a breach of the GDPR, the matter should be brought to the attention of the Data Protection Commission.

question: 1324. Deputy Danny Healy-Rae asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the position regarding a stamp 4 visa application for a person; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19628/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The person referred to by the Deputy applied to renew their immigration permission on 03 March 2026 and this application is currently in the queue for consideration. The Registration Office within Immigration Service Delivery of my Department provide a live processing date, which is updated every Monday, and is available at the following link: www.irishimmigration.ie/registering-your-immigration-permission/how-to-renew-your-current-permission/renewing-your-registration-permission-if-you-live-in-the-republic-of-ireland/#processing They are currently processing applications submitted from 22 December 2025. In order to ensure a fair and equitable service, renewals are processed in order of date submitted. If the application is approved, the person concerned can expect to receive their new Irish Residence Permit (IRP) card within the following 10-15 working days. answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Road traffic laws are enforced by Gardaí assigned to Roads Policing and as part of the day-to-day duties of uniformed Gardaí nationwide. question: 1328. Deputy Peter 'Chap' Cleere asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration for an update on the Garda vetting card; the timeframe for this to go live; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19669/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 1304 and 1328 together. The primary purpose of vetting carried out by the Garda National Vetting Bureau (GNVB) is to ensure the safety of children and vulnerable adults. This requires a robust Garda vetting process that reassures the public, and in particular parents, that appropriate checks are conducted on people taking on positions of trust. However, the Government is aware that concerns have been raised regarding certain aspects of the vetting process and I have listened carefully to the views of the sectors affected. In this regard I'm conscious that aspects of the current vetting system result in a highly-segmented process. Furthermore, I believe that the vetting system should be updated to ensure that the burden of seeking vetting disclosures, particularly on volunteers and organisations working in their communities, is minimised to the greatest extent possible, while maintaining the present high standards. Further to the work carried out by the Garda Vetting Review Group, steps are now being taken to implement a number of key changes to the vetting process that will ensure it remains robust and effective while improving the service to customers. It is my objective to ensure the vetting system is fit for purpose and, to the greatest extent possible, efficient and future-proofed to continue to protect our children. In practice, and subject to a general requirement that vetting be renewed every three years, it is envisaged that this will mean that when a person is vetted for the work they will be or are likely to be involved in as part of their employment or volunteering within identified risk categories, the person would not be required to repeat the process if they were to move to another role within the same risk category. These changes will require amending legislation and updated technical systems to support the revised approach and will make the process more efficient for volunteers and organisations, without compromising the essential safeguards that protect those in our care. The Garda National Vetting Bureau received 633,563 applications for vetting disclosures in 2025. The current processing time for 85% of vetting applications is 8/9 working days.

question: 1329. Deputy John Brady asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the current number of Garda reserve applicants who have passed the final interview in a Garda station but are awaiting vetting or drug testing clearance; the average processing time from the final interview to the vetting process being completed; and if he will make a statement on the matter. answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Garda Commissioner is responsible for the management and administration of An Garda Síochána under section 33 of the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024, which includes the recruitment and vetting of Garda personnel, including the Garda Reserve, throughout the State. Following the recruitment campaign in 2024, the first cohort of 19 successful candidates entered Templemore in 2025 and 17 of these attested in November 2025. The Garda (Trainee and Reserve Trainee) Vetting Policy implements a vetting clearance process for all candidates which is consistent, streamlined, holistic, embraces diversity and reflects the ethical standards and behaviours required of new entrants in a modern police service. The vetting clearance process for Garda Reserve Trainees is underpinned by regulation 3(1)(a) of the Garda Síochána (Reserve Members) Regulations (S.I No. 64/2024). I am further advised that all qualified candidates submitted to the Garda National Vetting Bureau are receiving attention, and their respective applications are being processed as expeditiously as possible. As each candidate’s vetting history is personal and reflects their individual circumstances, timelines cannot be provided.
